project.descriptionHtml:
HOW TO FUTURE?

The future remains an exciting mystery. It brings fractures and disruptions to our expectations as everything evolves faster and differently than anticipated. But with each shift, new possibilities emerge—possibilities that challenge business models, redefine habits, and reshape the way we live. Now is the time to be courageous and seize the opportunities to actively shape the future!

We are the creators of our own future. With an entrepreneurial spirit, we shape the world of tomorrow. Instead of passively watching, we ask ourselves: How do we shape the future? We take the initiative and make bold moves. Technologies and innovations are our tools to influence the future purposefully. Together, we can create a world that we dream of.

GUIDANCE INNOVATION MAP

The Innovation Map offers a dynamic, global overview of 105 cutting-edge technologies and innovations — always up to date. As a platform for discovery, orientation, and inspiration, it helps companies strengthen their competitiveness, develop future-proof strategies, and contribute to a resilient Austrian economy. Our five clusters — Data Era, Human Expansion, Generate & Drive, Agritech & Food, and Smart Living — offer insights into technologies that are shaping the future.

COLLABORATIVE PERSPECTIVE TOWARD THE FUTURE

Together with experts, renowned research institutions, and universities worldwide, we have designed the dynamically evolving Innovation Map – the ultimate radar for cutting-edge technologies and trends! It showcases 105 groundbreaking technologies that have the potential to profoundly influence our lives, society, and entrepreneurial actions.

project.clustersintro:
The 105 technologies with the potential to reshape how we live and work are organized into five main clusters. These future fields range from data as a key resource of the 21st century to technologies that blur the boundaries between nature and technology – and tackle fundamental questions like how we will move, live, and eat in the future. This thematic structure offers orientation, reveals interconnections, and helps identify innovation potential where it often emerges – at the intersection of disciplines, industries, and everyday life.

Click on a cluster to explore its technologies and learn more about each future field.
project.sdgintro:
Innovative technologies play a decisive role in achieving the United Nations’ 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). These goals define a global framework for sustainable development related to the environment, the economy, and society. Every technology featured on the Innovation Map is linked to at least one of these SDGs. This mapping not only helps with orientation, it also highlights how closely technological development is tied to social responsibility – and how innovation can be a driver in solving global challenges.

Click on an SDG to see which technologies contribute to achieving it. Learn more at: sdgs.un.org/goals
project.about:
THE AUSTRIAN FEDERAL ECONOMIC CHAMBER: SHAPING THE ECONOMY OF TOMORROW

The Austrian Federal Economic Chambers (WKÖ) represent more than 590,000 member companies. As the voice of Austrian business, we are committed to forward-looking policies which benefit the economy. We boost the economy through our comprehensive services and support Austrian companies with an extensive educational offering.

The Innovation Map is part of the WKÖ’s Innovation & Digitalization Department. Our goal is to offer a global, real-time overview of technologies and innovations — helping businesses boost competitiveness and develop future-ready strategies.

THE INNOVATION MAP AS A KEY ROLE

Together with experts, renowned research institutions, and universities worldwide, we have designed the dynamically evolving Innovation Map – the ultimate radar for cutting-edge technologies and trends! It showcases 105 groundbreaking technologies that have the potential to profoundly influence our lives, society, and entrepreneurial actions. Our constantly moving world bears witness to an endless stream of opportunities and inspiring sources. In sync with this movement, the Innovation Map perpetually develops and expands. Every 24 months, we release a new iteration. Thereby we rely on vibrant participation and continuous advancement through open innovation. Together, we actively shape the future, not only adapting to it but also creating new perspectives.

THE INNOVATION MAP AS A TOOL

The Innovation Map is more than just an overview of new technologies. It is a tool that fosters conversation, provides orientation, and sparks strategic inspiration – making the future tangible and exciting. The content of the Innovation Map is prepared for the Austrian entrepreneurial community in target group-specific formats – enabling knowledge transfer and a true future mindset.

  • Open Innovation
    Ongoing analysis and identification activities to drive a dynamic innovation process.

  • Keynotes & Impulse Talks
    Bringing the future to life and encouraging dialogue between business, research, and society.

  • Discussion Rounds
    Discussion formats that offer insights into current challenges and possible visions for the future.

  • Workshops
    Collaborative workshops designed to actively shape the future.

  • How to Future
    A format for foresight enthusiasts, offering exclusive insights into innovative companies combined with open discussion.

  • Future Journeys
    Connecting companies and promoting cooperation on an international level.

The technologies presented do not constitute a recommendation by the Austrian Federal Economic Chamber for or against their use. Rather, they are intended to highlight both opportunities and risks, and to encourage an informed – including critical – discussion of these technologies.

All images and visualisations featured in the Innovation Map were created using the AI image generation platform Midjourney. They are intended to illustrate possible future technology scenarios and do not depict real objects or people.

collections.name: Smart Living
collections.descriptionHTML:
The City as an Intelligent Ecosystem

By 2045, cities could become not only smarter but more adaptive. Buildings will respond dynamically to their environment. Autonomous systems will manage traffic and energy flows in real time. AI-driven governance will make urban planning more flexible and forward-thinking. Self-driving vehicles will merge with hyper-connected infrastructure, while drones transform urban logistics and security. Smart urban living is more than just technology – it’s a vision of a connected, sustainable, and human-centered cityscape where innovation and efficiency translate into better quality of life.

collections.name: Agritech & Food
collections.descriptionHTML:
Rethinking Food

By 2045, the way we produce, distribute, and consume food could be fundamentally transformed. Agriculture and nutrition will no longer exist in isolation but become part of an intelligent, interconnected ecosystem. Precision farming with autonomous machinery, AI-powered yield forecasting, and sensor-based environmental monitoring will make food production more efficient and resource-conscious. At the same time, groundbreaking nutritional concepts are emerging – from personalized nutrient solutions to alternative protein sources cultivated in cell cultures or vertical bioreactors. This cluster showcases innovations that not only make food systems more sustainable but also reimagine them in alignment with individual needs.

collections.name: Generate & Drive
collections.descriptionHTML:
Technology & Energy Revolution

Emerging technologies are transforming how we generate, store, and consume energy. By 2045, they could unlock not only the full potential of our planet but even space as a future energy source. Breakthroughs in storage and smart grids are paving the way for affordable and sustainable supply. At the same time, these innovations help reduce our ecological footprint and support the regeneration of natural resources. This cluster brings together solutions that turn energy from a limited and limiting factor into a driver of a sustainable and boundless future.

collections.name: Human Expansion
collections.descriptionHTML:
The Future of Life

The line between nature and technology continues to blur. By 2045, breakthroughs in synthetic biology, advanced materials, biotechnology, nanotechnology, and robotics could open entirely new dimensions of human development. From rethinking the ageing process to self-operating smart materials and optimized biological systems, the possibilities are vast. As we decode the mechanisms of life with increasing precision, our understanding of human progress will be fundamentally redefined across many domains.

collections.name: Data Era
collections.descriptionHTML:
Creating New Value from Data

Data is the key resource of the 21st century – and the driving force behind a smarter, more connected world. By 2045, it will unlock new value not only for business and public services, but also for environmental and health solutions. The Data Era signals the rise of a new digital reality where smart technologies, AI-powered insights, and interconnected systems work seamlessly together. Combined with the four other clusters, it forms a dynamic ecosystem that accelerates innovation and pushes the boundaries of what’s possible.

description.shortText: This autonomous, shared electric compact pod is designed to provide an efficient, comfortable, and flexible alternative to traditional public transportation in urban areas. It can be hailed through a mobile app, functioning similarly to ride-hailing services but with a focus on communal mobility.
description.longTextHtml:
Driverless public pods are autonomous, electric-powered vehicles designed for shared use in urban environments. These pods can be hailed via a mobile app, operating similarly to ride-hailing services but without a human driver. Using advanced vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V) and vehicle-to-infrastructure (V2I) communication, along with real-time sensors and image processing, they navigate efficiently through city streets.

Designed for sustainability, these pods run on clean energy, typically using electric or hydrogen-based power sources. Their compact form and 360-degree steering system allow for smooth navigation in congested urban areas and tight parking spaces. Unlike traditional self-driving cars, these pods prioritize communal transport and can be customized for various applications, including ride-sharing, food delivery, and mobile office spaces. Some models are also designed to operate on dedicated networks such as elevated tracks or underground shuttle systems.

Future Perspectives

As urban populations grow, cities must embrace smarter mobility solutions that balance efficiency, accessibility, and sustainability. Driverless public pods have the potential to revolutionize urban transport by reducing congestion, lowering emissions, and offering an adaptable alternative to conventional public transit.

In the coming years, the integration of these pods into urban infrastructure will depend on regulatory frameworks, safety advancements, and the development of supportive ecosystems such as dedicated lanes and smart traffic management. While autonomous technology is expected to reduce accidents caused by human error, public trust and robust cybersecurity measures will be critical to widespread adoption.

Future iterations of driverless public pods could leverage artificial intelligence to optimize routes dynamically based on demand, integrate with smart city networks for seamless multimodal transport, and even incorporate biometric authentication for personalized commuting experiences. If widely adopted, this technology could contribute to a shift from private car ownership to a more efficient, shared mobility model.

description.shortText: By merging sensor data, computer vision, and spatial mapping, spatial computing creates dynamic digital twins of physical spaces that enhance machine perception and mixed-reality experiences.
description.longTextHtml:
Spatial computing is an advanced technology that integrates the digital world with the physical environment, enabling users and robots to interact with digital content in real-world spaces. It forms the foundation for mixed-reality (MR) technologies such as augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR) by combining computer vision, sensor technologies, and spatial mapping techniques to create immersive and interactive experiences.

At its core, spatial computing relies on the ability to perceive and understand the physical world through various sensors—including cameras, 3D cameras, depth sensors, spatial trackers, and GPS—that capture real-time information about the environment, such as a user’s position, movement, and the characteristics of nearby objects and surfaces. The gathered data is processed using advanced computer vision algorithms, machine learning, and edge computing frameworks to generate a dynamic digital twin—often represented as a spatial map or point cloud—that accurately reflects the geometry and layout of the physical space. This digital model allows for the seamless overlay and integration of virtual content into reality via head-mounted displays, smartphones, projection systems, and haptic interfaces.

In addition to revolutionizing entertainment and gaming, spatial computing is transforming diverse fields such as medicine, remote collaboration, digital twin modeling, robotics, logistics, mining, industrial maintenance, architecture, design, and training by enabling more precise, context-aware, and real-time interactions between digital and physical worlds.

Future Perspectives

Spatial computing is the engine behind the increasingly blurred line between digital and physical realities. As sensor precision, miniaturization, and processing power continue to improve, this technology is poised to become ubiquitous across industries. In the near future, spatial computing could enable the creation of digital twins of entire cities, fundamentally transforming traffic management, energy optimization, and public safety.

The convergence of spatial computing with emerging technologies like quantum computing and next-generation wireless networks may allow for ultra-high-resolution, real-time mapping of environments at a planetary scale, revolutionizing disaster response, environmental monitoring, and global logistics. Moreover, as blockchain secures data exchanges and synthetic biology advances human-machine integration, new paradigms of interaction will emerge. AI assistants could evolve into holographic guides or virtual beings that seamlessly navigate both augmented and fully virtual spaces, redefining how we interact with our environment and paving the way for transformative innovations.

Apple’s entrance into the market is a big step for the technology, but the idea has been in development for years. Now, spatial computing is already starting to make an impact, including on communication and co-presence, manufacturing, gaming, human resources, media, sports and entertainment, and data visualization.

attachments.name: A New Definition of Spatial Computer: The Fourth Paradigm
attachments.description: Welcome to the launch of our Spatial Computing Agency, Infinite Retina, which offers consulting services and research, a new video series, a new newsletter, a new podcast series, new industry databases (coming later this year), and a new book, coming in 2020. Along with our consulting services aimed at helping companies and entrepreneurs build new Spatial Computing projects and getting them funded and launched, we are very apt to helping everyone truly understand what the new paradigm of personal computing will be.

attachments.name: Spatial Computing and Social Media in the Context of Disaster Management
attachments.description: The growing trend of using smartphones and other GPS-enabled devices has provided new opportunities for developing spatial computing applications and technologies in unanticipated and unprecedented ways. Some capabilities of today's smartphones highlight the potential of citizen sensors to enable the next generation of geoinformatics. One promising application area for this is social media and its application to disaster management. Dynamic, real-time incident information collected from onsite human responders about the extent of damage, the evolution of the event, the community's needs, and responders' ability to deal with the situation, combined with information from the larger emergency management community, could lead to more accurate and real-time situational awareness. This would enable informed decisions, better resource allocation and thus a better response and outcome to the total crisis. In this context, the US Department of Homeland Security's Science & Technology Directorate (DHS-S&T) has initiated the Social Media Alert and Response to Threats to Citizens" (SMART-C) program, which aims to develop citizen participatory sensing capabilities for decision support throughout the disaster life cycle via a multitude of devices and modalities. Here, the authors provide an overview of the envisioned SMART-C system's capabilities and discuss some of the interesting and unique challenges that arise due to the combination of spatial computing and social media within the context of disaster management.

attachments.name: What is Spatial Computing
attachments.description: Spatial computing broadly characterizes the processes and tools used to capture, process and interact with 3D data. Components of spatial computing can include IoT, digital twins, ambient computing, augmented reality, virtual reality, AI and physical controls.

attachments.name: Spatial Computing 101
attachments.description: TL;DR — Vision Pro gives us the possibility of injecting a middle-layer between ourselves and the always-changing dynamic reality. This can help us understand, interpret and react to the world — but we have yet to define new design patterns for it.

attachments.name: Working memory control dynamics follow principles of spatial computing
attachments.description: Working memory (WM) allows us to remember and selectively control a limited set of items. Neural evidence suggests it is achieved by interactions between bursts of beta and gamma oscillations. However, it is not clear how oscillations, reflecting coherent activity of millions of neurons, can selectively control individual WM items. Here we propose the novel concept of spatial computing where beta and gamma interactions cause item-specific activity to flow spatially across the network during a task. This way, control-related information such as item order is stored in the spatial activity independent of the detailed recurrent connectivity supporting the item-specific activity itself. The spatial flow is in turn reflected in low-dimensional activity shared by many neurons. We verify these predictions by analyzing local field potentials and neuronal spiking. We hypothesize that spatial computing can facilitate generalization and zero-shot learning by utilizing spatial component as an additional information encoding dimension.

description.shortText: A biofabrication technique that uses 3D printing to create tissue-like structures and fully functional artificial organs from living cells and biomaterials. By employing patient-specific cells, this technology enables regenerative treatments and addresses organ donor shortages.
description.longTextHtml:
3D Bioprinting is an advanced bioengineering method that constructs living tissue and artificial organs using layer-by-layer deposition of bio-inks—composed of living cells, biopolymers, and growth-supportive substances. These bio-printed constructs are designed to replicate the form and function of natural biological systems.

The process typically begins with harvesting the patient's own stem cells or differentiated cells, which are expanded in vitro and embedded in a hydrogel matrix. Sophisticated bioprinters then assemble these cells into complex, tissue-like architectures, including vascular channels to ensure viability and integration post-implantation. These structures may be matured in bioreactors and supplemented with growth factors to promote functional development.

This technology bridges the fields of regenerative medicine and organ replacement. Applications range from engineered cartilage, bone, and skin to the development of fully functional organs like kidneys, livers, or lungs. Bioprinted organs can restore essential physiological functions for patients with organ failure and drastically reduce the reliance on human donors.

Additionally, 3D bioprinting supports drug testing, personalized medicine, and the development of organ-on-a-chip systems. Its precision enables the fabrication of life-like anatomical models for surgical training, and even prosthetics such as artificial joints that mimic biological materials.

Future Perspectives

3D Bioprinting could fundamentally change healthcare by enabling on-demand production of organs tailored to each individual. Hospitals of the future might host on-site bioprinters capable of fabricating patient-specific tissue and organs, eliminating transplant waiting lists and reducing surgical complications.

Beyond immediate medical uses, the technology is poised to support education and training with hyper-realistic bio-models, enhance prosthetics with biologically integrated components, and drive innovation in fields like cosmetics and neurotechnology. The creation of neural and sensory tissue may one day restore lost functions or augment human abilities.

On a longer horizon, the integration of genetic engineering and synthetic biology could lead to the design of custom, enhanced human organs and bio-synthetic systems — redefining human enhancement and resilience. In space exploration, bioprinting could offer a sustainable path to healthcare autonomy in extraterrestrial missions, enabling astronauts to generate tissues and organs in microgravity environments.

attachments.name: Recent progress of 3D printed vascularized tissues and organs
attachments.description: • The latest progress of 3D printed vascularized tissues and organs were reviewed. • The 3D printed models included heart, liver, lung, kidney, and penis. • Application status and potential of the 3D printed models were discussed. • Further requirement of 3D printing technology for manufacturing clinically useable vascularized tissues were proposed.

attachments.name: Natural 3D-Printed Bioinks for Skin Regeneration and Wound Healing: A Systematic Review
attachments.description: Three-dimensional bioprinting has rapidly paralleled many biomedical applications and assisted in advancing the printing of complex human organs for a better therapeutic practice. The objective of this systematic review is to highlight evidence from the existing studies and evaluate the effectiveness of using natural-based bioinks in skin regeneration and wound healing. A comprehensive search of all relevant original articles was performed based on prespecified eligibility criteria. The search was carried out using PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, Medline Ovid, and ScienceDirect. Eighteen articles fulfilled the inclusion and exclusion criteria. The animal studies included a total of 151 animals with wound defects. A variety of natural bioinks and skin living cells were implanted in vitro to give insight into the technique through different assessments and findings. Collagen and gelatin hydrogels were most commonly used as bioinks. The follow-up period ranged between one day and six weeks. The majority of animal studies reported that full wound closure was achieved after 2–4 weeks. The results of both in vitro cell culture and in vivo animal studies showed the positive impact of natural bioinks in promoting wound healing. Future research should be focused more on direct the bioprinting of skin wound treatments on animal models to open doors for human clinical trials.

attachments.name: When we’ll be able to 3D-print organs and who will be able to afford them
3D Printed Organs: How, Why & When
attachments.description: When talking about 3D printed organs, it is important to note that we humans are not yet at the stage where we can implant 3D printed hearts into our bodies. In this article, we will dive deeper into the topic and give a good view of what is to come.

attachments.name: Printed human body parts could be available for human transplants within few years
attachments.description: Every year about 120,000 organs, mostly kidneys, are transplanted from one human being to another. Sometimes the donor is a living volunteer. Usually, though, he or she is the victim of an accident, stroke, heart attack or similar sudden event that has terminated the life of an otherwise healthy individual. But a lack of suitable donors, particularly as cars get safer and first-aid becomes more effective, means the supply of such organs is limited. Many people therefore die waiting for a transplant. That has led researchers to study the question of how to build organs from scratch.

attachments.name: Polysaccharide-Based Bioink Formulation for 3D Bioprinting of an In Vitro Model of the Human Dermis
attachments.description: Limitations in wound management have prompted scientists to introduce bioprinting techniques for creating constructs that can address clinical problems. The bioprinting approach is renowned for its ability to spatially control the three-dimensional (3D) placement of cells, molecules, and biomaterials. These features provide new possibilities to enhance homology to native skin and improve functional outcomes. However, for the clinical value, the development of hydrogel bioink with refined printability and bioactive properties is needed. In this study, we combined the outstanding viscoelastic behavior of nanofibrillated cellulose (NFC) with the fast cross-linking ability of alginate (ALG), carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC), and encapsulated human-derived skin fibroblasts (hSF) to create a bioink for the 3D bioprinting of a dermis layer. The shear thinning behavior of hSF-laden bioink enables construction of 3D scaffolds with high cell density and homogeneous cell distribution. The obtained results demonstrated that hSF-laden bioink supports cellular activity of hSF (up to 29 days) while offering proper printability in a biologically relevant 3D environment, making it a promising tool for skin tissue engineering and drug testing applications.

attachments.description: Significant progress has been made over the past 25 years in the development of in vitro-engineered substitutes that mimic human skin, either to be used as grafts for the replacement of lost skin, or for the establishment of in vitro human skin models.

attachments.name: Overview of Current Advances in Extrusion Bioprinting for Skin Applications
attachments.description: Bioprinting technologies, which have the ability to combine various human cell phenotypes, signaling proteins, extracellular matrix components, and other scaffold-like biomaterials, are currently being exploited for the fabrication of human skin in regenerative medicine. We performed a systematic review to appraise the latest advances in 3D bioprinting for skin applications, describing the main cell phenotypes, signaling proteins, and bioinks used in extrusion platforms. To understand the current limitations of this technology for skin bioprinting, we briefly address the relevant aspects of skin biology. This field is in the early stage of development, and reported research on extrusion bioprinting for skin applications has shown moderate progress.

attachments.name: The Future of Artificial Organ Transplants
attachments.description: Given the cost of artificial organ transplants, countries that focus on attracting medical tourists could greatly benefit from the growth of this market.

attachments.name: Artificial organs that look and bleed like the real thing take surgical practice to the next level
attachments.description: To provide surgeons and students with an alternative to a living human being to work on, a pair of physicians at URMC have developed a way to use 3D printing to create artificial organs that look, feel, and even bleed like the real thing.​

attachments.name: 3DBio conducts successful human ear reconstruction with 3D bioprinted AuriNovo implant
attachments.description: Regenerative medicine company 3DBio Therapeutics and the Microtia-Congenital Ear Deformity Institute have successfully completed a human ear reconstruction using the former’s novel 3D printed AuriNovo living tissue implant for the first time.  The first-in-human Phase 1/2a clinical trial evaluated the safety and efficacy of AuriNovo for patients with microtia, a rare congenital deformity where one or both outer ears are absent or underdeveloped. 3DBio’s patient-specific living tissue implant was developed using 3D bioprinting technology to provide a viable treatment alternative to rib cartilage grafts and traditionally-used synthetic materials.

attachments.name: 3D-printed heart tissue, imbued with solar tech, regulates heart rhythm in preclinical study
attachments.description: New research suggests that engineered tissues could one day do some of the work of traditional electrical stimulation devices while offering more customizable and biologically friendly solutions.

attachments.name: Startup Biomotion: 3D bioprinting to create human tissue
attachments.description: Biomotion Technologies is shaping the future of industrial biofabrication with its latest 3D bioprinting system. UAS Technikum Wien welcomes the startup to the Entrepreneurship in Technology program. The new partners will move into premises at Technikum and collaborate on content with the Life Science Engineering faculty.

attachments.name: First Ever Clinical Long-Term Follow-Up Study on 3D-Printed Bioceramic Implants Proves over 92% Total Success Rate with Lithoz LithaBone Material
attachments.description: The clinical paper scientifically proves that 3D-printed beta-TCP patient-specific implants (PSI), made from Lithoz LithaBone material, are ideal as osteoconductive1 and osteoinductive2 personalized bone substitutes

attachments.name: Vienna-based HeartBeat.bio raises €4.5 million to develop 3D human tissue-based drug discovery platform for heart disease
attachments.description: HeartBeat.bio, a biotech company building a highly scalable human organoid and AI-supported drug discovery platform for heart disease, announced the closing of a €4.5 million pre-Series A round co-led by i&i Biotech Fund, Invest AG, aws Gründungsfonds II, and Tensor Ventures.

attachments.name: Cellbricks Reports Preclinical Success with Bioprinted Tissue in Mice
attachments.description: German startup Cellbricks Therapeutics, a spin-off of the Technical University of Berlin, has announced successful preclinical results for its 3D-bioprinted adipose tissue implants. In a study conducted on mice, the company reported full integration of the implants into host tissue after seven weeks, without signs of fibrosis or rejection.

description.shortText: By merging AI techniques and protein design, this technology is set to revolutionize the field of protein engineering. It enables and accelerates the creation of tailored proteins with desired properties, addressing specific challenges in domains such as medicine and agriculture, and opening up new possibilities for drug discovery, materials science, and other fields.
description.longTextHtml:
By combining generative artificial intelligence (AI) and protein design, it is possible to create tailored protein structures and functions for specific individuals or applications. AI-Powered Protein Design brings together the power of machine-learning algorithms and computational modeling to revolutionize protein engineering and optimization.

The technology uses a vast database of protein sequences and structure data to train AI models. These models learn the patterns and relationships between amino acid sequences and protein properties, allowing for the assessment of stability, binding affinity, or enzymatic activity. Once trained, the algorithms can quickly generate new custom protein sequences or optimize existing ones based on desired characteristics, designed to address specific challenges and meet individual needs. After that, the protein can be synthesized in a laboratory and then tested and validated.

In medicine, this technology can create therapeutic proteins with enhanced efficacy and reduced side effects that could be used in vaccines or novel drugs. These proteins can be customized to interact with specific targets in the body, such as disease-causing molecules or receptors, increasing their specificity and effectiveness. In agriculture, AI-Powered Protein Design can be employed to improve crop yield or resistance to diseases and environmental stress. In industrial applications, personalized proteins can be designed for enhanced enzyme activity, allowing for more efficient biofuel production or waste degradation, for instance.

This technology accelerates the protein design process by reducing the reliance on time-consuming and costly experimental methods. AI-Powered Protein Design enables researchers to explore and identify optimal protein variants with desired properties more efficiently. Additionally, this technology expands the boundaries of protein design by allowing the creation of proteins that may not exist naturally. By leveraging AI models, scientists can explore protein structures and functions beyond what has been observed in nature, opening up new possibilities for drug discovery, materials science, and other fields.

Future Perspectives

AI-Powered Protein Design holds significant potential for various applications and fields. It can drive the personalized medicine movement, since designing custom protein therapies could be tailored to an individual's genetic makeup, disease characteristics, and response patterns. It can also be key in the advancement of synthetic biology, allowing for the design of novel proteins with non-natural functions and properties. These proteins can be engineered to perform specific tasks, such as biosensing, biocatalysis, or even the creation of entirely new metabolic pathways. Also, this technology can assist in designing proteins for the development of sustainable materials, such as biodegradable plastics or renewable-energy devices. Customized proteins can exhibit desired properties like high strength, flexibility, or environmental compatibility.

attachments.name: This AI Can Design Complex Proteins Perfectly Tailored to Our Needs
attachments.description: Building proteins with AI is like furnishing a house.  There are two main strategies. One is the IKEA approach: you buy pre-made pieces that easily snap together, but can only hope the furniture somewhat fits your space. While relatively simple, you have no control over the dimensions or functions of the final product.

attachments.name: AI tools are designing entirely new proteins that could transform medicine
attachments.description: Digital art techniques can now devise custom, working biomolecules on demand.

attachments.name: Revolutionary Breakthrough: AI-Driven Systems Create Custom Proteins with Precision
attachments.description: Proteins, those intriguing fundamental building blocks of life, are involved in vital roles across various biological processes, such as digestion and immune response. The captivating idea of creating new proteins has long fascinated researchers, as it holds the potential to revolutionize drug discovery and other applications. However, crafting proteins from scratch has proven to be an immense challenge, requiring a deep understanding of protein structure and function. Thankfully, the benevolent intervention of artificial intelligence (AI) has come to the rescue, empowering scientists with the development of AI systems capable of generating bewilderingly novel proteins that perfectly fulfill intricate structural design targets.

attachments.name: An AI that can design new proteins could help unlock new cures and materials
attachments.description: The machine-learning tool could help researchers discover entirely new proteins not yet known to science.

attachments.name: AI Proteins
attachments.description: Harnessing the power of synthetically designed proteins to cure diseases

attachments.name: Now AI Can Be Used to Design New Proteins
attachments.description: Machine learning can be harnessed to synthesize artificial light-bearing enzymes that actually work in cells.

attachments.name: A.I. Turns Its Artistry to Creating New Human Proteins
attachments.description: Inspired by digital art generators like DALL-E, biologists are building artificial intelligences that can fight cancer, flu and Covid.

attachments.name: AI-powered start-up puts protein discovery on the fast track
attachments.description: Technology that combines directed evolution with machine learning holds promise for optimizing potential drugs.

attachments.name: PROTEIN_GENERATOR: Unleashing AI for Protein Design
attachments.description: Have you ever wanted to design your own protein but didn't know where to start? We’ve launched a new platform that puts powerful machine learning tools behind a user-friendly web interface, making protein design accessible to anyone.

attachments.name: Generative design of de novo proteins based on secondary-structure constraints using an attention-based diffusion model
attachments.description: The design of de novo protein sequences has great potential in achieving superior combinations of novel functions and mechanical properties beyond known, natural proteins. However, the tremendous number of possible sequences and the cost of experimental testing make the effective search and validation of superior de novo protein candidates extremely challenging. Here, we leverage a diffusion-model-based deep-learning framework to efficiently generate novel protein sequences that meet a desired overall secondary-structure fractional content or per-residue type of secondary structure. The generated sequences show novelty beyond existing, natural ones. By robustly generating various novel sequences with the desired structural features, our model provides rapid strategies for a target-guided de novo protein design that leads to novel discoveries of superior protein materials for various biological and engineering applications and can be extended for other design objectives in future work.

attachments.name: AI-enhanced protein design makes proteins that have never existed
attachments.description: Protein engineers are drawing on rapidly evolving machine learning tools, deep reservoirs of data, and the structure-predicting firepower of AlphaFold2 to pursue more sophisticated de novo protein designs.

attachments.name: AlphaProteo generates novel proteins for biology and health research
attachments.description: New AI system designs proteins that successfully bind to target molecules, with potential for advancing drug design, disease understanding and more.

attachments.name: Five protein-design questions that still challenge AI
attachments.description: Tools such as Rosetta and AlphaFold have redefined the protein-engineering landscape. But some problems remain out of reach — for now.

attachments.name: Generative artificial intelligence for de novo protein design
attachments.description: Engineering new molecules with desirable functions and properties has the potential to extend our ability to engineer proteins beyond what nature has so far evolved. Advances in the so-called ‘de novo’ design problem have recently been brought forward by developments in artificial intelligence. Generative architectures, such as language models and diffusion processes, seem adept at generating novel, yet realistic proteins that display desirable properties and perform specified functions. State-of-the-art design protocols now achieve experimental success rates nearing 20%, thus widening the access to de novo designed proteins. Despite extensive progress, there are clear field-wide challenges, for example, in determining the best in silico metrics to prioritise designs for experimental testing, and in designing proteins that can undergo large conformational changes or be regulated by post-translational modifications. With an increase in the number of models being developed, this review provides a framework to understand how these tools fit into the overall process of de novo protein design. Throughout, we highlight the power of incorporating biochemical knowledge to improve performance and interpretability.

description.shortText: Microscopic grooves inspired by shark skin that reduce friction in air and water, improving energy efficiency across transportation and fluid dynamics systems.
description.longTextHtml:
Riblet technology mimics the dermal microstructures of shark skin by applying tiny, aligned grooves — called riblets — to surfaces exposed to fluid flows. These structures disrupt the turbulent vortices that form as air or water moves across a surface, significantly reducing drag without requiring active energy input. Riblets function as a passive solution to aerodynamic and hydrodynamic resistance, making them particularly suitable for industries where drag reduction translates into meaningful energy or fuel savings.

The most notable applications of riblet films or coatings are in aviation (aircraft fuselages and wings), maritime transport (hulls of ships), and wind energy (turbine blades). Riblet coatings tests on commercial aircraft have shown fuel savings of up to 1%, which represents substantial economic and environmental benefits. Similarly, shipping companies and turbine manufacturers are exploring riblet applications to optimize performance and reduce emissions.

Future Perspectives

In the long-term future, riblet technology may evolve beyond industrial coatings into adaptive smart materials capable of dynamically altering their surface texture in response to flow conditions. This could lead to next-generation aircraft and ships with programmable exteriors, enhancing fuel efficiency even further in real-time.

Combined with AI and sensor integration, riblet surfaces could become self-healing and responsive, adapting to wear or environmental factors to maintain optimal drag reduction throughout their lifespan. In aerospace, the future might see space shuttles or planetary rovers using riblet-enhanced surfaces to navigate atmospheric entry or fluidic resistance in other planetary environments. The concept may also find novel biomedical uses, such as reducing resistance in catheters or bloodstream navigation devices.

attachments.name: Aeroshark
attachments.description: Just by using the sharkskin technology, the global fleet of long-haul aircraft could save close to five million tons of kerosene per year. AeroSHARK is a durable bionic film that successfully mimics the skin of sharks and optimizes the airflow thus enabling significant fuel savings.   Together with the leading global chemicals and coatings manufacturer BASF, we developed a functional biomimetic technology: a film with a barely perceptible ribbed texture of small protrusions – riblets. Sized in patches for easy and targeted application, the film has millions of these prism-shaped riblets, each one 50 micrometers high.  Applied to the aircraft in a specific manner and aligned with the airflow, the riblets achieve efficiency gains, by reduced friction, similar to those of their counterparts in nature, and can also improve lift if attached on wings.  The riblet film is easy to apply, even on large commercial aircraft - approximately 800 square meters of AeroSHARK riblet film are for example applied to the Boeing 777F cargo aircraft on fuselage and nacelles by hand. Once applied, there are no special requirements for cleaning. The riblet film is extremely resilient, withstands large temperature shifts, pressure differentials and the ultra violet radiation on high flight levels.

attachments.name: AeroSHARK - Innovation inspired by nature
attachments.description: The innovative surface film lowers fuel consumption and reduces CO2 emissions

attachments.name: Shark-style skins are cutting aircraft fuel use – and could have other benefits
attachments.description: With rows of razor-sharp teeth and nostrils capable of smelling blood from hundreds of metres, sharks are some of the ocean’s most accomplished hunters. But they also have another weapon in their arsenal – their skin.

attachments.name: AeroSHARK from Lufthansa Technik and BASF now certified for Boeing 777
attachments.description: Drag-reducing riblet film helps airlines to save fuel and reduce emissions Supplemental Type Certificate (STC) paves the way for series modification of 777-300ER and 777F Next modification layovers at SWISS and Lufthansa Cargo to commence already in January

attachments.name: Marine drag reduction of shark skin inspired riblet surfaces
attachments.description: Shark skin inspired riblet surfaces have been known to have drag reduction effect for the over past 40 years. It first drew the attention from the aircraft industry. With the property of low drag and self-cleaning (antifouling), shark skin inspired riblet surfaces can also be used on navigation objects. In this paper, different marine drag reduction technologies are discussed, and a review of riblet performance studies is also given. Experimental parameters include riblet geometry, continuous and segmented configurations, fluid velocity (laminar and turbulent flow), fluid viscosity (water, oil and gas), and wettability are analyzed. However, force is obtained by area-weighted integral of shear stress distributions. So area of riblet surfaces is a crucial factor which has not been considered in many previous studies. An experiment is given to discuss the impact of area. This paper aims not only to contribute to a better understanding of marine drag reduction, but also to offer new perspectives to improve the current evaluation criteria of riblet drag reduction.

attachments.name: Drag Reduction Using Riblet Film Applied to Airfoils for Wind Turbines
attachments.description: This paper presents results of a study that was commissioned by the 3M Renewable Energy Division to measure the drag reduction by using riblet film on airfoils specifically designed for wind turbine applications. The DU 96-W-180 airfoil was tested with four different symmetrical V-shaped riblet sizes (44, 62, 100 and 150-µm) at three Reynolds numbers (1, 1.5 and 1.85 million) and at angles of attack spanning the low drag range of the airfoil. Tests were run with riblet film covering different sections of the airfoil in order to determine the optimal riblet location in terms of drag reduction. Results showed that the magnitude of drag reduction depended on the angle of attack, Reynolds number, riblet size, and riblet location. For some configurations, riblets produced significant drag reduction of up to 5%, while for others riblets were detrimental. Trends in the results indicated an optimum riblet size of 62-µm for the range of Reynolds numbers at which tests were conducted. The airfoil chord was 18 in (0.457 m). Results also showed that each riblet size performed best at a given Reynolds number with the optimal Reynolds number decreasing with an increase in riblet size.

attachments.name: Drag reduction of large wind turbine blades through riblets: Evaluation of riblet geometry and application strategies
attachments.description: Wind tunnel experiments were performed to quantify the drag reduction on a wind turbine airfoil partially or fully covered with riblets. A full-scale 2.5 MW wind turbine airfoil section, typical for the near tip, was placed in the free stream flow of the wind tunnel at the Saint Anthony Falls Laboratory, University of Minnesota. Various sizes and geometries of experimental riblets were provided by 3M Company and tested at angles of attack ranging from 0° ≤ α ≤ 10° (0.25 ≤ CL ≤ 1.14) and at a Reynolds number of Re = 2.2 × 106. Mean drag was measured via wake survey (momentum deficit) and with a sensitive force balance. Lift was measured directly from the force balance. Tests included the cases of complete and partial riblet coverage on the wing. Results indicated that riblets could provide an overall reduction of skin friction drag, and that the amount of the decrease varied with riblet height and geometry. Partial riblet coverage appears in some cases more efficient than its complete coverage counterpart. The percentage of drag the riblets reduced varied greatly and in some cases the riblets were even detrimental to the airfoil. The most efficient riblet for a completely covered airfoil was found to be the V-groove shape of 100 μm height. It produced a reduction of roughly 6% in the operational range expected in a turbine airfoil. On the other hand, the most efficient riblet size for partial coverage was also a V-groove shape and seemed to shift slightly to a smaller peak height of 80 μm. This configuration produced a reduction of roughly 4% in the range of angle of attack that is typical for operation in the field. The average non-dimensional square root of the groove cross-section, l+, defined in terms of the drag coefficient at design angle of attack for the optimum riblet configuration in the fully coverage case was found to be  , which is very close to the optimum value found for planar surfaces. Based on our results we propose a formulation for the optimum riblet size in airfoil considering the mean drag coefficient and chord length Reynolds number. Even though the optimum full coverage case showed better performance that the partial case, the additional drag reduction benefit may be offset by the additional application cost.

attachments.name: Biomimicry: engineering in nature’s style
attachments.description: Airbus engineers study the natural world for modern aircraft design solutions  The growing science of biomimicry focuses on what humanity can learn from the world, and Airbus engineers are learning quite a lot about efficient solutions for aircraft design that nature has spent millions of years refining.

attachments.name: Sharks in the Sky: Lufthansa Technik’s AeroSHARK Coating Reduces CO2 Emissions
attachments.description: Biomimetics is the science (or art) of engineering natural phenomena. Sharks are known to be extremely efficient swimmers and this is helped, in part, by their skin, which is covered in denticles, or small riblets. These smooth the flow of water and reduce drag. As the science of hydrodynamics and that of aerodynamics are similar, this has been of interest to aviation for some time but has taken on a new lease of life with the increased push towards the reduction of CO2 emissions.

attachments.name: Shrinking the carbon footprint and improving the bottom line
attachments.description: Close to 5 million tons of kerosene per year. That’s the fuel savings the global fleet of aircraft could achieve with AeroSHARK coating technology. And we’re well past proof of concept.

attachments.name: Hulls that glide through the water like sharks – and stay smooth
attachments.description: The potential of drag reduction through a textured surface is widely known. In real world scenarios, however, the advantages are quickly negated if fouling control properties are not integrated. A new project developed a biocide-free solution to this problem.

attachments.name: The evolution of Riblet technology
attachments.description: As a biomimetic technology, Riblet surfaces have their origins in nature and are directly inspired by the structure of sharkskin. While the physical mechanism in this sense is millions of years old, the scientific field of Riblets is rather young. Their discovery took place in the 1960s and intense research in this subject started in the late 1970s and 1980s. Considering the technology’s status quo in respect of its young age, the speed and advancement of its evolution is remarkable. Especially the development of high-performance computing tools plays a major role for the progress of Riblet research and its industrial exploitation.

attachments.name: Riblet processing
attachments.description: Riblets form a fine artificial structure with a shark-skin-like pattern. It is widely understood that frictional resistance is reduced by using a fine triangular convex structure on a surface that is in contact with air or water. Nikon adds a fine structure called a riblet structure to various products utilizing our proprietary laser processing technology to reduce equipment energy losses and contribute to improving fuel consumption and reducing CO2 emissions.

attachments.name: Experiments on drag-reducing surfaces and their optimization with an adjustable geometry
attachments.description: Previous research has established that surfaces with tiny ribs (riblets) aligned in the streamwise direction can reduce the turbulent wall-shear stress below that of a smooth surface. Typical skin-friction reductions have been found to be about 5%. The results of the present investigation, however, demonstrate a considerable improvement over this value. This improvement is achieved by a systematic experimental optimization which has been guided by theoretical concepts.

attachments.name: 30 Jahre Riblet-Forschung am Berliner Ölkanal des DLR
attachments.description: Die Forschung an widerstandsvermindernden Riblet-Strukturen hat eine über 40jährige Geschichte in Deutschland, erst in Göttingen und später in Berlin wurde an diesen Mikrorillen (Riblets) geforscht. Die Riblets reduzieren den turbulenten Reibungswiderstand um bis zu 10% gegenüber glatten Flächen. Erste Experimente fanden in Windkanälen statt, wegen der Kleinheit der Strukturen wurde ein mit Öl befüllter Kanal gebaut. Dieser Kanal ermöglicht mit einer differentiell messenden Waage hochgenaue Widerstandsmessungen an stark vergrößerten Modellen. Mit einem theoretischen Ansatz und Parameterstudien wurden die Rillenstrukturen optimiert und eine anwendungstaugliche Geometrie für den Flugbetrieb entwickelt. Die Riblets kamen 2021 in den kommerziellen Betrieb für Verkehrsflugzeuge.

description.shortText: AI-powered robots designed to assist the elderly and individuals with disabilities in daily activities, offering personalized support and companionship.
description.longTextHtml:
Robot caregivers are AI-driven machines designed to monitor and assist the elderly and people with disabilities in performing routine tasks. These robots integrate machine learning, computer vision, and natural language processing to adapt their actions to each individual's specific needs. By analyzing gestures, verbal commands, and non-verbal cues, they provide personalized care.

These robots can assist with mobility, transferring patients from bed to wheelchair, aiding in bathroom use, preparing meals, and administering medication. Advanced models incorporate emotional recognition to offer companionship and mitigate loneliness. Some also support therapists in treating depression, anxiety, and PTSD by facilitating interactive engagement and monitoring mental well-being.

Japan, South Korea, and parts of Europe have pioneered the integration of robotic caregivers in eldercare facilities, yet widespread adoption remains limited by ethical concerns, regulatory barriers, and technological constraints. Current systems still require human oversight, particularly in high-risk scenarios such as emergency medical interventions or handling fragile patients.

Future Perspectives

As AI continues to evolve, robot caregivers are expected to become more autonomous and emotionally intelligent. Future iterations may integrate sophisticated biometric monitoring, allowing real-time health assessments and predictive diagnostics, reducing the need for constant human supervision. AI could also enhance their capacity to respond empathetically, simulating human-like interactions to better support emotional and mental well-being.

The increasing reliance on robotic caregivers could alleviate workforce shortages in healthcare and eldercare, but it also raises concerns about job displacement and the erosion of human-to-human care. Ethical debates will intensify over issues such as privacy, consent, and the emotional limitations of AI-driven companionship. To ensure a balanced transition, policymakers and healthcare institutions must proactively implement training programs, regulations, and hybrid care models that integrate both human and robotic assistance.

A fully autonomous, highly capable robot caregiver is still years away, but with the rapid advancement of AI, robotics, and sensor technologies, we may witness significant progress within the next decade.

attachments.name: Would You Let a Robot Take Care of Your Mother?
attachments.description: Robotic companions are being promoted as an antidote to the burden of longer, lonelier human lives. At stake is the future of what it means to be human.

attachments.name: How Robot Caregivers Will Help an Aging U.S. Population
attachments.description: Robots are being used to keep age 65-plus people healthy and alert. Learn more on how robot caregivers will help fill the upcoming caregiving void in the U.S.

attachments.name: ‘Care bots’: a dream for carers or a dangerous fantasy?
attachments.description: Robots that can assist caregivers have been talked up as being transformative. But some researchers fear such technology could take more than it gives

attachments.name: Care of the future: Can robots care for the elderly or the sick?
attachments.description: Experts agree on the potential of machines to take on specific tasks, such as reminding someone to take medication, or tracking a patient’s moods. However, they warn that robotics alone isn’t enough

attachments.name: Whatever Happened to All Those Care Robots?
attachments.description: So far, companion robots haven’t lived up to the hype—and might even exacerbate the problems they’re meant to solve.

attachments.name: Taking Care With Caregiving Robots
attachments.description: If caregiving is the very essence of being human, why would we consider turning it over to robots? Technology—and artificial intelligence (AI, in particular—have created a world in which automation is prioritized and digital is seen as an improvement on analog—more accurate, more portable, and more controllable. Caregiving is as analog as it gets and it is a field with a serious labor shortage. That makes it ripe for automation—and in fact, the robot caregivers are already here.

attachments.name: Emotional and 'culturally aware' robots could soon be looking after the elderly
attachments.description: The three-year project to create a 'culturally-aware' robot will be led by teams from Middlesex University and the University of Bedfordshire.

attachments.name: Applications of Artificial Intelligence in Elderly Care Robotics
attachments.description: In this article, we look at prevalence of artificial intelligence being deployed in elder care robots currently and what is in store for the the future

attachments.name: Could a robot care for grandma?
attachments.description: In the future, machines could be programmed to assist and comfort the elderly—and help meet the escalating demand for caregivers.

attachments.name: Can Robots Ease the Caregiver Burden?
attachments.description: A small robot army is being test-driven in long-term care facilities throughout Toronto to fill an urgent need—to look after our elderly. But what is lost when we outsource caregiving to machines?

attachments.name: Pepper Robots for Enhanced Elderly Health
attachments.description: The rise in the elderly population these decades has paved the way for innovations catering to elderly health care. One of them, Pepper Robots, is on point.

attachments.name: AI Could Provide Moment-by-Moment Nursing for a Hospital’s Sickest Patients.
attachments.description: In the intensive care unit, artificial intelligence can keep watch at a patient’s bedside

attachments.name: Meet Zora, the Robot Caregiver
attachments.description: This robot is at the center of an experiment in France to change care for elderly patients.

attachments.name: Elderly care? Bring in the robots!
attachments.description: Robots have come a long way. For years they have been supporting human activity – enabling exploration in dangerous and unreachable environments like out in space and deep in the oceans. A new generation of robots are being designed to stay closer to home – caring for ageing adults and young children.

attachments.name: The Future of Robot Caregivers.
attachments.description: Elderly people need everyday help, and there aren’t enough humans to provide it.

attachments.name: Inside Japan’s long experiment in automating elder care
attachments.description: The country wanted robots to help care for the elderly. What happened?

attachments.name: The Application Potential of the Humanoid Socially Assistive Robot AMIGO for Motivation and Assessment in Dementia Care
attachments.description: Background: The increase in dementia causes an increase of the use of health care resources. At the same time there is a decreasing number of available caregivers. Consequently, technologies, like socially assistive robots, have been developed to assist caregivers and persons with dementia (PWD) in promoting independence. Most robots were tested in laboratory settings with mainly elderly people without dementia. Therefore, there is a lack of knowledge about their use in real care situations of persons with dementia, such as, the potential for motivating PWD to perform meaningful activities and furthermore to analyse the PWD’s mental state. Methodology: The project AMIGO explores the experience of PWD, relatives, caregivers and dementia trainers in applying the humanoid socially assistive robot Pepper in private households. In Companion mode Pepper provides entertainment, reminders and tailored dialogues. In Coach mode it specifically motivates to use a tablet computer based, playful multimodal stimulation for intervention, by commenting, applauding and comforting during gameplay. In a first stage pilot study about the usability of the application, Pepper spent 1 week in each of 3 Austrian households. In total 12 participants (3 of each target group) were included to collect questionnaire and interview data.

attachments.name: Care-O-bot 4
attachments.description: Care-O-bot® is the product vision of a mobile robot assistant to actively support humans in domestic environments. The meanwhile fourth generation of this successful development series is more agile and modular than its predecessors and offers various ways of interaction. It also stands out through the use of cost-reducing construction principles. In this way, large parts of its internal construction feature folding sheet metal, which is economical to produce in small quantities. The enhanced agility of Care-O-bot 4 is owed to the patented spherical joints around discreet pivot points on its neck and hips. They extend the robot’s working space and allow 360 degree rotations of head and torso.

description.shortText: Drones and autonomous aerial platforms equipped with wireless technologies can expand internet access to remote areas and provide emergency connectivity in disaster-stricken zones.
description.longTextHtml:
Aerial Wireless Networks use drones and high-altitude platforms to deliver internet access where traditional infrastructure is unavailable or unreliable. These autonomous aircraft act as floating cell towers, relaying data signals between users on the ground and existing communication networks, such as satellites or fiber-optic hubs. By hovering over remote regions or disaster-stricken areas, they provide temporary or supplementary coverage, ensuring continuous connectivity.

Most current systems rely on pre-programmed flight paths, maintaining a steady altitude while distributing signals. Advanced models are being developed with AI-driven navigation, allowing them to adapt to real-time demand and environmental conditions. Despite their potential, these networks face challenges such as limited battery life, regulatory hurdles, and vulnerability to extreme weather. As technology advances, improvements in energy efficiency and predictive analytics could make them a more viable long-term solution.

Future Perspectives

As aerial networks evolve, they could become integral components of smart cities and global connectivity initiatives. Future developments may integrate AI-powered adaptive routing to optimize coverage dynamically and edge computing capabilities to reduce latency for time-sensitive applications. These platforms could also support fog computing, enabling UAVs to perform local data processing and offload tasks from user devices.

Despite their potential, current solutions are vulnerable to adverse weather conditions, power limitations, and high operational costs. Advancements in energy storage, such as solar-powered high-altitude platforms and fuel-efficient UAVs, may improve the feasibility of long-term aerial networks. Additionally, predictive analytics could enhance operational efficiency by anticipating weather disruptions and adjusting UAV deployment accordingly.

attachments.name: Connecting Internet of Drones and Urban Computing: Methods, protocols and applications
attachments.description: This comprehensive survey explores the connection between the Internet of Drones (IoD) and Urban Computing (UC). Drones offer substantial benefits across diverse urban applications encompassing public safety, transportation management, delivery services, and emergency response, among others. To ensure the seamless operation of these applications, efficient airspace management is imperative. Consequently, an essential foundation is to establish a communication infrastructure coupled with an accompanying supportive system that caters to drones, control bases, service providers, and the Internet. Termed the IoD, this framework facilitates drones’ control management, synchronization, coordination and monitoring of drones to attain their objectives effectively. Moreover, IoD applications are poised to propel societal advancement by aligning with the goals of UC. UC is an interdisciplinary domain to enhances human well-being by harnessing data from various sources, including the Global Positioning System (GPS), cameras, proximity sensors, and social networks. This survey thoroughly examines and analyzes multifaceted aspects underpinning how the IoD can significantly benefit UC. It encompasses applications, their requisites, design protocols specific to IoD, and the challenges inherent within this evolving realm. To the best of our knowledge, our work is one of the first studies to directly relate and show how the IoD can contribute to all UC-applications categories.

attachments.name: An NFV-Based Energy Scheduling Algorithm for a 5G Enabled Fleet of Programmable Unmanned Aerial Vehicles
attachments.description: The fifth generation of mobile networks (5G) is expected to provide diverse and stringent improvements such as greater connectivity, bandwidth, throughput, availability, improved coverage, and lower latency. Considering this, drones or Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) and Internet of Things (IoT) devices are perfect examples of existing technology that can take advantage of the capabilities provided by 5G technology. In particular, UAVs are expected to be an important component of 5G networks implementations and support different communication requirements and applications. UAVs working together with 5G can potentially facilitate the deployment of standalone or complementary communications infrastructures, and, due to its rapid deployment, these solutions are suitable candidates to provide network services in emergency scenarios, natural disasters, and search and rescue missions. An important consideration in the deployment of a programmable drone fleet is to guarantee the reliability and performance of the services through consistent monitoring, control, and management scheme. In this regard, the Network Functions Virtualization (NFV) paradigm, a key technology within the 5G ecosystem, can be used to perform automation, management, and orchestration tasks. In addition, to ensure the coordination and reliability in the communications systems, considering that the UAVs have a finite lifetime and that eventually they must be replaced, a scheduling scheme is needed to guarantee the availability of services and efficient resource utilization. To this end, in this paper is presented an UAV scheduling scheme which leverages the potential offered by NFV. The proposed strategy, based on a brute-force search combinatorial algorithm, allows obtaining the optimal scheduling of UAVs in time, in order to efficiently deploy network services. Simulation results validate the performance of the proposed strategy, by providing the number of drones needed to meet certain levels of service availability. Furthermore, the strategy allows knowing the sequence of replacement of UAVs to ensure the optimal resource utilization.

attachments.name: A Tutorial on UAVs for Wireless Networks: Applications, Challenges, and Open Problems
attachments.description: The use of flying platforms such as unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), popularly known as drones, is rapidly growing. In particular, with their inherent attributes such as mobility, flexibility, and adaptive altitude, UAVs admit several key potential applications in wireless systems. On the one hand, UAVs can be used as aerial base stations to enhance coverage, capacity, reliability, and energy efficiency of wireless networks. On the other hand, UAVs can operate as flying mobile terminals within a cellular network. Such cellular-connected UAVs can enable several applications ranging from real-time video streaming to item delivery. In this paper, a comprehensive tutorial on the potential benefits and applications of UAVs in wireless communications is presented. Moreover, the important challenges and the fundamental tradeoffs in UAV-enabled wireless networks are thoroughly investigated. In particular, the key UAV challenges such as 3D deployment, performance analysis, channel modeling, and energy efficiency are explored along with representative results. Then, open problems and potential research directions pertaining to UAV communications are introduced. Finally, various analytical frameworks and mathematical tools, such as optimization theory, machine learning, stochastic geometry, transport theory, and game theory are described. The use of such tools for addressing unique UAV problems is also presented. In a nutshell, this tutorial provides key guidelines on how to analyze, optimize, and design UAV-based wireless communication systems.

attachments.name: Self-Energized UAV-Assisted Scheme for Cooperative Wireless Relay Networks
attachments.description: Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) have recently been envisaged as an enabling technology of 5G. UAVs act as an intermediate relay node to facilitate uninterrupted, high quality communication between information sources and their destination. However, UAV energy management has been a major issue of consideration due to limited power supply, affecting flight duration. Thus, we introduce in this paper a unified energy management framework by resorting to wireless power transfer (WPT), simultaneous wireless information and power transfer (SWIPT) and self-interference (SI) energy harvesting (EH) schemes, in cooperative relay communications. In our new technique, UAVs are deployed as relays equipped with a decode and forward protocol and EH capability operating in a full-duplex (FD) mode. The UAV assists information transmission between a terrestrial base station and a user. The UAV's transmission capability is powered exclusively by the energy harvested from WPT, radio frequency signal transmitted from the source via time-switching SWIPT protocol and SI exploitation. We improve the overall system throughput by the use of FD based UAV-assisted cooperative system. In this proposed system, we formulate two optimization problems to minimize end-to-end outage probability, subject to UAV's power profile and trajectory for a DF relay scheme, respectively. The KKT conditions have been used to obtain closed-form solutions for the two formulated problems. Numerical simulation results validate all the theoretical results. We demonstrate that the performance of our proposed unified EH scheme outperforms that of existing techniques in the literature.

Internet of drones security: Taxonomies, open issues, and future directions
attachments.description: Drones have recently become one of the most important technological breakthroughs. They have opened the horizon for a vast array of applications and paved the way for a diversity of innovative solutions. Integrating drones with the Internet has led to the emergence of a new paradigm named the Internet of Drones (IoD). Several works dealt with the security of the IoD, and various surveys have been published on this topic over the past few years. The existing surveys either have limited scope or offer partial coverage of cybersecurity countermeasures. To address these gaps, in this paper, we provide a comprehensive survey related to the cyber and physical security of IoD. Differently from many surveys that only provide a classification of attacks/threats, we also propose three taxonomies that are related to (1) the assets of drones, (2) attacks, and (3) countermeasures. The first taxonomy is a two-level classification of the assets in the IoD. The first level considers the coarse-grained assets, which refer to the IoD's tangible elements, and the second level considers the fine-grained assets, which refer to the elements composing the coarse-grained assets. Based on the asset classification, we propose a taxonomy of attacks targeting the coarse and fine-grained assets, which allows a finer level of granularity to identify threats, and thus ensure better security. Also, we evaluate the risk of cyber and physical attacks by introducing a novel concept, named Chain of Impact, which connects four types of impacts, namely, Direct, Mission, Drone, and Environment. We propose a taxonomy of technical and non-technical countermeasures according to two implementation phases: Pre-incident, and Post-incident (or recovery). The pre-incident countermeasures are further classified as: preventive and detective. In addition, we present the countermeasures along with their performance and limitations. Finally, open research challenges are identified and ranked according to the level of attention they should receive from the research community. Also, future research directions and suggestions are presented for the security of the IoD.

description.shortText: Materials derived from renewable biological sources—such as plants, fungi, and microorganisms—offering a sustainable alternative to fossil fuel-based materials. These materials reduce carbon footprints, support circular economies, and enhance material performance across various industries.
description.longTextHtml:
Biobased materials leverage biological sources to produce functional materials that replace conventional fossil-derived products. These materials originate from plant-based polymers like cellulose, starch, and lignin, as well as oils and proteins. They can also be produced through microbial fermentation, enzymatic processes, or engineered metabolic pathways to generate specific compounds such as bioplastics, bioresins, and biocoatings.

Fungi-based materials, particularly mycelium, are cultivated into structures that mimic traditional materials such as leather, foam, and insulation. Advanced processing techniques enable biobased materials to match or exceed the properties of conventional materials, offering competitive mechanical strength, thermal stability, and biodegradability.

Compared to petroleum-based materials, biobased alternatives significantly reduce greenhouse gas emissions, often requiring less energy for production. Many of these materials are biodegradable or compostable, minimizing environmental impact at the end of their lifecycle. However, sustainability depends on factors such as agricultural land use, water consumption, and waste management. The integration of life cycle assessments (LCAs) ensures a holistic evaluation of their environmental footprint.

Biobased materials are already transforming industries such as packaging, textiles, automotive, and construction. Applications include biobased films, coatings, adhesives, foams, and engineered composites that maintain high-performance standards while reducing reliance on finite resources.

Future Perspectives

As research advances, biobased materials are expected to play a transformative role in diverse fields. In electronics, they could enable biodegradable circuits, flexible substrates, and conductive inks derived from plant-based polymers. Innovations in energy storage may lead to bio-derived battery components, including electrodes, separators, and electrolytes.

3D printing applications are expanding, with biobased filaments enabling customized, biodegradable products across manufacturing, healthcare, and consumer goods. High-performance biocomposites could replace traditional carbon- and glass-fiber composites in aerospace, automotive, and construction industries, improving sustainability without compromising strength or durability.

In medicine, biobased materials have the potential to enhance biocompatible implants, drug delivery systems, and tissue engineering scaffolds. Future breakthroughs could include programmable biobased materials that self-heal or adapt to environmental changes, driving a shift towards smart and responsive materials.
