description.shortText: A computational method that optimizes crop growth. It collects data from real crops in the field and creates a mathematical model to simulate how yields perform in any given circumstance.
description.longTextHtml:
In silico farming refers to the use of computer simulations and data-driven models to create digital representations—often called digital twins—of crops and their growing environments. These crop-level digital twins integrate biological, environmental, and agronomic data to replicate and forecast how plants respond to varying conditions such as water stress, soil quality, sunlight exposure, nutrient levels, and pest threats.

By combining plant physiology models with remote sensing, sensor data, and machine learning, in silico systems can simulate plant development, optimize growing strategies, and anticipate outcomes across scales—from individual plants to entire fields. This technology is particularly valuable in selective breeding, climate adaptation research, and precision agriculture, where it enables virtual trials that would be too costly or time-consuming to perform physically.

Current applications range from greenhouse experiments to large-scale field trials, supporting decisions around irrigation, fertilization, and yield prediction. Although access remains limited for smallholders, in silico farming is increasingly adopted by research institutions, governments, and agri-tech firms seeking to test “what-if” scenarios and design more resilient food systems.

Future Perspectives

As machine learning and remote sensing become more integrated with crop science, the convergence of top-down models (e.g., satellite-based forecasting) with bottom-up in silico simulations could radically increase predictive precision. This hybrid modeling could allow entire farming ecosystems — monocultures, polycultures, and agroforestry systems — to be virtually tested for resilience and yield before any seeds are planted.

With global food security under pressure from climate change, in silico farming could move from being a research tool to a decision-making need. It might enable policymakers to forecast shortages and manage food reserves preemptively. On a local level, democratizing access to these tools — via cloud computing, open datasets, or farmer cooperatives — could transform agricultural planning, reduce input waste, and promote more sustainable and adaptive farming systems.

attachments.name: In silico modelling of physiologic systems.
attachments.description: In silico modelling, in which computer models are developed to model a pharmacologic or physiologic process, is a logical extension of controlled in vitro experimentation. It is the natural result of the explosive increase in computing power available to the research scientist at continually decreasing cost. In silico modelling combines the advantages of both in vivo and in vitro experimentation, without subjecting itself to the ethical considerations and lack of control associated with in vivo experiments. Unlike in vitro experiments, which exist in isolation, in silico models allow the researcher to include a virtually unlimited array of parameters, which render the results more applicable to the organism as a whole. In silico modelling is best known for its extensive use in pharmacokinetic experimentation, the best-known example of which is the development of the three-compartment model. In addition, complex in silico models have been applied to pathophysiological problems to provide information which cannot be obtained practically or ethically by traditional clinical research methods. These experiments have led to the development of significant insights in subject matters ranging from pure physiology to congenital heart surgery, obstetric anaesthesia airway management, mechanical ventilation and cardiopulmonary bypass/ventricular support devices. The utility of these models is based on both the validity of the model framework as well as the corresponding assumptions. In vivo experimentation has validated some, but not all of the in silico strategies employed. We present a review illustrating by example how in silico modelling has been applied to a number of cardio-respiratory problems in states of health and disease, the purpose of which is to give the reader a sense of the complexity and assumptions which underlie this diverse and underappreciated research strategy, as well as an introduction to a research strategy that will likely continue to grow in importance.

attachments.name: Modeling and Mapping Agroforestry Aboveground Biomass in the Brazilian Amazon Using Airborne Lidar Data
attachments.description: Agroforestry has large potential for carbon (C) sequestration while providing many economical, social, and ecological benefits via its diversified products. Airborne lidar is considered as the most accurate technology for mapping aboveground biomass (AGB) over landscape levels. However, little research in the past has been done to study AGB of agroforestry systems using airborne lidar data. Focusing on an agroforestry system in the Brazilian Amazon, this study first predicted plot-level AGB using fixed-effects regression models that assumed the regression coefficients to be constants. The model prediction errors were then analyzed from the perspectives of tree DBH (diameter at breast height)—height relationships and plot-level wood density, which suggested the need for stratifying agroforestry fields to improve plot-level AGB modeling. We separated teak plantations from other agroforestry types and predicted AGB using mixed-effects models that can incorporate the variation of AGB-height relationship across agroforestry types. We found that, at the plot scale, mixed-effects models led to better model prediction performance (based on leave-one-out cross-validation) than the fixed-effects models, with the coefficient of determination (R2) increasing from 0.38 to 0.64. At the landscape level, the difference between AGB densities from the two types of models was ~10% on average and up to ~30% at the pixel level. This study suggested the importance of stratification based on tree AGB allometry and the utility of mixed-effects models in modeling and mapping AGB of agroforestry systems.

attachments.name: Crops In Silico: Generating Virtual Crops Using an Integrative and Multi-scale Modeling Platform
attachments.description: Multi-scale models can facilitate whole plant simulations by linking gene networks, protein synthesis, metabolic pathways, physiology, and growth. Whole plant models can be further integrated with ecosystem, weather, and climate models to predict how various interactions respond to environmental perturbations. These models have the potential to fill in missing mechanistic details and generate new hypotheses to prioritize directed engineering efforts. Outcomes will potentially accelerate improvement of crop yield, sustainability, and increase future food security. It is time for a paradigm shift in plant modeling, from largely isolated efforts to a connected community that takes advantage of advances in high performance computing and mechanistic understanding of plant processes. Tools for guiding future crop breeding and engineering, understanding the implications of discoveries at the molecular level for whole plant behavior, and improved prediction of plant and ecosystem responses to the environment are urgently needed. The purpose of this perspective is to introduce Crops in silico (cropsinsilico.org), an integrative and multi-scale modeling platform, as one solution that combines isolated modeling efforts toward the generation of virtual crops, which is open and accessible to the entire plant biology community. The major challenges involved both in the development and deployment of a shared, multi-scale modeling platform, which are summarized in this prospectus, were recently identified during the first Crops in silico Symposium and Workshop.

attachments.name: From Simulation to Field Validation: A Digital Twin-Driven Sim2real Transfer Approach for Strawberry Fruit Detection and Sizing
attachments.description: Typically, developing new digital agriculture technologies requires substantial on-site resources and data. However, the crop’s growth cycle provides only limited time windows for experiments and equipment validation. This study presents a photorealistic digital twin of a commercial-scale strawberry farm, coupled with a simulated ground vehicle, to address these constraints by generating high-fidelity synthetic RGB and LiDAR data. These data enable the rapid development and evaluation of a deep learning-based machine vision pipeline for fruit detection and sizing without continuously relying on real-field access. Traditional simulators often lack visual realism, leading many studies to mix real images or adopt domain adaptation methods to address the reality gap. In contrast, this work relies solely on photorealistic simulation outputs for training, eliminating the need for real images or specialized adaptation approaches. After training exclusively on images captured in the virtual environment, the model was tested on a commercial-scale strawberry farm using a physical ground vehicle. Two separate trials with field images resulted in F1-scores of 0.92 and 0.81 for detection and a sizing error of 1.4 mm (R2 = 0.92) when comparing image-derived diameters against caliper measurements. These findings indicate that a digital twin-driven sim2real transfer can offer substantial time and cost savings by refining crucial tasks such as stereo sensor calibration and machine learning model development before extensive real-field deployments. In addition, the study examined geometric accuracy and visual fidelity through systematic comparisons of LiDAR and RGB sensor outputs from the virtual and real farms. Results demonstrated close alignment in both topography and textural details, validating the digital twin’s ability to replicate intricate field characteristics, including raised bed geometry and strawberry plant distribution. The techniques developed and validated in this strawberry project have broad applicability across agricultural commodities, particularly for fruit and vegetable production systems. This study demonstrates that integrating digital twins with simulation tools can significantly reduce the need for resource-intensive field data collection while accelerating the development and refinement of agricultural robotics algorithms and hardware.

attachments.name: Accessing the Effect of Phyllotaxy and Planting Density on Light Use Efficiency in Field-Grown Maize using 3D Reconstructions
attachments.description: High-density planting is a widely adopted strategy to enhance maize productivity, yet it introduces challenges such as increased interplant competition and shading, which can limit light capture and overall yield potential. In response, some maize plants naturally reorient their canopies to optimize light capture, a process known as canopy reorientation. Understanding this adaptive response and its impact on light capture is crucial for maximizing agricultural yield potential. This study introduces an end-to-end framework that integrates realistic 3D reconstructions of field-grown maize with photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) modeling to assess the effects of phyllotaxy and planting density on light interception. In particular, using 3D point clouds derived from field data, virtual fields for a diverse set of maize genotypes were constructed and validated against field PAR measurements. Using this framework, we present detailed analyses of the impact of canopy orientations, plant and row spacings, and planting row directions on PAR interception throughout a typical growing season. Our findings highlight significant variations in light interception efficiency across different planting densities and canopy orientations. By elucidating the relationship between canopy architecture and light capture, this study offers valuable guidance for optimizing maize breeding and cultivation strategies across diverse agricultural settings.

description.shortText: This device converts chemical energy from hydrogen into electrical energy through an electrochemical reaction. It serves as a clean energy source for various applications, including transportation and backup power systems.
description.longTextHtml:
A hydrogen fuel cell generates electricity by combining hydrogen and oxygen in an electrochemical reaction, producing water and heat as byproducts. It consists of two electrodes (anode and cathode) separated by an electrolyte membrane. At the anode, hydrogen molecules split into protons and electrons. The protons travel through the electrolyte, while the electrons create an external electric current before recombining at the cathode with oxygen to form water.

Hydrogen can be produced using multiple methods, including steam methane reforming (SMR) from natural gas, which emits carbon dioxide, and electrolysis, which uses electricity to split water molecules into hydrogen and oxygen. Electrolysis powered by renewable energy (green hydrogen) is the most environmentally friendly option, while SMR remains the most widely used method due to cost considerations.

Hydrogen fuel cells are currently less efficient than traditional electric batteries in energy conversion but have a higher energy density, making them attractive for long-range applications. When compared to combustion engines, hydrogen fuel cells are roughly 40% more energy-efficient. They offer fast refueling times and longer operational ranges, making them a viable alternative to conventional fuels in sectors where batteries fall short, such as heavy transportation and aviation.

Future Perspectives

Hydrogen fuel cells have the potential to revolutionize multiple industries by offering a clean, scalable energy solution. In transportation, they could power a variety of vehicles, including cars, trucks, buses, trains, ships, and even aircraft, reducing reliance on fossil fuels. Hydrogen fuel cells also hold promise for stationary applications, such as decentralized power generation, grid stabilization, and backup power for critical infrastructure.

If coupled with renewable hydrogen production, hydrogen fuel cells could contribute significantly to a zero-emission energy system. In the future, advancements in fuel cell efficiency, hydrogen storage, and production methods could lower costs and improve the feasibility of widespread adoption. Innovations such as solid oxide fuel cells and biohydrogen production are being explored to enhance performance and sustainability.

However, large-scale implementation faces major challenges, including the high costs of production, distribution, and storage infrastructure. Hydrogen's low volumetric energy density makes storage and transport complex, requiring specialized facilities. Additionally, hydrogen's flammability necessitates stringent safety measures. Overcoming these hurdles will require policy support, investment in green hydrogen production, and advancements in storage and distribution technologies.

description.shortText: This set of solutions converts motion into electricity, capturing energy from human activities like walking or cycling, as well as from environmental movements such as wind and ocean waves. This renewable energy source offers a sustainable alternative to traditional power generation.
description.longTextHtml:
Kinetic energy refers to the energy of motion, which can be harnessed from a variety of sources, including human movement, vehicle vibrations, wind, and ocean waves. The energy can be captured and converted into electricity using electromechanical transducers, such as piezoelectric, electromagnetic, or triboelectric generators.

Recent advancements have focused on microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) and triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs), which use surface charge interactions to produce electricity. One notable breakthrough is the integration of MEMS plasma switches with TENGs, which enhances energy conversion efficiency. These small-scale devices can be embedded in wearable textiles, footwear, and urban infrastructure to generate power from everyday activities.

In urban settings, kinetic energy harvesting can be applied to smart pavement systems that generate electricity as people walk over them, powering nearby streetlights or sensors. Wearable solutions, such as shoes embedded with conductive liquid-based TENGs, can harvest approximately 7 watts per step—enough to charge small electronic devices.

Another innovative use case is in electric bicycles, where kinetic energy from pedaling and braking is converted into stored electricity, reducing reliance on external charging sources. This technology has the potential to enhance urban mobility by creating self-sustaining transportation systems.

Future Perspectives

As personal devices become more integrated into daily life, kinetic energy harvesting could enable continuous, self-sufficient power generation, reducing the need for external charging. Wearable electronics, from fitness trackers to smart glasses, could run indefinitely using the wearer’s movement as an energy source.

On a broader scale, entire cities could be reimagined as energy ecosystems, where sidewalks, roads, and even clothing contribute to a decentralized power grid. Future advancements may incorporate AI-driven optimization, directing energy where it is most needed in real-time.

Additionally, gamification strategies could incentivize sustainable behaviors, rewarding pedestrians and cyclists with credits for generating power. This could drive urban mobility trends away from motorized transport, encouraging more environmentally friendly habits. As smart cities evolve, kinetic energy harvesting may become an integral part of the Internet of Things (IoT), enabling self-powered sensors and communication networks that require minimal external energy input.

attachments.name: Movers and Shakers: Kinetic Energy Harvesting for the Internet of Things
attachments.description: Numerous energy harvesting wireless devices that will serve as building blocks for the Internet of Things (IoT) are currently under development. However, there is still only limited understanding of the properties of various energy sources and their impact on energy harvesting adaptive algorithms. Hence, we focus on characterizing the kinetic (motion) energy that can be harvested by a wireless node with an IoT form factor and on developing energy allocation algorithms for such nodes. In this paper, we describe methods for estimating harvested energy from acceleration traces. To characterize the energy availability associated with specific human activities (e.g., relaxing, walking, cycling), we analyze a motion dataset with over 40 participants. Based on acceleration measurements that we collected for over 200 hours, we study energy generation processes associated with day-long human routines. We also briefly summarize our experiments with moving objects. We develop energy allocation algorithms that take into account practical IoT node design considerations, and evaluate the algorithms using the collected measurements. Our observations provide insights into the design of motion energy harvesters, IoT nodes, and energy harvesting adaptive algorithms.

attachments.name: High-Performance Piezoelectric Energy Harvesters and Their Applications - ScienceDirect
attachments.description: With the rapid advances in wireless sensors, implantable electronics, and wearable devices, the demand for high-power-density and long-lifespan power sources is becoming increasingly stronger. Energy harvesting, emerging as an alternative energy solution to batteries, holds great potential to achieve self-powered autonomous operations of such low-power electronic devices, and thus has recently attracted much attention from both academia and industry. The piezoelectric effect is widely adopted to convert mechanical energy to electrical energy, due to its high energy conversion efficiency, ease of implementation, and miniaturization. This paper presents a comprehensive and critical review of state-of-the-art research on piezoelectric energy harvesting. From the viewpoint of applications, we are most concerned about whether an energy harvester can generate sufficient power under variable excitation. Therefore, here we concentrate on methodologies leading to high power output and broad operational bandwidth. A variety of designs, nonlinear methods, optimization techniques, and harvesting materials are reviewed and discussed in depth. The study also evaluates different figures of merit and presents a systematic performance comparison on recently proposed energy harvesters. Furthermore, we identify four promising applications: shoes, artificial pacemakers, tire pressure monitoring systems, and bridge and building monitoring. The excitation characteristics of each application are analyzed and corresponding harvesting methods discussed.

attachments.name: Employing a MEMS plasma switch for conditioning high-voltage kinetic energy harvesters
attachments.description: Triboelectric nanogenerators have attracted wide attention due to their promising capabilities of scavenging the ambient environmental mechanical energy. However, efficient energy management of the generated high-voltage for practical low-voltage applications is still under investigation. Autonomous switches are key elements for improving the harvested energy per mechanical cycle, but they are complicated to implement at such voltages higher than several hundreds of volts. This paper proposes a self-sustained and automatic hysteresis plasma switch made from silicon micromachining, and implemented in a two-stage efficient conditioning circuit for powering low-voltage devices using triboelectric nanogenerators. The hysteresis of this microelectromechanical switch is controllable by topological design and the actuation of the switch combines the principles of micro-discharge and electrostatic pulling, without the need of any power-consuming control electronic circuits. The experimental results indicate that the energy harvesting efficiency is improved by two orders of magnitude compared to the conventional full-wave rectifying circuit.

attachments.name: Electrochemical kinetic energy harvesting mediated by ion solvation switching in two-immiscible liquid electrolyte
attachments.description: Kinetic energy harvesting has significant potential, but current methods, such as friction and deformation-based systems, require high-frequency inputs and highly durable materials. We report an electrochemical system using a two-phase immiscible liquid electrolyte and Prussian blue analogue electrodes for harvesting low-frequency kinetic energy. This system converts translational kinetic energy from the displacement of electrodes between electrolyte phases into electrical energy, achieving a peak power of 6.4 ± 0.08 μW cm−2, with a peak voltage of 96 mV and peak current density of 183 μA cm−2 using a 300 Ω load. This load is several thousand times smaller than those typically employed in conventional methods. The charge density reaches 2.73 mC cm−2, while the energy density is 116 μJ cm−2 during a harvesting cycle. Also, the system provides a continuous current flow of approximately 5 μA cm−2 at 0.005 Hz for 23 cycles without performance decay. The driving force behind voltage generation is the difference in solvation Gibbs free energy between the two electrolyte phases. Additionally, we demonstrate the system’s functionality in a microfluidic harvester, generating a maximum power density of 200 nW cm−2 by converting the kinetic energy to propel the electrolyte through the microfluidic channel into electricity.

attachments.name: Overview of Human Kinetic Energy Harvesting and Application
attachments.description: In the Internet of Things era, wearable electronics and sensors have become essential for health monitoring and human computer interaction. However, a continuous power supply is an urgent demand in the field of distributed sensing. Energy harvesting from daily human activities and its conversion into electricity are expected to replace traditional batteries and wearable power supplying electronic devices. This article reviews the electromagnetic, piezoelectric, and triboelectric energy harvesting technologies from human motions, including joint rotation, limb swing, force application, fold stretching, and organ motion. It also discusses and analyzes the advantages and disadvantages of various recently proposed human energy harvesters. In addition, possible applications of active sensing and wearable powered electronic devices driven by human body kinetic energy harvesting are provided. Finally, the concept of a human energy and information exchange center based on energy harvesting is proposed as a future prospect.

attachments.name: Kinetic energy harvesting based sensing and IoT systems: A review
attachments.description: The rapid advance of the Internet of Things (IoT) has attracted growing interest in academia and industry toward pervasive sensing and everlasting IoT. As the IoT nodes exponentially increase, replacing and recharging their batteries proves an incredible waste of labor and resources. Kinetic energy harvesting (KEH), converting the wasted ambient kinetic energy into usable electrical energy, is an emerging research field where various working mechanisms and designs have been developed for improved performance. Leveraging the KEH technologies, many motion-powered sensors, where changes in the external environment are directly converted into corresponding self-generated electrical signals, are developed and prove promising for multiple self-sensing applications. Furthermore, some recent studies focus on utilizing the generated energy to power a whole IoT sensing system. These systems comprehensively consider the mechanical, electrical, and cyber parts, which lead a further step to truly self-sustaining and maintenance-free IoT systems. Here, this review starts with a brief introduction of KEH from the ambient environment and human motion. Furthermore, the cutting-edge KEH-based sensors are reviewed in detail. Subsequently, divided into two aspects, KEH-based battery-free sensing systems toward IoT are highlighted. Moreover, there are remarks in every chapter for summarizing. The concept of self-powered sensing is clarified, and advanced studies of KEH-based sensing in different fields are introduced. It is expected that this review can provide valuable references for future pervasive sensing and ubiquitous IoT.

description.shortText: A computing system that enables local data processing, providing safer, low-latency responses for automated devices like factory machines, autonomous vehicles, and IoT ecosystems.
description.longTextHtml:
Edge computing is a method of managing workloads by positioning computation closer to data sources. This approach eliminates the need to transmit data to centralized cloud servers for processing, thereby reducing latency and enhancing real-time responsiveness. It's particularly advantageous for applications requiring immediate data handling, such as industrial automation and autonomous systems.

By integrating machine learning algorithms, edge devices can make decisions independently without relying solely on cloud infrastructures. For instance, autonomous vehicles equipped with edge computing can operate in areas with limited connectivity, processing sensor data in real-time to navigate safely. In manufacturing, machines with on-board edge processors can function autonomously, improving reliability and reducing dependence on external networks.

Additional benefits of edge computing include efficient handling of high-bandwidth data and enhanced data security, as sensitive information remains on local devices. This localized processing minimizes exposure to potential cyber threats associated with data transmission to centralized servers.

Future Perspectives

As edge computing continues to evolve, its integration with artificial intelligence (AI) is poised to revolutionize various sectors. The deployment of AI at the edge enables devices to perform complex tasks locally, leading to faster decision-making and improved user experiences. For example, smartphones and personal computers are increasingly capable of running sophisticated AI models directly on-device, facilitating real-time applications without relying on cloud connectivity. This shift not only enhances performance but also addresses privacy concerns by keeping data processing on the user's device. The trend towards edge AI signifies a move towards more decentralized and efficient computing paradigms, potentially transforming industries ranging from healthcare to retail.

Another emerging trend is the rise of open-source edge computing. By enabling developers and enterprises to collaboratively build and deploy edge solutions, open-source frameworks lower adoption barriers and accelerate innovation. Open-source platforms allow businesses to customize edge applications without being locked into proprietary ecosystems, fostering interoperability between different edge computing environments. Startups and research institutions are already developing open-source edge architectures that could democratize access to edge computing, making it more adaptable across industries. As these open frameworks gain traction, we could see a broader range of edge-powered applications in smart cities, healthcare, and industrial automation, shaping a more decentralized and resilient digital infrastructure.

description.shortText: This system captures and redirects excess thermal energy from servers to heat nearby buildings or support industrial processes, improving energy efficiency and reducing environmental impact.
description.longTextHtml:
Data center heat reuse systems are designed to convert the waste heat generated by data centers into a usable energy source. When servers operate, they produce a significant amount of heat, which is typically managed through air or liquid cooling systems and then dissipated into the environment. Instead of allowing this energy to go unused, heat reuse systems capture it using heat exchangers and transfer it — often via water-based thermal loops — to adjacent infrastructures such as residential or office buildings, greenhouses, or district heating networks.

These systems may incorporate advanced control technologies to manage temperature levels and optimize energy flow based on seasonal or operational demand. In colder climates especially, the reuse of data center heat can cover a substantial portion of a building’s heating needs. Companies like Amazon and Microsoft have begun implementing such systems in urban areas, making data centers not only energy-intensive hubs but also contributors to circular energy economies.

Future Perspectives

In the long term, data center heat reuse systems could become standard components of urban planning. As smart cities emerge, data centers might serve as distributed thermal nodes in a city’s broader energy ecosystem — intelligently rerouting heat to schools in the morning, hospitals in the evening, and urban agriculture projects overnight. The integration of AI-driven demand forecasting could further optimize heat distribution in real time, reducing reliance on traditional heating systems and fossil fuels.

Looking further ahead, ultra-efficient closed-loop ecosystems might emerge, where the waste heat from data centers directly supports energy-positive architecture. In extreme climates, entire neighborhoods or vertical cities might be sustained by the waste heat of localized computing clusters. Data centers could become a backbone of regenerative urban infrastructure—turning digital infrastructure into thermal utility providers.

attachments.name: Optimizing Data Center Waste Heat Reuse: Case Studies and Environmental Implications
attachments.description: As data centers (DCs) are the backbones of information and communications technology (ICT), internet and big data, the utilization of energy by DCs has increased exponentially, which presents a significant impact on the environment. To simultaneously solve the dilemma of DC  huge amount of electricity  used for cooling on the one hand and a large amount of waste  heat  that is converted from nearly  all the consumed electricity on the other hand, better use of low -grade waste heat from DCs represents a significant source of energy savings for both future fourth generation of district heating (DH) networks and reducing environmental impact. This study presents an innovative waste heat reuse approach and develops a generalizable methodology that employs a simple dynamic estimate  of the potential for reutilising DC waste heat in the heat demand in DH for buildings. Brief economic calculations for building operators are also provided. The proposed modeling method is a two-stage approach for calibration and validation based on two real DCs in Finland. After validation,  the  model is  then  applied for  investigating  the potential  environmental  impacts of  a  real  DC in its design  phase.    The analysis  demonstrates  that  reusing waste  heat  from  an 18  MW  data  center to  heat  400,000  m 2 greenhouse and buildings results in a substantial reduction of 603,366 tons of carbon dioxide (CO2)  emissions over a 25-year period. From the building owners' perspective, the payback time is remarkably short, spanning only five years. The  results  highlight  the  feasibility  and  effectiveness  of  the  DC  waste  heat  recovery  to  tackle  the  energy  and environmental problems.

attachments.name: Aquasar: A hot water cooled data center with direct energy reuse | IBM

The prototype also has an air cooled part to help compare the coolants's performances. For example, a chip/coolant temperature differential of only 15 °C was sufficient for chip cooling using water. The air cooled side, however, required air pre-cooling down to 23 °C and a chip/coolant temperature differential of 35 °C. Whereas extra exergy was expended for air pre-cooling, the higher thermal conductivity and specific heat capacity of water enabled coolant temperatures to be safely raised to 60 °C. Using such hot water not only eliminated the need for chillers, it also opened up the possibility of heat reuse. The latter was realized by using the hot water from Aquasar for building heating. A heat recovery efficiency of 80% and an exergetic efficiency of 34% were achieved with a water temperature of 60 °C. All these results establish hot water as a better coolant compared to air. A novel concept of economic value of heat was introduced to evaluate different reuse strategies such as space heating and refrigeration using adsorption chillers. It was shown that space heating offers the highest economic value for the heat recovered from data centers. © 2012 Elsevier Ltd.

description.shortText: This emerging field explores the interaction between light (photons) and matter at the quantum scale, laying the foundation for technologies like quantum computing, ultra-secure communication, and next-generation sensors.
description.longTextHtml:
Quantum optics is a field of physics that investigates how photons — the fundamental particles of light — interact with atoms, molecules, and other quantum systems. At this microscopic scale, light exhibits behaviors that defy classical expectations, such as entanglement and superposition. These phenomena are harnessed to develop technologies that operate under the rules of quantum mechanics rather than conventional electronics.

This field plays a central role in quantum information science. For example, quantum cryptography uses entangled photons to guarantee secure communication that is theoretically immune to eavesdropping. Quantum sensors based on photon interference allow for ultra-precise measurements of time, acceleration, and magnetic fields—useful in navigation, medicine, and geology. Furthermore, photonic quantum processors, which use light instead of electrons, promise scalable and potentially room-temperature quantum computing with reduced decoherence compared to traditional quantum bits.

As the technology matures, quantum optics is expected to enable the development of quantum networks that interconnect quantum computers and sensors via optical fibers or free-space links. These networks rely on the manipulation of photons to transmit quantum information over long distances, integrating seamlessly with today’s internet infrastructure.

Future Perspectives

Looking ahead, quantum optics could redefine how information is transmitted, processed, and secured globally. In the long-term future, we may see the emergence of a quantum internet — an infrastructure where entangled photons enable instantaneous, unhackable communication across continents. This would transform sectors like diplomacy, finance, and national defense, offering unprecedented levels of privacy and trust.

In healthcare, quantum-optical biosensors could detect diseases at the molecular level in real-time, revolutionizing diagnostics and precision medicine. In space exploration, photon-based quantum compasses could allow for GPS-independent navigation across deep space, facilitating autonomous spacecraft coordination.

Eventually, photonic quantum computers — powered entirely by light — could surpass classical and even current quantum systems in speed and energy efficiency, leading to breakthroughs in artificial intelligence, climate modeling, and new materials discovery. As quantum optics technologies become miniaturized and commercially viable, they might be embedded into everyday devices, democratizing access to quantum-enhanced capabilities.

attachments.name: Room-Temperature entangled quantum processor on integrated semiconductor photonics platform
attachments.description: The rise of the 4H-silicon-carbide-on-insulator (SiCOI) platform marks a promising pathway towards the realization of monolithic quantum photonic networks. However, the challenge of establishing room-temperature entangled registers on these integrated photonics platforms remains unresolved. Herein, we demonstrate the first entangled processor on the SiCOI platform. We show that both deterministic generation of single divacancy electron spins and near-unity spin initialization of a single 13C nuclear spin can be achieved on SiCOI at room temperature. Besides coherently manipulating the single nuclear spin, a maximally entangled state with a fidelity of 0.89 has been prepared on this CMOS-compatible semiconductor-integrated photonics system. This work establishes the foundation for compact and on-chip solutions within existing defect-based computing and sensing protocols, positioning the SiCOI platform as the most promising candidate for integrated monolithic quantum photonic networks.

attachments.description: A transition is underway – from theoretical quantum science to real-world applications across industries. The year 2025 marks a century since the formalization of quantum mechanics, and the United Nations has designated it as the International Year of Quantum Science and Technology (IYQ 2025). Quantum technologies hold the potential to drive advancements across key sectors, offering new possibilities for addressing global challenges. For example, quantum computing is accelerating drug discovery by simulating complex molecular interactions, quantum-safe cryptography is enhancing cybersecurity with robust encryption, and quantum sensors are improving climate monitoring and precision agriculture. However, for many low- and middle-income countries, the high costs, infrastructure requirements, and limited accessibility of quantum technologies present major barriers.

attachments.name: Quantum for Good: Frontier Technology for the SDGs

attachments.name: Introduction to Quantum Optics
attachments.description: These are the lecture notes for a course that I am teaching at Zhiyuan College of Shanghai Jiao Tong University (available at this https URL), though the first draft was created for a previous course I taught at the University of Erlangen-Nuremberg in Germany. It has been designed for students who have only had basic training on quantum mechanics, and hence, the course is suited for people at all levels. The notes are a work in progress, meaning that some proofs and many figures are still missing. However, I've tried my best to write everything in such a way that a reader can follow naturally all arguments and derivations even with these missing bits. Quantum optics treats the interaction between light and matter. We may think of light as the optical part of the electromagnetic spectrum, and matter as atoms. However, modern quantum optics covers a wild variety of systems, including superconducting circuits, confined electrons, excitons in semiconductors, defects in solid state, or the center-of-mass motion of micro-, meso-, and macroscopic systems. Moreover, quantum optics is at the heart of the field of quantum information. The ideas and experiments developed in quantum optics have also allowed us to take a fresh look at many-body problems and even high-energy physics. In addition, quantum optics holds the promise of testing foundational problems in quantum mechanics as well as physics beyond the standard model in table-sized experiments. Quantum optics is therefore a topic that no future researcher in quantum physics should miss.

attachments.name: Quantum Matter and Optics

attachments.name: Elements of Quantum Optics
attachments.description: Elements of Quantum Optics gives a self-contained and broad coverage of the basic elements necessary to understand and carry out research in laser physics and quantum optics, including a review of basic quantum mechanics and pedagogical introductions to system-reservoir interactions and to second quantization. The text reveals the close connection between many seemingly unrelated topics, such as probe absorption, four-wave mixing, optical instabilities, resonance fluorescence and squeezing. It also comprises discussions of cavity quantum electrodynamics and atom optics. The 4th edition includes a new chapter on quantum entanglement and quantum information, as well as added discussions of the quantum beam splitter, electromagnetically induced transparency, slow light, and the input-output formalism needed to understand many problems in quantum optics. It also provides an expanded treatment of the minimum-coupling Hamiltonian and a simple derivation of the Gross-Pitaevskii equation, an important gateway to research in ultracold atoms and molecules.

description.shortText: By harnessing the laws of quantum physics, Quantum Cryptography provides a future-proof method for secure communication that remains unbreakable—even in the face of emerging quantum computing threats.
description.longTextHtml:
This solution exploits the fundamental principles of quantum mechanics to secure communication channels. Unlike classical methods that depend on the computational difficulty of solving complex mathematical problems, Quantum Cryptography leverages phenomena such as quantum superposition, entanglement, and the no‐cloning theorem to detect any eavesdropping.

In practice, one party encodes information onto quantum particles (typically photons), which are transmitted via optical fibres or free-space lasers. The quantum states of these particles, often prepared in various polarization bases, collapse upon measurement; any interception alters their state, alerting the communicators to potential tampering. Practical systems also employ techniques like decoy states and quantum error correction to ensure that only undisturbed, genuine key bits are retained for subsequent encryption using conventional algorithms. Field demonstrations, including terrestrial networks and satellite-based links, underline the technology’s potential for integrating with existing communication infrastructures.

Future Perspectives

As cyber threats evolve and quantum computing advances, governments, defence agencies, and financial institutions are increasingly turning to Quantum Cryptography to secure sensitive data and ensure information sovereignty. In the coming years, we may witness the development of a global quantum network—a quantum internet—that interconnects cities and continents via satellite links and ground-based quantum repeaters.

This network would enable almost latency-free, ultra-secure communications that could underpin critical infrastructures and digital economies. The technology might also evolve to integrate with next-generation Internet of Things (IoT) ecosystems, enhancing urban security and smart city operations. As research pushes the boundaries of quantum transmission distances and key distribution rates, the fusion of quantum cryptography with classical networks will likely redefine digital security standards, offering a resilient backbone for the data-driven societies of tomorrow.

attachments.name: Quantum Cryptography: Theory and Applications
attachments.description: Quantum cryptography is an attempt to allow two users to communicate using more secure methods than those guaranteed by traditional cryptography. Traditionally, cryptographic security relied on mathematics and took into account the limited computation powers that we have developed. Breaking a cryptographic code would involve factoring extremely large numbers into two primes, typically of over 100 digits in length, which was assumed to be impossible in a reasonable amount of time (less than a million years) even if all of the available computers today worked exclusively on one such problem. However, just because there is no algorithm efficient enough to do the factoring quickly, does not mean that such an algorithm could not be found eventually. Quantum cryptography, which uses photons and relies on the laws of quantum physics instead of "extremely large numbers," is the cutting edge discovery which seems to guarantee privacy even when assuming eavesdroppers with unlimited computing powers.

description.shortText: A deep-learning model that learns while it performs a task, adapting to new data inputs in real-time, enabling speed and adaptability for machine learning.
description.longTextHtml:
Current machine learning methods first go through a training phase before being deployed in real-world applications, meaning they remain static unless retrained. Liquid neural networks take a different approach, allowing models to continuously adapt by changing their underlying equations in response to new data. Dubbed “liquid” because of their flexibility, these networks can analyze information in real-time, making them highly effective for applications requiring constant learning and adjustment. Their ability to anticipate future behavior based on incoming data can accelerate the development of emerging technologies like self-driving cars, medical diagnosis tools, financial forecasting, and other systems that rely on fast, adaptive decision-making.

Future Perspectives

The development of liquid neural networks could fundamentally reshape how artificial intelligence interacts with dynamic environments. Autonomous vehicles could safely and accurately navigate roads by reacting instantly to real-time obstacles, traffic patterns, and weather conditions, making self-driving cars more viable. Delivery drones, which rely on instant decision-making, could use these networks to avoid collisions and optimize routes as conditions change. In the medical field, liquid neural networks could enable more precise diagnostics by learning from patient data in real-time, helping detect diseases earlier and improving treatment recommendations. In financial markets, these networks could enhance robo-advisors and algorithmic trading strategies by continuously adapting to fluctuations, potentially generating greater wealth for investors. The energy sector could also benefit, as liquid neural networks may allow power grids to analyze fluctuations more accurately, enabling energy suppliers to predict and respond to shifts in demand more efficiently. With climate change making weather patterns more volatile, liquid neural networks could significantly improve weather forecasting, offering more accurate predictions for both everyday conditions and extreme natural disasters. As AI systems continue evolving, liquid neural networks may become a cornerstone technology for real-time adaptability, unlocking new possibilities across industries.

attachments.name: Liquid Time-constant Networks
attachments.description: We introduce a new class of time-continuous recurrent neural network models. Instead of declaring a learning system's dynamics by implicit nonlinearities, we construct networks of linear first-order dynamical systems modulated via nonlinear interlinked gates. The resulting models represent dynamical systems with varying (i.e., liquid) time-constants coupled to their hidden state, with outputs being computed by numerical differential equation solvers. These neural networks exhibit stable and bounded behavior, yield superior expressivity within the family of neural ordinary differential equations, and give rise to improved performance on time-series prediction tasks. To demonstrate these properties, we first take a theoretical approach to find bounds over their dynamics and compute their expressive power by the trajectory length measure in latent trajectory space. We then conduct a series of time-series prediction experiments to manifest the approximation capability of Liquid Time-Constant Networks (LTCs) compared to classical and modern RNNs. Code and data are available at this https URL

attachments.name: The Reinforced Liquid State Machine: A New Training Architecture for Spiking Neural Networks
attachments.description: This work presents a novel Spiking Neural Network training architecture based on a deepened Liquid State Machine integrating Winner-Takes-All computation and Reward-Modulated Synaptic Plasticity. The networks performance is evaluated on the Heidelberg Dataset for spoken digit recognition. A two-layer liquid configuration improves classification accuracy by 5% over a single-layer baseline, while incorporating feedback between liquid layers. This architecture demonstrates that deep liquid models, combined with feedback and reward-driven learning, can effectively capture complex spatio-temporal patterns, offering significant advantages in terms of accuracy over traditional Liquid State Machines.

attachments.name: LTC-SE: Expanding the Potential of Liquid Time-Constant Neural Networks for Scalable AI and Embedded Systems
attachments.description: We present LTC-SE, an improved version of the Liquid Time-Constant (LTC) neural network algorithm originally proposed by Hasani et al. in 2021. This algorithm unifies the Leaky-Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) spiking neural network model with Continuous-Time Recurrent Neural Networks (CTRNNs), Neural Ordinary Differential Equations (NODEs), and bespoke Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs). The enhancements in LTC-SE focus on augmenting flexibility, compatibility, and code organization, targeting the unique constraints of embedded systems with limited computational resources and strict performance requirements. The updated code serves as a consolidated class library compatible with TensorFlow 2.x, offering comprehensive configuration options for LTCCell, CTRNN, NODE, and CTGRU classes. We evaluate LTC-SE against its predecessors, showcasing the advantages of our optimizations in user experience, Keras function compatibility, and code clarity. These refinements expand the applicability of liquid neural networks in diverse machine learning tasks, such as rob

These pioneers of the air are not living creatures, but rather a product of deliberate innovation: drones. But these aren’t your typical flying bots, humming around like mechanical bees. attachments.description: This study investigates the realm of liquid neural networks (LNNs) and their deployment on neuromorphic hardware platforms. It provides an in-depth analysis of Liquid State Machines (LSMs) and explores the adaptation of LNN architectures to neuromorphic systems, highlighting the theoretical foundations and practical applications. We introduce a pioneering approach to image classification on the CIFAR-10 dataset by implementing Liquid Neural Networks (LNNs) on state-of-the-art neuromorphic hardware platforms. Our Loihi-2 ASIC-based architecture demonstrates exceptional performance, achieving a remarkable accuracy of 91.3% while consuming only 213 microJoules per frame. These results underscore the substantial potential of LNNs for advancing neuromorphic computing and establish a new benchmark for the field in terms of both efficiency and accuracy.

description.shortText: Biodegradable polymers made from insect biomass offer a sustainable alternative to petroleum-based plastics.
description.longTextHtml:
Insect-based bioplastics are an emerging class of biodegradable materials created using biomass and byproducts from insect farming. Chief among these is chitin, a fibrous substance found in the exoskeletons of insects, which can be chemically processed into chitosan and further into bioplastics. These plastics are non-toxic, biodegradable, and can be engineered to possess a variety of properties depending on the processing techniques.

The production process typically involves harvesting insect waste or exoskeletons, extracting chitin, deacetylating it into chitosan, and blending it with natural polymers or additives to enhance flexibility, durability, or water resistance. This results in a versatile bioplastic that can be molded or extruded like traditional plastics. Use cases include compostable packaging, agricultural films, controlled-release fertilizers, wound dressings, and drug delivery systems.

This technology supports the principles of a circular bioeconomy by utilizing insect waste — often a byproduct of protein farming — thereby closing material loops and reducing the environmental burden of plastic production.

Future Perspectives

In the long term, insect-based bioplastics could become a vital component of decentralized material production systems, especially in regions investing in insect agriculture for food or feed. As farming insects becomes more widespread due to their high efficiency and low environmental footprint, the volume of usable biowaste will also increase, offering a cheap and abundant source for polymer production.

In more speculative futures, these bioplastics may be engineered for smart biodegradation — programmed to degrade only under certain environmental conditions — or enhanced with biosensors to monitor product use, freshness, or contamination. With advancements in synthetic biology, customized insects could be bred specifically for high-chitin yields, creating a new intersection of farming and materials engineering.

In space or remote environments, insect-based bioplastics could be a sustainable solution for waste reuse and closed-loop manufacturing, turning biological waste into useful materials on demand.

attachments.name: Advances in the insect industry within a circular bioeconomy context: a research agenda
attachments.description: The agri-food industry is increasingly recognizing the environmental impact of the over-exploitation of natural resources and waste production, which has prompted a search for sustainable alternatives based on circular bioeconomy principles. Insects can efficiently transform food substrates into reusable biomass, thus making them valuable contributors to a circular bioeconomy system. However, the relationship between the circular bioeconomy and the insect industry has so far appeared relatively unexplored in the existing research. To address this gap, a meta-synthesis has been conducted through a systematic literature review. By identifying the state of the art and assessing the role of insects in the transition of closed-loop systems, the aim of this research has been to shed light on the opportunities and challenges of integrating insects in circular bioeconomy strategies. The research revealed three main topics: (1) waste management by insects, i.e., the use of insects as a tool for waste management and with which to create high-value substrates; (2) insect-based feeds, namely the use of insects as alternative food sources in farming systems; (3) insect-based food acceptance by consumers. The results underscore the significant potential of this market within the circular bioeconomy context, highlighting the obstacles that need to be addressed and future strategies that could be adopted.

attachments.name: Biodegradable Chitosan-Based Films as an Alternative to Plastic Packaging
attachments.description: The impact of synthetic packaging on environmental pollution has been observed for years. One of the recent trends of green technology is the development of biomaterials made from food processing waste as an alternative to plastic packaging. Polymers obtained from some polysaccharides, such as chitosan, could be an excellent solution. This study investigated the biodegradability of chitosan–metal oxide films (ZnO, TiO2, Fe2O3) and chitosan-modified graphene films (CS-GO-Ag) in a soil environment. We have previously demonstrated that these films have excellent mechanical properties and exhibit antibacterial activity. This study aimed to examine these films’ biodegradability and the possibility of their potential use in the packaging industry. The obtained results show that soil microorganisms were able to utilize chitosan films as the source of carbon and nitrogen, thus providing essential evidence about the biodegradability of CS, CS:Zn (20:1; 10:1), and CS:Fe2O3 (20:1) films. After 6 weeks of incubation, the complete degradation of the CS-Fe2O3 20:1 sample was noted, while after 8 weeks, CS-ZnO 20:1 and CS-ZnO 10:1 were degraded. This is a very positive result that points to the practical aspect of the biodegradability of such films in soil, where garbage is casually dumped and buried. Once selected, biodegradable films can be used as an alternative to plastic packaging, which contributes to the reduction in pollution in the environment.

description.shortText: To enhance food safety and prevent storage losses, this autonomous robotic device navigates through granular bulks such as grains, beans, and pellets. It continuously monitors humidity and temperature to detect early signs of mold and pest accumulation.
description.longTextHtml:
A Granular Drone is an autonomous robotic device designed to navigate within bulk solids and powders, aiding grain merchants and farmers in preventing significant losses during long-term storage.

The drone features a rotating body with retractable segments that enable it to "swim" through granular materials like protein crops, beans, cereal grains, and pellets. Equipped with advanced sensors, it measures temperature and humidity, allowing for real-time monitoring of storage conditions and early detection of risks such as mold growth and pest infestation, crucial for food safety and supply chain resilience.

Current models are tethered to an external system via a long cable, which supplies power and facilitates real-time data transmission. The collected data is visualized in a software interface, offering a 3D representation of the storage conditions, enabling users to take timely corrective actions.

Future Perspectives

As granular drones evolve, they could extend beyond food storage applications. Future advancements may allow them to operate untethered, improving maneuverability and integration with AI-driven monitoring systems. Potential applications include subterranean probing for geological surveys, archeological excavation assistance, and seabed exploration.

In the long term, these drones could play a role in space exploration by conducting soil analysis on extraterrestrial surfaces such as Mars or the Moon. Their ability to move through granular material could make them valuable for studying regolith properties, assisting in resource extraction, and supporting planetary habitat development.

attachments.name: The Crover Effect

Crover's method of movement in granular materials is made possible by a new ground-breaking physical discovery and patented (UK) technology enabling locomotion in bulk solids (e.g. sand, grains, powders).    Like plane or drone wings in air, or a boat's rotor in water, it allows an object to move through solid grains.    It works in any environment made of bulk solids and powers, like sand dunes, heaps of grain, mineral bulks, chemical powders and even loose Martian terrain.

The project aims to further the development of the CROVER robot, the world's first 'granular drone' (in the sense of a device able to move through bulk solids and powders), in order to create a system that not only provides condition monitoring of granular bulks, but also the ability to manage them autonomously.  The project is made possible by the Crover proprietary technology for locomotion in bulk solids (e.g. sand, grains, powders) and it is based around the CROVER: the world's first 'granular drone', in the sense of a device able to move through bulk solids and powders.

description.shortText: By deploying orbital platforms equipped with solar panels and mirrors, sunlight can be captured, converted into electrical energy, transformed into microwaves or lasers, and beamed down to receiving stations on Earth.
description.longTextHtml:
Space-Based Solar Power (SBSP) is a proposed method of harnessing solar energy in space and transmitting it wirelessly to Earth. Unlike terrestrial solar farms, which are subject to weather conditions and limited by night cycles, SBSP benefits from uninterrupted exposure to sunlight, significantly increasing energy efficiency. This is made possible by placing solar power satellites (SPS) in geostationary orbit or other advantageous locations where they can continuously collect solar radiation without atmospheric interference.

The core principle of SBSP involves massive solar arrays or mirrors that capture sunlight and convert it into electrical energy. This energy is then converted into microwave or laser beams, which are transmitted to ground-based receiving stations—often called rectennas (rectifying antennas). These rectennas convert the beamed energy back into electricity, which is fed into the existing power grid.

One of the major advantages of SBSP is its potential for 24/7 clean energy generation, eliminating the intermittency issues associated with conventional solar power. Additionally, the ability to beam energy wirelessly to different locations could provide flexible power distribution, supporting both developed energy grids and remote regions. Furthermore, it reduces the reliance on fossil fuels, significantly contributing to global efforts to mitigate climate change.

Despite its promise, SBSP faces significant technological and economic challenges. The launch and assembly of large-scale space solar platforms require substantial investment, advancements in wireless power transmission, and innovations in space-based manufacturing. Moreover, concerns regarding beam safety, energy conversion efficiency, and geopolitical control over orbital power infrastructure remain active areas of research and debate.

Future Perspectives

In the long term, SBSP could serve as a primary energy source for Earth and beyond. It has the potential to power remote regions, disaster-stricken areas, and high-altitude platforms such as autonomous drones or airships, extending their operational endurance for telecommunications, surveillance, and atmospheric research.

Looking further ahead, SBSP could be integral to space exploration and colonization. Future lunar or Martian colonies could rely on space-based solar infrastructure to generate energy independently, reducing reliance on supply missions from Earth. SBSP could also support interplanetary travel, powering spacecraft and deep-space stations on long-duration missions.

The development of in-orbit manufacturing and assembly technologies, such as robotic fabrication or asteroid mining, could make SBSP more economically viable. If components are produced and assembled in space rather than launched from Earth, the costs could decrease dramatically, accelerating adoption. If successful, SBSP could redefine how humanity generates and distributes energy, creating a truly global, sustainable, and decentralized power grid.

description.shortText: Physical AI merges artificial intelligence with robotics and material science to enable intelligent systems that operate effectively within the constraints of the physical world.
description.longTextHtml:
Physical AI refers to intelligent systems that integrate artificial intelligence with robotics, advanced sensors, and material science to operate directly within the physical world. These systems are designed to perceive, reason, and act while constrained by the laws of physics—such as gravity, friction, and energy dynamics—allowing for real-time adaptation to their environment. Rather than remaining in purely digital domains, Physical AI is embodied in machines that must make context-aware decisions based on tactile, visual, spatial, and kinetic inputs.

Applications are expanding rapidly across multiple sectors. In industry, collaborative robots (co-bots) work side-by-side with humans on production lines, learning from their surroundings to safely assist with tasks like assembly, inspection, or logistics. In healthcare, surgical robots equipped with AI improve precision and responsiveness in complex procedures, enhancing patient outcomes. Autonomous vehicles, including self-driving cars, depend on Physical AI to interpret dynamic road conditions and navigate safely through urban environments. In built environments, smart spaces and IoT-enabled systems use embedded intelligence to manage lighting, energy, security, and environmental comfort based on human presence and activity.

These systems combine AI’s cognitive capabilities with physical embodiment, bridging the gap between computation and the tangible world. By enabling machines to adapt intelligently in real time, Physical AI supports a new class of autonomous agents capable of operating safely and effectively in unstructured, human-centric environments.

Future Perspectives

In the long term, Physical AI could become a foundation for machines that operate with almost lifelike adaptability and resilience. We may see the emergence of fully autonomous construction swarms that build shelters in disaster zones, intelligent wearables that assist with physical therapy in real time, or sentient-like exploration units capable of colonizing extreme environments — from deep ocean trenches to planetary surfaces.

As materials become smarter and AI systems more context-aware, Physical AI may evolve into what some theorists call “embodied intelligence,” where learning and cognition emerge directly from physical interaction. This could redefine the boundary between machines and living organisms, blurring the line between artificial and biological intelligence in a way that fundamentally shifts how we understand agency, autonomy, and intelligence itself.

In this world, AI agents don’t just guide work—they do the work, both digitally and physically.

attachments.name: The Next Wave of AI
Generative Physical AI in Vision: A Survey
attachments.description: Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) has rapidly advanced the field of computer vision by enabling machines to create and interpret visual data with unprecedented sophistication. This transformation builds upon a foundation of generative models to produce realistic images, videos, and 3D/4D content. Conventional generative models primarily focus on visual fidelity while often neglecting the physical plausibility of the generated content. This gap limits their effectiveness in applications that require adherence to real-world physical laws, such as robotics, autonomous systems, and scientific simulations. As generative models evolve to increasingly integrate physical realism and dynamic simulation, their potential to function as "world simulators" expands. Therefore, the field of physics-aware generation in computer vision is rapidly growing, calling for a comprehensive survey to provide a structured analysis of current efforts. To serve this purpose, the survey presents a systematic review, categorizing methods based on how they incorporate physical knowledge, either through explicit simulation or implicit learning. It also analyzes key paradigms, discusses evaluation protocols, and identifies future research directions. By offering a comprehensive overview, this survey aims to help future developments in physically grounded generation for computer vision. The reviewed papers are summarized at this https URL.

description.shortText: A credit-tracking system that evaluates and ranks citizen behavior, quantifying it into a type of social-credit code, producing a persistent and dynamic social trust profile linked to a permanent and nontransferable record.
description.longTextHtml:
A Social Credit System is a digital framework that collects, processes, and analyzes data to generate behavioral scores for individuals and organizations. Originating as a national policy initiative, these systems aim to promote trust and accountability by rewarding compliant behavior and discouraging misconduct.

Using a combination of AI-powered surveillance cameras, financial records, legal documents, and online behavior—including social media activity—algorithms calculate dynamic scores based on predefined government or institutional parameters. In some pilot versions, this data has been used to automatically restrict access to loans, travel, or jobs for low-scoring individuals, while offering fast-track privileges and incentives to high scorers.

While often portrayed as a monolithic national system, in reality, it consists of multiple fragmented regional and corporate experiments. Some target companies while others trial public behavior incentives, such as real-time “trustworthiness” rankings in public transport systems.

In theory, this type of system could be used to promote eco-friendly practices, penalize littering or fare evasion, and reward sustainable behavior through discounts or loyalty points. However, in practice, it raises critical concerns about mass surveillance, data privacy, political bias, and social inequality. Critics argue that it could reinforce digital authoritarianism and create a system of behavioral policing where citizens surveil one another or fear algorithmic misinterpretation.

Future Perspectives

As AI, biometric tracking, and ubiquitous computing advance, social credit systems could evolve into autonomous self-learning frameworks that continuously redefine social norms. Deep learning models might develop probabilistic profiles of individuals not only based on actions but inferred intentions, potentially judging micro-expressions, voice tone, and even subconscious behavior captured by urban sensors.

In the near future, individuals could be algorithmically clustered and flagged in real time based on context-specific risk assessments. These assessments might influence access to public services, automated job interviews, or even the pace at which government forms are processed. With generative AI and synthetic surveillance, entire urban ecosystems might respond to social credit metrics dynamically—altering pricing, access, or exposure to opportunities.

While offering a potential infrastructure for fostering civic responsibility and ecological consciousness, such systems also risk normalizing digital discrimination, amplifying existing biases, and reducing citizens to data points. The speculative frontier includes invisible nudging of behavior through personalized AI agents or predictive policing based on aggregated social credit risk—raising ethical questions about the future of freedom, reputation, and governance.

attachments.name: China just announced a new social credit law. Here’s what it means.

attachments.name: China’s Corporate Social Credit System and Its Implications
attachments.description: China’s corporate social credit system (CSCS) is a data-driven scoring system to rate the “trustworthiness” of all business entities registered in China. In the first publicly-available CSCS scores from Zhejiang Province, neither better-governed nor more profitable firms received higher overall scores, but highly-leveraged firms subject to higher default risks were associated with lower total scores. This research finds that politically-connected firms received higher CSCS scores, primarily by accumulating soft merits for charitable donations sanctioned by the party-state, volunteer activities, and awards from government organs. The findings underscore the CSCS’s potential to nudge firms to adopt the preferred policies of the CCP and to exhibit increasing fealty to the CCP.

The paper aims to discuss these issues.

attachments.name: China Social Credit System Explained – What is it & How Does it Work?
attachments.description: The China social credit system is a broad regulatory framework intended to report on the ‘trustworthiness’ of individuals, corporations, and governmental entities across China. In this introduction, we explain how the China social credit system works in 2024, how it differs from financial credit ratings elsewhere, and how it impacts individuals and companies operating within China.

attachments.name: Moral and Economic Governance: The Role of China's Social Credit System in Relation to the Welfare State
attachments.description: The Social Credit System is an expansive program which aims to rank Chinese citizens, companies, organizations, and government entities by their trustworthiness, which is measured through social credit points earned by complying with legal, professional, and moral standards in China. The early implementation of Social Credit has led to international concern over the system’s supposedly Orwellian nature. Counter to a public perception and historiography which is dominated by discussing the system’s function as a method of social control, this thesis asks how the SCS may alternatively be understood as part of China’s welfare state. In doing so, this thesis questions the tendency to cast the SCS as Orwellian by arguing that these critiques uncritically evaluate the SCS according to Western standards. As a result, the thesis calls for recognition of the cultural and political context in which the SCS exists if it is to be properly analyzed. The thesis then explores this cultural and political context in relation to China’s welfare state and demonstrates how the SCS can be shown to logically consistent with China’s Confucian history of welfare provision. It argues that the SCS provides vitally needed moral and economic governance in response to insecurities generated by China’s economic liberalization. By doing so, the SCS secures material and spiritual welfare in China. Both the program’s Confucian influence and response to the economic liberalization are demonstrated through analyzing the planning document for the SCS. The thesis concludes by arguing that understanding the SCS as part of China’s welfare state has significant explanatory power and should not be overlooked. Overall, it argues that analyzing the SCS through the lens of the welfare state is extremely relevant to understand how the social and economic spheres are linked in the view of Chinese governance. However, the thesis concludes by acknowledging that the program is too large to be adequately understood from any single frame of analysis and thus research should continue to be conducted from multiple frames of analysis.
