attachments.name: We’re just data: Exploring China’s social credit system in relation to digital platform ratings cultures in Westernised democracies
attachments.description: Social media platforms and apps have become increasingly important tools for governance and the centralisation of information in many nation states around the globe. In China, the government is currently piloting a social credit system in several cities in an ambitious attempt to merge a financial credit score system with a broader quantification of social and civic integrity for all citizens and corporations. China has already begun to experiment with metrics and quantification of the value and virtue of its citizens, going beyond the function of measuring workplace performance and health-related self-tracking to measuring one’s purchasing and consumption history, interpersonal relationships, political activities, as well as the tracking of one’s location history. China has also already begun to apply a reward and punishment system that rewards those who comply with the Chinese government’s ideals and punishes those who deviate from them. Although there are no such ambitiously unified systems currently proposed in Western liberal democratic countries, some aligned structures and cultures of social media use are already well in place. This article seeks to offer a comparative examination of the structures and cultures of China’s social credit system with those which are already present and in place in Western liberal democratic countries. While it may be convenient to digitise everyday social, political and economic life, China’s social credit system brings about a vision of what may be to come, should democratic countries continue to do so without stricter data use policies in place.

attachments.name: Forget public transit: In London, an app that rewards you for walking and cycling.
attachments.description: Coming to a city near you, too. Get off the bus or subway, even if only one stop early. Use your own two feet. Collect points! Get free underpants!

attachments.name: How IoT Tracking Devices are changing the Fleet Management Business
attachments.description:
Being in the fleet
business has never been easy, especially when it comes to the management of
vehicles and drivers on road. Earlier, it was all done with the help of phone
calls, but drivers used to evade the calls leaving the fleet manager clueless.  It
was a major challenge to track the drivers over phone, which was frustrating
for the fleet managers.

attachments.name: New Aussie Designed Coffee Cup That's Reusable And Pays With A Tap
attachments.description: A new Aussie coffee cup eliminates two problems with your daily coffee run: wasting all those paper (or heaven forbid, Styrofoam) cups and a sluggish line to the cashier. Frank green, a Melbourne-based company, has designed a reusable coffee cup (that doesn’t spill) and lets you pay with a tap -- [...]

attachments.name: China social credit system still in testing phase amid trials
attachments.description: China is forging ahead with efforts to create a national social credit system. Some analysts doubt authorities can reach their goal.

attachments.name: Government Credit, a Double‐Edged Sword: Evidence from the China Development Bank
attachments.description: Using proprietary data from the China Development Bank (CDB), this paper examines the effects of government credit on firm activities. Tracing the effects of government credit across different levels of the supply chain, I find that CDB industrial loans to state‐owned enterprises (SOEs) crowd out private firms in the same industry but crowd in private firms in downstream industries. On average, a $1 increase in CDB SOE loans leads to a $0.20 decrease in private firms' assets. Moreover, CDB infrastructure loans crowd in private firms. I use exogenous timing of municipal politicians' turnover as an instrument for CDB credit flows.

attachments.name: Driver Behavior Monitoring System for Fleet Safety Management
attachments.description: Driver behavior monitoring for enhanced fleet & fleet safety management- Analyze and receive violations in real-time of driving behavior events, giving you valuable insights to improving fleet safety management and driver safety. Start monitoring your fleet today!

attachments.name: Detroit: Become Human
attachments.description: Directed by David Cage.  With Valorie Curry, Bryan Dechart, Jesse Williams, Audrey Boustani. The game allows you to take control of three androids in their quest to discover who they really are.

attachments.name: Scoring—Analysis of the Social Credit System in the PRC and Scoring in the West
attachments.description: The joint project "Scoring - Analysis of the Social Credit System in the People's Republic of China and Scoring in the West" comprises two academic partners (University of Witten/Herdecke | Leuphana University).  Through the cooperation of different project partners from computer science and cultural studies as well as health sciences under the coordination of a project partner from Chinese studies, the scoring topic is examined for the first time in individual aspects, compared interculturally and thus analyzed across disciplines.

attachments.name: Citizenship governance in the age of Covid-19: the case of social credit
attachments.description: This project studied the social credit systems being developed in response to the COVID-19 crisis and their effects on society.

attachments.name: Zhima Credit
attachments.description: Zhima Credit (Chinese: 芝麻信用; pinyin: Zhīma Xìnyòng; also known as Sesame Credit) is a private company-run credit scoring and loyalty program system developed by Ant Group, an affiliate of Alibaba Group. It uses data from Alibaba's services to compile its score. Customers receive a score based on a variety of factors based on social media interactions and purchases carried out on Alibaba Group websites or paid for using its affiliate Ant Financial's Alipay mobile wallet. The rewards of having a high score include easier access to loans from Ant Financial and having a more trustworthy profile on e-commerce sites within the Alibaba Group.[1][2] It has frequently been confused with the Social Credit System.[3]

attachments.name: China’s Tencent is quietly testing a “social credit score” based on people’s online behavior
attachments.description: More scores that rate your trustworthiness are coming to China’s internet—which is great for a quick discount, but concerning for civil liberties.

description.shortText: A compact aerial first-response unit equipped with emergency medical tools, designed to dramatically reduce response times and improve survival chances during critical incidents.
description.longTextHtml:
An ambulance drone is a lightweight uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) developed to deliver emergency medical equipment—such as automated external defibrillators (AEDs), trauma kits, or even blood units—to the scene of a medical emergency in record time. Operated via GPS and LTE or 5G connectivity, these drones are guided to the precise coordinates of the incident, often provided through emergency dispatch systems or smartphone apps.

The concept has been tested in real-world conditions, most notably in Sweden, where trials showed drones delivering defibrillators to cardiac arrest cases faster than ambulances in 64% of cases within a 10 km range. The drone includes a video and audio interface, enabling medical professionals to remotely instruct bystanders on administering first aid or operating the AED.

More advanced applications include the secure and temperature-controlled transport of organs, blood, and medical samples. Onboard sensors monitor and transmit real-time health and transport data to hospitals or medical centers. Beyond emergency delivery, ambulance drones are being piloted for search-and-rescue operations, remote triage, and disaster relief in areas with obstructed ground access.

Future Perspectives

Ambulance drones could redefine the structure of emergency response systems. With fleets of autonomous units stationed across cities or rural areas, a mesh network of flying responders could intervene within minutes, drastically enhancing survival rates, especially in remote or traffic-congested zones. Hospitals may evolve into more distributed and agile hubs, focusing less on immediate intake and more on remote stabilization and virtual triage.

As AI and telemedicine advance, ambulance drones might become smart enough to assess patient vitals through cameras and biosensors, administer basic care, or even deploy robotic arms for simple interventions. In disaster zones or conflict areas, these drones could serve as frontline responders—delivering aid, performing diagnostics, or relaying real-time data to emergency teams and decision-makers.

attachments.name: Ambulance Drone, Engineering For Change
attachments.description: The Ambulance Drone is a prototype high speed drone that delivers Automated Defribrillators (AED) in the event of a cardiac arrest. The drone tracks emergency mobile calls and uses GPS to navigate to the emergency site. Using a live-stream webcam, the drone instructor or pilot can instruct on how to use the AEDs and provide instructions for giving emergency aid.

attachments.name: A Data-Driven Simulator for the Strategic Positioning of Aerial Ambulance Drones Reaching Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrests: A Genetic Algorithmic Approach
attachments.description: Objective: The Internet of Things provide solutions for many societal challenges including the use of unmanned aerial vehicles to assist in emergency situations that are out of immediate reach for traditional emergency services. Out of hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) can result in death with less than 50% of victims receiving the necessary emergency care on time. The aim of this study is to link real world heterogenous datasets to build a system to determine the difference in emergency response times when having aerial ambulance drones available compared to response times when depending solely on traditional ambulance services and lay rescuers who would use nearby publicly accessible defibrillators to treat OHCA victims. Method: The system uses the geolocations of public accessible defibrillators and ambulance services along with the times when people are likely to have a cardiac arrest to calculate response times. For comparison, a Genetic Algorithm has been developed to determine the strategic number and positions of drone bases to optimize OHCA emergency response times. Conclusion: Implementation of a nationwide aerial drone network may see significant improvements in overall emergency response times for OHCA incidents. However, the expense of implementation must be considered.

attachments.name: Drone vs. ambulance: How one Canadian paramedic service went beyond to deliver critical medical technology
attachments.description: A unique race between an ambulance and drone flying beyond the line of sight demonstrates what’s possible for emergency services in remote areas

attachments.name: Ambulance Drone
attachments.description: The first minutes after an accident are critical and essential to provide the right care to prevent escalation. Speeding up emergency response can prevent deaths and accelerate recovery dramatically. This is notably true for heart failure, drowning, traumas and respiratory issues. Lifesaving technologies such as an Automated External Defibrillator (AED), medication, Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (CPR) aids can be designed compact enough to be carried by a drone.

attachments.name: 'Ambulance drone' takes to the skies - BBC News
attachments.description: A Belgian student is seeking sponsors to get his prototype "ambulance drone" off the ground.

attachments.name: Zipline - Instant Delivery & Logistics
The Evolution of UAVs: The Ambulance Drone
attachments.description: The mere mention of the word "drone" tends to conjure up unpleasant images in the public mind. Whether it's unmanned hunter-killers armed with missiles, small surveillance drones monitoring people on the street, or the spectre of autonomous vehicles one-day patrolling our skies, the idea of unmanned machines being a threat to our privacy or our very existence seems rather popular these days. And yet, the reality of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) is quite different.

attachments.name: Alec Momont | Ambulance Drone
attachments.description: This prototype of an ambulance drone was developed during his graduation by Alec Momont (faculty of Industrial Design TU Delft) in cooperation with the innovation platform Living Tomorrow. In cases of emergencies like a coronary attack, the autonomously navigating drone can deliver a defibrillator in no time; through a video and voice connection, the people on location receive feedback and instructions. The application determines the location of a victim based on the telephone signal of the caller, and finds its way thanks to GPS. The drone achieves speeds of around hundred km/h, weighs four kilogrammes and can carry loads of up to four kilogrammes.

attachments.name: Our ambulance drone concept
attachments.description: Last month we revealed our ambulance drone concept; a look into the (near) future of how this new emergency vehicle can better serve patients and responders, reduce response times and provide more reliability compared to the helicopters used today.

attachments.name: In Sweden, Drones Are Beating Ambulances to the Scene — and Saving Lives
attachments.description: New technology is intervening in the moments where speed matters more than anything. Welcome to the future of emergency medicine.

attachments.name: Sky's the limit for drone-delivered defibrillators
attachments.description: THE Welsh Ambulance Service is moving closer to using drones to fly defibrillators to patients.

attachments.name: Red Cross tests delivery of blood bag by drone
attachments.description: In Austria, every 90 seconds a person needs a blood supply. When a hospital calls for reserves, a car with a driver sets off to deliver the life-saving blood. The Red Cross is now testing new ways to save time and resources: For the first time, a blood bag was delivered by drone. Fully automatically. The action is symbolic, the flight from the Red Cross district office in Lilienfeld to the nearby state hospital only took a few minutes, but it shows how drones can make it easier to help in the future.

attachments.name: Sophisticated rescuers with rotors
attachments.description: The University of Klagenfurt and the Medical University of Graz are jointly researching the use of drones in medical missions. The first test flights have now been completed in Bodental.

attachments.name: New drone type transports life-saving defibrillator
attachments.description: For cardiac arrest victims, minutes can mean the difference between life and death. It’s vital that medical emergency response teams get to them quickly, but in more remote, rural areas this can sometimes be difficult. “HORYZN” is an initiative of students at the Technical University of Munich (TUM) and has developed a remote-controlled, AI-supported rescue drone with a defibrillator on board for just such emergencies.

description.shortText: By turning waste into a tradable asset, communities can reduce landfill overflow while creating income opportunities. Through systems that exchange trash for money, goods, or services, this model incentivizes recycling, supports low-income populations, and fosters circular economies.
description.longTextHtml:
Waste as a currency is a model that transforms both plastic and organic waste from environmental burdens into economic value. In this system, individuals collect waste and exchange it at designated centers for money, digital tokens, or essential services such as food, transportation, school tuition, or mobile phone charging. Plastic waste is typically sorted, cleaned, and processed into pellets, which are sold to manufacturers as recycled raw materials. Organic waste, on the other hand, can be composted and used in local agriculture or converted into biogas, adding further utility and value.

Some projects have implemented blockchain and app-based platforms that register waste contributions and convert them into digital currencies or tokens. These tokens can be redeemed in local shops or markets, creating a circular economy that incentivizes recycling and supports economic inclusion. In parallel, some cities are experimenting with reward-based systems for households that correctly separate recyclables, reinforcing responsible behaviour through gamified platforms and micro-rewards.

By aligning economic incentives with environmental action, this approach strengthens recycling infrastructures, provides income to underserved populations, and reduces plastic pollution through localized, closed-loop economies.

Future Perspectives

As awareness of ecological responsibility spreads, brands and retailers are beginning to accept waste as payment—a symbolic shift that both empowers consumers and positions companies as sustainability allies. Waste as a currency may evolve beyond grassroots movements and become embedded into formal waste management and economic systems. Blockchain and IoT integration could allow for seamless waste traceability, smart-contract rewards, and dynamic pricing based on material types and market demand.

However, as the value of waste rises, unintended consequences could emerge. In regions lacking strict regulation, there is a risk of incentivizing the production of waste purely for economic gain. To mitigate such risks, transparency mechanisms and ethical guidelines must evolve alongside the technology. On the brighter side, as remanufacturing technologies improve, especially in chemical recycling, the ecosystem for waste-based economies could expand dramatically—enabling cities to turn waste surpluses into material wealth and distributed economic resilience.

Rather than viewing it as garbage, Plastic Bank empowers local communities by paying them to collect this waste and bring it to a Plastic Bank facility. From there, it is recycled and repurposed, to create raw pellets of Social Plastic for reuse in other industries. attachments.name: Recycleye launches new currency to help increase recycling

So backing Waste2Crypto means investing directly to save the planet by stopping waste going to landfill.

attachments.name: Green Currency: Exchanging organic waste for money
attachments.description: Organic waste represents more than 50% of the waste generated in Brazil, and constitutes a major urban problem. For many years, Santiago has been committed to environmental education, which is one of the goals of the Charter of Educating Cities. In this way, the city consolidated its selective waste collection service in all neighbourhoods, accustoming citizens to separate organic waste (food leftovers, fruit peel, vegetables, etc.) from recyclable waste (glass, paper and metal) on different collection days.

De Gezonde Stad’s ambition is to contribute to a circular economy with the Zero Waste Lab scheme and create awareness about the value of waste. The Zero Waste Lab by De Gezonde Stad is a local spot used to collect and upcycle waste. The community’s rubbish is exchanged for a local currency which can be used to buy goods and services at local shops. A first Zero Waste Lab opened in Amsterdam in 2016 and a second one came along in 2017.

attachments.name: RecycleMich app proves to be a digital addition to the new deposit system
attachments.description: Only 20% of packaging will fall under the new Austrian deposit system from 2025 – but what will happen to the remaining 80%? This is precisely where the innovative Austrian app RecycleMich comes in. With clear sorting information, new features and a user-friendly reward system, it provides orientation and motivation for proper waste separation. With over 2.5 million items of packaging registered, RecycleMich has already had a significant impact on recycling behaviour and resource conservation in Austria.

attachments.name: When school fees are paid with plastic waste
attachments.description: A Nigerian social enterprise found an innovative way to tackle the twin problems of mounting plastic waste and lack of education access.

attachments.name: PLASTICPAY: Turning Waste into Money
attachments.description: Plasticpay is a social movement based on a digital platform, which invites people to change plastic waste that damages the environment into something useful and good.  The collected plastic waste will be exchanged for Plasticpay Points, then it will be recycled and turned into granules, Recycled Polyester Staple Fiber (“Re-PSF”), yarn and fabric. The result is Eco-friendly fibre and recycled fabric that meets all high-quality standards that can be used for pillows, dolls, bedding, carpets, furniture, automotive interiors, and non-woven / woven products.

description.shortText: Advanced neural networks generate photorealistic, full-body avatars adaptable to various poses and camera angles, enabling dynamic augmented reality experiences for virtual social interactions.
description.longTextHtml:
Dynamic Neural Avatars utilize deep neural networks to create lifelike, full-body renderings of individuals in motion, accommodating diverse body poses and camera perspectives. By training convolutional neural networks on extensive datasets of images and videos depicting human movements, these systems synthesize realistic, animated figures without requiring the exact individual to be present in the training data. This allows for the generation of multiple unique avatars from a single dataset.

Recent advancements employ neural radiance fields (NeRFs) and neural light fields (NeLFs) to enhance the realism of these avatars. NeRF-based models implicitly represent the geometry and appearance of the human head, enabling photorealistic reconstructions from monocular videos. However, traditional NeRFs face challenges with slow rendering speeds due to dense point sampling. To address this, models like LightAvatar leverage NeLFs to achieve efficient head avatar rendering, significantly improving rendering speeds while maintaining high-quality outputs.

Future Perspectives

The evolution of Dynamic Neural Avatars holds transformative potential across various sectors. In entertainment, they could revolutionize filmmaking and gaming by enabling the creation of digital actors who perform without physical presence, reducing production costs and time. In social media and marketing, virtual influencers—entirely digital personas—could engage audiences and endorse products which aims to supercharge the virtual influencer market using AI . However, these advancements also raise ethical concerns. The ability to produce indistinguishable deepfake videos poses risks of misinformation and challenges the authenticity of digital content. As this technology becomes more accessible, establishing guidelines and detection mechanisms will be crucial to mitigate potential misuse.

attachments.name: Video-based Characters – Creating New Human Performances from a Multi-view Video Database
attachments.description:
We present a method to synthesize plausible video sequences of
humans according to user-defined body motions and viewpoints.
We first capture a small database of multi-view video sequences
of an actor performing various basic motions. This database needs
to be captured only once and serves as the input to our synthesis
algorithm. We then apply a marker-less model-based performance
capture approach to the entire database to obtain pose and geometry
of the actor in each database frame. To create novel video sequences
of the actor from the database, a user animates a 3D human skeleton
with novel motion and viewpoints.

attachments.name: DensePose: Dense Human Pose Estimation In The Wild
attachments.description: In this work, we establish dense correspondences between RGB image and a surface-based representation of the human body, a task we refer to as dense human pose estimation. We first gather dense correspondences for 50K persons appearing in the COCO dataset by introducing an efficient annotation pipeline. We then use our dataset to train CNN-based systems that deliver dense correspondence 'in the wild', namely in the presence of background, occlusions and scale variations. We improve our training set's effectiveness by training an 'inpainting' network that can fill in missing groundtruth values and report clear improvements with respect to the best results that would be achievable in the past. We experiment with fully-convolutional networks and region-based models and observe a superiority of the latter; we further improve accuracy through cascading, obtaining a system that delivers highly0accurate results in real time. Supplementary materials and videos are provided on the project page this http URL

attachments.name: Textured Neural Avatars
attachments.description: Textured Neural Avatars

attachments.name: Dynamic Neural Radiance Fields for Monocular 4D Facial Avatar Reconstruction
attachments.description: We present dynamic neural radiance fields for modeling the appearance and dynamics of a human face. Digitally modeling and reconstructing a talking human is a key building-block for a variety of applications. Especially, for telepresence applications in AR or VR, a faithful reproduction of the appearance including novel viewpoint or head-poses is required. In contrast to state-of-the-art approaches that model the geometry and material properties explicitly, or are purely image-based, we introduce an implicit representation of the head based on scene representation networks. To handle the dynamics of the face, we combine our scene representation network with a low-dimensional morphable model which provides explicit control over pose and expressions. We use volumetric rendering to generate images from this hybrid representation and demonstrate that such a dynamic neural scene representation can be learned from monocular input data only, without the need of a specialized capture setup. In our experiments, we show that this learned volumetric representation allows for photo-realistic image generation that surpasses the quality of state-of-the-art video-based reenactment methods.

attachments.name: LightAvatar: Efficient Head Avatar as Dynamic Neural Light Field
attachments.description: Recent works have shown that neural radiance fields (NeRFs) on top of parametric models have reached SOTA quality to build photorealistic head avatars from a monocular video. However, one major limitation of the NeRF-based avatars is the slow rendering speed due to the dense point sampling of NeRF, preventing them from broader utility on resource-constrained devices. We introduce LightAvatar, the first head avatar model based on neural light fields (NeLFs). LightAvatar renders an image from 3DMM parameters and a camera pose via a single network forward pass, without using mesh or volume rendering. The proposed approach, while being conceptually appealing, poses a significant challenge towards real-time efficiency and training stability. To resolve them, we introduce dedicated network designs to obtain proper representations for the NeLF model and maintain a low FLOPs budget. Meanwhile, we tap into a distillation-based training strategy that uses a pretrained avatar model as teacher to synthesize abundant pseudo data for training. A warping field network is introduced to correct the fitting error in the real data so that the model can learn better. Extensive experiments suggest that our method can achieve new SOTA image quality quantitatively or qualitatively, while being significantly faster than the counterparts, reporting 174.1 FPS (512x512 resolution) on a consumer-grade GPU (RTX3090) with no customized optimization.

attachments.name: Dynamic Neural Garments
attachments.description: A vital task of the wider digital human effort is the creation of realistic garments on digital avatars, both in the form of characteristic fold patterns and wrinkles in static frames as well as richness of garment dynamics under avatars’ motion. Existing workflow of modeling, simulation, and rendering closely replicates the physics behind real garments, but is tedious and requires repeating most of the workflow under changes to characters’ motion, camera angle, or garment resizing. Although data-driven solutions exist, they either focus on static scenarios or only handle dynamics of tight garments. We present a solution that, at test time, takes in body joint motion to directly produce realistic dynamic garment image sequences. Specifically, given the target joint motion sequence of an avatar, we propose dynamic neural garments to jointly simulate and render plausible dynamic garment appearance from an unseen viewpoint. Technically, our solution generates a coarse garment proxy sequence, learns deep dynamic features attached to this template, and neurally renders the features to produce appearance changes such as folds, wrinkles, and silhouettes. We demonstrate generalization behavior to both unseen motion and unseen camera views. Further, our network can be fine-tuned to adopt to new body shape and/or background images. We also provide comparisons against existing neural rendering and image sequence translation approaches, and report clear quantitative improvements.

attachments.name: AutoAvatar: Autoregressive Neural Fields for Dynamic Avatar Modeling
attachments.description: Neural fields such as implicit surfaces have recently enabled avatar modeling from raw scans without explicit temporal correspondences. In this work, we exploit autoregressive modeling to further extend this notion to capture dynamic effects, such as soft-tissue deformations. Although autoregressive models are naturally capable of handling dynamics, it is non-trivial to apply them to implicit representations, as explicit state decoding is infeasible due to prohibitive memory requirements. In this work, for the first time, we enable autoregressive modeling of implicit avatars. To reduce the memory bottleneck and efficiently model dynamic implicit surfaces, we introduce the notion of articulated observer points, which relate implicit states to the explicit surface of a parametric human body model. We demonstrate that encoding implicit surfaces as a set of height fields defined on articulated observer points leads to significantly better generalization compared to a latent representation. The experiments show that our approach outperforms the state of the art, achieving plausible dynamic deformations even for unseen motions.

attachments.name: Improving online teaching with mixed reality: Fraunhofer HHI launches BMBF-funded project VoluProf
attachments.description: The Fraunhofer Heinrich Hertz Institute (HHI) has started the new project VoluProf (Volumetric Mixed Reality Professor for Omnipresent and User-Optimized Teaching). It was recently launched at the “3IT - Innovation Center for Immersive Imaging Technologies ”. The project will use mixed reality (MR) technologies to make online teaching more direct, interactive, and user-centered. For this purpose, the researchers develop photo- and audio-realistic avatars of real lecturers. The project started in September 2021 and will run until August 2024. The Federal Ministry of Education and Research (BMBF) is funding the project with 1.98 million euros.

attachments.name: EVA: Expressive Virtual Avatars from Multi-view Videos
attachments.description: EVA generates high-fidelity, real-time human renderings from arbitrary camera views, skeletal motion, and expression parameters. It leverages an expressive template geometry as a geometric proxy for its 3D Gaussian appearance model, enabling disentangled control over body, hands, and face

attachments.name: gDNA: Towards Generative Detailed Neural Avatars
attachments.description: To make 3D human avatars widely available, we must be able to generate a variety of 3D virtual humans with varied identities and shapes in arbitrary poses. This task is challenging due to the diversity of clothed body shapes, their complex articulations, and the resulting rich, yet stochastic geometric detail in clothing. Hence, current methods that represent 3D people do not provide a full generative model of people in clothing. In this paper, we propose a novel method that learns to generate detailed 3D shapes of people in a variety of garments with corresponding skinning weights. Specifically, we devise a multi-subject forward skinning module that is learned from only a few posed, un-rigged scans per subject. To capture the stochastic nature of high-frequency details in garments, we leverage an adversarial loss formulation that encourages the model to capture the underlying statistics. We provide empirical evidence that this leads to realistic generation of local details such as wrinkles. We show that our model is able to generate natural human avatars wearing diverse and detailed clothing. Furthermore, we show that our method can be used on the task of fitting human models to raw scans, outperforming the previous state-of-the-art.

description.shortText: This solution integrates IoT sensors, big data, and AI to monitor and optimize logistics in real time. By leveraging cloud computing, these systems enhance transparency, automate decision-making, and streamline supply chain operations.
description.longTextHtml:
A cloud-connected supply chain integrates digital technologies to provide real-time visibility, automation, and operational efficiency across logistics networks. It relies on Internet of Things (IoT) sensors, AI-driven analytics, and, in emerging cases, blockchain for secure, transparent, and immutable data sharing. These systems track assets, predict maintenance needs, optimize inventory, and enhance end-to-end logistics management.

By linking assets directly to the cloud and blockchain, supply chain entities—from manufacturers to retailers—can monitor products throughout their journey, ensuring compliance, quality, and security. Sensors track factors such as temperature, location, and condition of goods, while AI predicts demand and optimizes routes. Automated transactions and smart contracts facilitate seamless business operations, reducing costs and inefficiencies.

However, challenges remain. While blockchain ensures data integrity, privacy concerns persist, particularly regarding compliance with regulations like the GDPR. Traditional blockchain architectures, which store data permanently, conflict with GDPR requirements for data deletion. Emerging solutions such as zero-knowledge proofs and hybrid blockchain models aim to resolve this paradox, allowing selective disclosure and controlled data erasure without compromising security.

Future Perspectives

The evolution of cloud-connected supply chains could redefine logistics, making global trade more efficient, sustainable, and resilient. Future advancements in AI and predictive analytics will enable autonomous decision-making, reducing human intervention in supply chain operations. Enhanced IoT integration may lead to fully self-regulating supply chains, where goods autonomously navigate distribution networks.

In agri-food systems, blockchain-enabled traceability could improve food safety and sustainability by verifying authenticity and reducing waste. As global trade expands, cloud-based logistics can mitigate environmental impact, particularly in ports, where pollution and resource consumption are significant concerns. Smart auditing and sustainability enforcement mechanisms could transform supply chains into greener, more efficient networks.

Additionally, AI-powered supply chains may integrate generative AI to optimize inventory forecasting and logistics planning, reducing inefficiencies and waste. The convergence of digital twins and blockchain could create fully virtualized supply chain models, allowing businesses to simulate scenarios and preemptively address disruptions.

attachments.name: Tomorrow's world today, as automated 'rapid logistics' begin to optimise supply chains.
attachments.description: Software start-up Yojee is using artificial intelligence (AI) and blockchain technology to optimise freight movements and develop a new type of “collaborative economy” logistics model.

attachments.description: To succeed in this evolving marketplace, companies need to transform linear supply chains into autonomous supply chain ecosystems.

description.shortText: A sustainable and automated construction method using bio-based materials like surplus wood waste and mycelium to create 3D-printed homes with minimal environmental impact.
description.longTextHtml:
This technology employs large-scale 3D printing to fabricate homes using bio-based materials such as surplus wood waste, sawdust, paper pulp, and mycelium. These materials are combined with bio-resins or other biodegradable polymers to create durable, low-carbon construction materials. The process allows for precise and waste-free building, significantly reducing carbon emissions and construction waste.

By using locally sourced and renewable materials, 3D-printed bio-homes address supply chain disruptions, labor shortages, and the rising costs of housing. The automated nature of 3D printing enables rapid, off-site manufacturing, minimizing on-site construction time and making sustainable housing more affordable and scalable.

Future Perspectives

As this technology scales, 3D-printed bio-homes could revolutionize the housing industry by providing customizable, low-cost, and environmentally sustainable homes, particularly in regions facing housing shortages or natural disasters. The potential for integrating smart features, self-sustaining energy systems, and even bioreceptive surfaces could further enhance their efficiency and adaptability.

In the long term, bio-based 3D printing might contribute to extraterrestrial colonization, using locally available regolith on the Moon or Mars combined with bioengineered binders to create self-sustaining habitats for space missions. The integration of artificial intelligence and robotic construction could further automate and optimize housing solutions worldwide.

description.shortText: A government-backed digital currency built on blockchain infrastructure, combining elements of fiat and crypto to ensure legal tender status, accountability, and algorithmic monetary policy.
description.longTextHtml:
Sovereign cryptocurrencies are digital currencies issued or authorized by nation-states, designed to function as legal tender while leveraging blockchain infrastructure for transparency, efficiency, and programmable governance. Unlike traditional cryptocurrencies, which are decentralized and often volatile, sovereign cryptocurrencies typically integrate fiat backing or regulatory oversight to stabilize value and ensure compliance with existing financial laws.

These digital currencies are often built on third-generation blockchains using consensus mechanisms like Delegated Proof-of-Stake (DPoS) or Avalanche protocols, which allow high throughput, energy efficiency, and built-in governance structures. Transactions and supply rules are embedded directly into the protocol via smart contracts and DAOs (Decentralized Autonomous Organizations), allowing algorithmic issuance, real-time audits, and more equitable distribution models. For example, rather than directing newly issued funds to banks, some implementations envision distributing them directly to verified citizens.

Sovereign cryptocurrencies differ from Central Bank Digital Currencies (CBDCs) primarily in their hybrid governance models—often involving public-private partnerships—and their potential programmability for social policies (such as conditional cash transfers or automated tax deductions). They can promote interoperability across financial systems while minimizing energy usage and enhancing trust through cryptographic proofs and transparent ledger systems.

Future Perspectives

In the coming decade, sovereign cryptocurrencies may evolve into programmable infrastructure for the digital economy—integrating with IoT systems, smart contracts, and digital identity frameworks. This could allow individuals to autonomously manage taxes, licenses, social benefits, and cross-border transactions, all embedded within a regulated yet decentralized network. In low-trust or inflation-prone environments, sovereign crypto could replace or supplement fragile monetary systems. Additionally, programmable currency policies may enable real-time macroeconomic adjustments, direct stimulus distribution, or region-specific monetary governance. As more jurisdictions seek alternatives to traditional financial intermediaries, sovereign cryptocurrencies could underpin a new era of inclusive, transparent, and automated economic interaction.

attachments.name: Sovereign Digital Currencies: Reshaping the Design of Money and Payments Systems
attachments.description: This paper focuses on how technology might reshape payments going forward. It considers the policy issues and choices associated with crypto-currencies, stablecoins and sovereign digital currencies and emphasises that there is no single model for sovereign digital currency design. While Bitcoin and its progenies could be safely ignored by regulators, Facebook’s proposal for Libra, a global stablecoin, brought an immediate and potent response from regulators globally. Any proposal by the private sector to move into the creation of currency — the traditional preserve of sovereigns — was always likely to trigger such a regulatory response, as well as the launch of sovereign digital currencies by other major central banks. While China has moved first, dozens of other countries are now investigating their own central bank digital currencies or other forms of sovereign digital currency. This paper argues that central banks should first focus not on rolling out novel new forms of sovereign digital currencies, but rather on transforming their payment systems. In time, domestic money and payment systems are expected to evolve so that central banks cooperate with (new and old) private entities to launch digital currencies that better underpin monetary and payment systems at the domestic, regional and international levels.

description.shortText: Electronic devices constructed on advanced flexible substrates that enable bending, stretching, rolling, folding, and conforming to various shapes while maintaining full functionality.
description.longTextHtml:
Flexible Electronics are electronic systems built using materials such as polymers, plastic, metal foils, paper, smart textiles, flex glass, or thin films, allowing them to conform to diverse shapes and contours. Unlike conventional rigid electronics, these devices can be stretched, bent, folded, or rolled without compromising performance.

The technology leverages specialized materials and advanced fabrication methods. Conductive polymers, thin metal films, and printed electronics techniques are employed to create flexible circuits and interconnections that retain conductivity even under mechanical strain. Manufacturing approaches include inkjet, screen, gravure, and 3D printing, enabling the deposition of functional electronic components on flexible substrates. Organic semiconductors, flexible thin-film transistors, stretchable batteries, and bendable displays contribute to the adaptability and durability of Flexible Electronics.

This adaptability unlocks new possibilities for integration into unconventional form factors, significantly impacting industries such as wearables, healthcare, aerospace, and automotive. Wearable electronics, including smart textiles, fitness trackers, and biosensors, benefit from seamless body conformity. In healthcare, electronic skin (e-skin) and flexible medical implants improve patient monitoring and treatment outcomes. In the automotive and aerospace industries, lightweight and shock-resistant Flexible Electronics enhance cockpit displays, structural sensors, and adaptive surfaces. Additionally, the space-saving nature of flexible circuitry supports IoT applications, allowing sensors and communication modules to be embedded into compact, non-traditional environments.

Future Perspectives

By overcoming the constraints of rigid electronics, Flexible Electronics enable a future where technology seamlessly integrates into everyday life, creating devices that are more intuitive, wearable, and durable. As this field advances, electronics could become an unobtrusive part of our surroundings, effectively blurring the line between the digital and physical worlds.

One transformative possibility is the self-powered flexible device—energy-harvesting electronics embedded in clothing, accessories, or even urban infrastructure. These could capture ambient energy from body heat, motion, or light, reducing the dependence on traditional batteries. Additionally, intelligent packaging solutions incorporating Flexible Electronics could revolutionize retail, logistics, and healthcare by enabling dynamic freshness indicators, real-time tracking, and personalized user interactions.

Future advancements may also include biodegradable Flexible Electronics, reducing electronic waste and supporting sustainability initiatives. As material science and nanotechnology progress, fully stretchable circuits with integrated AI capabilities may emerge, enabling dynamic, shape-adaptive computing surfaces. Ultimately, Flexible Electronics could lead to a new paradigm of ubiquitous, unobtrusive, and highly resilient electronic ecosystems.

attachments.name: Recent progress in silk fibroin-based flexible electronics
attachments.description: With the rapid development of the Internet of Things (IoT) and the emergence of 5G, traditional silicon-based electronics no longer fully meet market demands such as nonplanar application scenarios due to mechanical mismatch. This provides unprecedented opportunities for flexible electronics that bypass the physical rigidity through the introduction of flexible materials. In recent decades, biological materials with outstanding biocompatibility and biodegradability, which are considered some of the most promising candidates for next-generation flexible electronics, have received increasing attention, e.g., silk fibroin, cellulose, pectin, chitosan, and melanin. Among them, silk fibroin presents greater superiorities in biocompatibility and biodegradability, and moreover, it also possesses a variety of attractive properties, such as adjustable water solubility, remarkable optical transmittance, high mechanical robustness, light weight, and ease of processing, which are partially or even completely lacking in other biological materials. Therefore, silk fibroin has been widely used as fundamental components for the construction of biocompatible flexible electronics, particularly for wearable and implantable devices. Furthermore, in recent years, more attention has been paid to the investigation of the functional characteristics of silk fibroin, such as the dielectric properties, piezoelectric properties, strong ability to lose electrons, and sensitivity to environmental variables. Here, this paper not only reviews the preparation technologies for various forms of silk fibroin and the recent progress in the use of silk fibroin as a fundamental material but also focuses on the recent advanced works in which silk fibroin serves as functional components. Additionally, the challenges and future development of silk fibroin-based flexible electronics are summarized.

attachments.name: What are Flexible Electronics?
attachments.description: Flexible electronics are being designed into a wide range of products on the market today, including both consumer and industrial segments. These products include components in today's cell phones and displays, human and health performance tools, security tags, sensor componentry in cars and airplanes, agricultural and environmental sensors, strain gauges in bridges and equipment, just to name a few. Find more information on the technology and the wide range of application segments and markets in SEMI's member-only information section, including presentations from the leading integrators of flexible electronics technology.

attachments.name: Flexible Electronics: Status, Challenges and Opportunities
attachments.description: The concept of flexible electronics has been around for several decades. In principle, anything thin or very long can become flexible. While cables and wiring are the prime example for flexibility, it was not until the space race that silicon wafers used for solar cells in satellites were thinned to increase their power per weight ratio, thus allowing a certain degree of warping. This concept permitted the first flexible solar cells in the 1960s (Crabb and Treble, 1967). The development of conductive polymers (Shirakawa et al., 1977), organic semiconductors, and amorphous silicon (Chittick et al., 1969; Okaniwa et al., 1983) in the following decades meant huge strides toward flexibility and processability, and thus these materials became the base for electronic devices in applications that require bending, rolling, folding, and stretching, among other properties that cannot be fulfilled by conventional electronics (Cheng and Wagner, 2009) (Figure 1).

attachments.name: Flexible Electronics | Nature
The Future of Flexible Electronics
attachments.description: Flexible electronics are game-changers in the world of technology. There are many advantages of flexible electronics., and since they’re so lightweight and malleable, they change the capabilities of products and equipment in a variety of industries. To understand the potential of flexible electronics, you’ll first need to know more about what flexible electronics are, why they’re used, and who uses them. Then, you’ll be ready to understand the current trends in flex circuit technology, along with what the future holds for the technology.

attachments.name: The Evolution of Flexible Electronics: From Nature, Beyond Nature, and To Nature
attachments.description: The flourishing development of multifunctional flexible electronics cannot leave the beneficial role of nature, which provides continuous inspiration in their material, structural, and functional designs. During the evolution of flexible electronics, some originated from nature, some were even beyond nature, and others were implantable or biodegradable eventually to nature. Therefore, the relationship between flexible electronics and nature is undoubtedly vital since harmony between nature and technology evolution would promote the sustainable development. Herein, materials selection and functionality design for flexible electronics that are mostly inspired from nature are first introduced with certain functionality even beyond nature. Then, frontier advances on flexible electronics including the main individual components (i.e., energy (the power source) and the sensor (the electric load)) are presented from nature, beyond nature, and to nature with the aim of enlightening the harmonious relationship between the modern electronics technology and nature. Finally, critical issues in next-generation flexible electronics are discussed to provide possible solutions and new insights in prospective exploration directions.

attachments.name: Flexible Electronics using Liquid Silicon
attachments.description: A team led by EEMCS associate professor Ryoichi Ishihara has successfully fabricated flexible, super-fast transistors on plastic foil. Their technology considerably improves on transistor fabrication based on printing techniques, which has limited application for flexible electronic devices. The innovation opens new paths for flexible displays and many other applications, such as implantable sensors, flexiblesmart sensor tags with ultra-high frequency RF-ID, and flexible, stable solar-cells with high efficiency. A flexible polyimide substrate is coated with a special solution called ‘liquid silicon’. Using laser recrystallisation, a thin polysilicon layer is prepared with 3μm sized grains at predetermined positions. Transistors fabricated inside the grains show an unparalleled high carrier mobility of 461 cm2/Vs.

attachments.name: Flexible and Printed Electronics
attachments.description: Flexible and Printed Electronics is a multidisciplinary journal devoted to publishing cutting edge research articles on electronics that can be either flexible, plastic, stretchable, conformable or printed.  Research related to electronic materials, manufacturing techniques, components or systems which meets any one (or more) of the above criteria is suitable for publication in the journal.

attachments.name: Flexible Electronics | Science Direct
attachments.description: Flexible electronics refers to the technologies that process sensors, actuators, circuits and other electronic devices on flexible and stretchable substrates. Comprehensive studies on flexible materials and processing technologies began in 1960s since copper (Cu) was patterned on polyimide (PI) [1]. Compared with traditional electronics, flexible electronics exhibits advantages in many aspects, such as wearability, biocompatibility, and mechanical stability [2]. These features allow flexible electronics to fit into applications in chemical/bio sensors [3–7], human-computer interfaces [8–10], flexible optoelectronics and displays [11–13], electronics skins [14–17] and many others [18–22]. Traditional single-layer flexible electronics, however, has limited space for assembling functional components, and therefore suffers from low level of integration, limited spatial resolution and sensing modality, and insufficient capability in personalized configuration. The concept of multilayer design can leverage the vertical space to tackle the above limitations of single-layer flexible electronics.

attachments.name: Flexible and rigid-flexible printed circuit boards
attachments.description: Technological innovation of the kind we’re seeing in the medical sector or the automotive industry is mainly driven by the miniaturisation of electronic circuits. These days, a great many modern medical implants and LED car headlights make exacting demands of printed circuit boards, and require them to be installed in tiny spaces. AT&S can easily meet these demands by using flexible base materials. Flexible printed circuit boards can be bent or twisted during assembly, so they can be integrated into devices with almost any form factor and with space constraints. This is extremely important in devices like pacemakers.

attachments.name: A printed proximity-sensing surface based on organic pyroelectric sensors and organic thin-film transistor electronics
attachments.description: Large-area, flexible proximity-sensing surfaces are useful in a range of applications including process control, work security and robotics. However, current systems typically require rigid and thick electronics, which limit how they can be used. Here we report a flexible large-area proximity-sensing surface fabricated using printed organic materials and incorporating analogue front-end electronics in each pixel. The sensing surface is built with printed thin-film pyroelectric sensors based on poly(vinylidene fluoride-co-trifluoroethylene) co-polymers and printed organic thin-film transistors. A 5 × 10 matrix frontplane, consisting of long-wavelength infrared organic pyroelectric sensors, is laminated with an organic transistor analogue front-end backplane. The electronic front end provides sensor-signal amplification and pixel addressing to maximize the detection distance and reduce pixel crosstalk. An average yield of 82% fully working pixels for the backplane and a maximum system yield of 96%, which corresponds to 768 defect-free devices, are achieved. The system can detect a human hand approaching from different directions and track the position of a movable heat source up to a distance of around 0.4 m at a readout speed of 100 frames per second.

attachments.name: PLASTIC LOGIC GERMANY’S FLEXIBLE LECTUM® DISPLAYS
attachments.description: Plastic Logic manufactures flexible, glass-free electrophoretic active matrix displays of various sizes. These displays are perfectly readable under bright conditions, and they consume power only in case of display updates - without power the content remains for years. Compared to conventional electrophoretic displays Plastic Logic's organic transistor (OTFT) technology provides additional and unique features: Our displays are flexible, extremely robust, glass-free as well as lightweight and ultra-thin. Plastic Logic’s displays provide proven lifetimes of over five years and more than 10 million page updates. They are especially suited for applications and products in signage and logistics, mobile electronic devices, smart cards and wearables.

attachments.name: Aligning Nanowires for Stretchable Electronics
attachments.description: Researchers at Complex Materials and at the Laboratory of Biosensors and Bioelectronics (D-ITET) have developed stretchable electronics containing multilayers of oriented nanowires. This is useful for strain sensing applications in soft robotics, wearable electronics and E-skins.
