attachments.description: The mass production of conventional silicon chips relies on a successful business model with large ‘semiconductor fabrication plants’ or ‘foundries’. New research by KU Leuven and imec shows that this ‘foundry’ model can also be applied to the field of flexible, thin-film electronics. Adopting this approach would give innovation in the field a huge boost.

description.shortText: Biomimicry is an interdisciplinary design approach that draws inspiration from nature’s forms, processes, and systems to develop sustainable human technologies.
description.longTextHtml:
Biomimicry, or Biomimetics, refers to the practice of emulating nature’s strategies—shaped by billions of years of evolution—to solve human design challenges. This method draws insights from biology, materials science, engineering, and architecture to craft solutions that are efficient, resilient, and often radically innovative. Instead of merely extracting resources from nature, biomimicry looks to nature as a model, measure, and mentor.

Practical applications include buildings modeled after termite mounds to regulate temperature passively, water systems inspired by fog-harvesting beetles in deserts, and adhesives mimicking the microstructures of gecko feet. Biomimicry can also influence systems design, such as organizational models that reflect the decentralized efficiency of ant colonies or circular economic models based on forest ecosystems.

This approach helps industries develop low-impact materials, optimize energy use, and design integrated systems that reduce waste and improve resilience. It has been adopted in urban planning, product development, and even governance structures.

Future Perspectives

In the long-term future, biomimicry may serve as a foundational philosophy for post-anthropocentric design, leading to cities that function like forests — cleaning air and water, regulating climate, and regenerating waste into nutrients. Architecture could become adaptive and responsive, shaped by materials that grow, self-heal, and adapt to their environment, drawing directly from biological processes like photosynthesis or mycelial networks.

Entire infrastructures might evolve into living systems — bridges that grow stronger with use, roads that repair themselves, and buildings that breathe and evolve with their occupants. As synthetic biology and AI converge with biomimicry, we may also see programmable ecosystems engineered to reverse environmental degradation or even terraform new planetary habitats.

Ultimately, biomimicry could help transition humanity from being extractive to being symbiotic, deeply embedded in and responsive to the broader ecosystems we inhabit.

attachments.name: A Biomimicry Primer  | Janine Benyus
attachments.description: In this approachable eight-page essay, Janine Benyus defines biomimicry and the discipline's place in design and culture.

attachments.name: Termites Are Teaching Architects to Design Super-Efficient Skyscrapers
attachments.description: Mound termites are pros at building self-regulating homes. Human architects want to get in on the action.

attachments.name: Termite mould building – A comparative study on bio-memetics model
attachments.description: This paper seeks to adapt passive cooling techniques in buildings through an alternative approach of biomimetic. The biomimetic is a concept in which the biological design and model of nature are transformed into human entities and processes. This study presents the passive cooling ventilation system inspired by the termite nest, with which the building is cooled based on the natural process by the provision of vent pipes. The ultimate outcome was to deliver the effect of space cooling by means of ventilation with minimal consumption of electric energy. This method could develop an eco-friendly approach by avoiding the extensive usage of air conditioning systems. This concept has been successfully adopted in two commercial buildings around the world. In the present study, the model of a conventional multi-storeyed residential structure has been executed using REVIT software, with and without the provision of a ventilation system. The structural stability and the energy efficiency of the modelled building were analyzed and comprehensive designed was provided as an output. The ducts for the ventilation was provided in such a way that it should overcome the design limitations. This kind of building must be implemented in an urban environment, where there is a rapid increase in cumulative energy consumption, which leads to sustainable development.

attachments.name: A fog-collecting surface mimicking the Namib beetle: its water collection efficiency and influencing factors
attachments.description: Shortage of water resources and deterioration of water quality are becoming more and more serious today. Inspired by Namib Desert beetles, scientists designed biomimetic fog collection materials to obtain fresh water. The overview of this field is limited and mainly concerned with the preparation and application. In this paper, we focused on the water collection efficiency of surfaces inspired by beetles and discussed their influence on the water collection efficiency from three aspects: surface wettability, surface structure and surface pattern distribution.

attachments.name: Gecko-Inspired Controllable Adhesive: Structure, Fabrication, and Application
attachments.description: The gecko can achieve flexible climbing on various vertical walls and even ceilings, which is closely related to its unique foot adhesion system. In the past two decades, the mechanism of the gecko adhesion system has been studied in-depth, and a verity of gecko-inspired adhesives have been proposed. In addition to its strong adhesion, its easy detachment is also the key to achieving efficient climbing locomotion for geckos. A similar controllable adhesion characteristic is also key to the research into artificial gecko-inspired adhesives. In this paper, the structures, fabrication methods, and applications of gecko-inspired controllable adhesives are summarized for future reference in adhesive development. Firstly, the controllable adhesion mechanism of geckos is introduced. Then, the control mechanism, adhesion performance, and preparation methods of gecko-inspired controllable adhesives are described. Subsequently, various successful applications of gecko-inspired controllable adhesives are presented. Finally, future challenges and opportunities to develop gecko-inspired controllable adhesive are presented.

attachments.name: Ecosystem Biomimicry: A New Perspective on Urban Design
attachments.description: That’s where it all begins. It marked the start of the Industrial Revolution, a monumental step forward for our civilization. Although it propelled technological knowledge, this stage in human history solidified our impact on this planet IN THE WRONG WAY. Billions of tons of carbon dioxide have since been emitted into our atmosphere, millions of acres of forest have been destroyed, and a staggering two-thirds of the world’s wildlife populations have plummeted in the last 50 years. To put it simply, we’re killing our planet.

attachments.name: Biomimicry in Urban Design
attachments.description: Our life and lifestyle have been highly influenced by the Industrial revolution. Architecture has also seen aftereffects for the same. Architecture, as the urban design has been compromised in this process of ultimately trying to make it better.

attachments.name: Applications of biomimicry to urban planning: interrogating the relevance of emerging approaches to design cities by inspiring from nature.
attachments.description: Cities have an important role to play in tackling the challenges of climate change and the depletion of biodiversity. The way they were built has had a significant impact on biological and terrestrial systems. In this regard, a new generation of urban planners is attempting to address this problem by inventing new urban models, especially using biomimicry to create a real paradigm shift in the discipline. Nonetheless, it introduces a fresh perspective that refrains from viewing nature merely as a supplier of resources and energy, but instead recognizes it as a rich wellspring of wisdom. This approach is now unfolding in the realm of cities and territories as intricate systems. In fact, biomimicry is seen as a means towards more virtuous development models, aiming at the regeneration and resilience of living spaces in symbiosis with the environment. Researchers and theorists have put forth diverse ideas and concepts to incorporate the principles derived from nature into urban projects. However, several challenges are raised when trying to mimic how a biological system works to plan cities which are much more complex due to human social attributes. Although there are a few current examples of biomimicry being applied to urban planning, they need to be assessed to determine if this approach is relevant, particularly in the social field. This study employs a qualitative approach whereby the narrative review of literature has been applied which focusing on the applicability and impact of biomimicry in urban systems. Six-step framework for review articles are used to address three key research questions regarding the adoption of biomimicry principles in urban contexts. We aim to summarize and categorize the variety of applications of biomimicry to urban planning by the literature review method and to initiate an inquiry into their relevance and utility in responding to contemporary urban challenges.

attachments.name: Biomimetic Urban and Architectural Design: Illustrating and Leveraging Relationships between Ecosystem Services
attachments.description: Redesigning and retrofitting cities so they become complex systems that create ecological and cultural–societal health through the provision of ecosystem services is of critical importance. Although a handful of methodologies and frameworks for considering how to design urban environments so that they provide ecosystem services have been proposed, their use is not widespread. A key barrier to their development has been identified as a lack of ecological knowledge about relationships between ecosystem services, which is then translated into the field of spatial design. In response, this paper examines recently published data concerning synergetic and conflicting relationships between ecosystem services from the field of ecology and then synthesises, translates, and illustrates this information for an architectural and urban design context. The intention of the diagrams created in this research is to enable designers and policy makers to make better decisions about how to effectively increase the provision of various ecosystem services in urban areas without causing unanticipated degradation in others. The results indicate that although targets of ecosystem services can be both spatially and metrically quantifiable while working across different scales, their effectiveness can be increased if relationships between them are considered during design phases of project development.

attachments.name: Biomimicry as a way to create adaptable urban environments
attachments.description: The relatively novel theory of ‘biomimicry’ might provide opportunities for the construction of adaptable designs. A biomimicry design approach tries to learn from nature’s successes in order to solve human problems. The theory proposes three levels of learning from nature: the level of form, the level of process, and the level of system. Learning on the level of form is predominantly practised in current applications of biomimicry within fields of research other than urban design.

attachments.name: Applying Biomimicry to Cities: The Forest as Model for Urban Planning and Design
attachments.description: The idea of applying biomimicry to cities is attracting increasing attention as a way of achieving sustainability. Undoubtedly the most frequently evoked natural model in this context is the forest, though it has not yet been investigated with any great scientific rigour. To overcome this lacuna, we provide: first, a justification of the model of the forest via what we call the arguments from “fittingness”, “scale”, and “complexity”; second, an exploration of various key innovations made possible by this model in the fields of urban planning, urban water systems, urban energy and transport systems, and urban food and nutrient systems.

attachments.name: Biomimicry and Sustainable Urban Design
Biomimicry: How Nature Can Streamline Your Business For Innovation
attachments.description: Windows that prevent bird collisions by mimicking the UV-reflective qualities of spider webs; a train that travels faster, uses less energy and makes less noise after it was redesigned to resemble a bird’s beak; highly efficient wind turbine blades that mimic the bumpy edges of a whale’s flippers.

attachments.name: From seashells to cement, nature inspires tougher building material
attachments.description: Inspired by the material that makes up oyster and abalone shells, engineers at Princeton have created a new cement composite that is 17 times more crack-resistant than standard cement and 19 times more able to stretch and deform without breaking. The findings could eventually help increase the crack resistance of a wide range of brittle ceramic materials, from concrete to porcelain.

attachments.name: TU WIen | Biomimetics Group
attachments.description: The Biomimetics group of Ille C. Gebeshuber deals with physical principles of organisms and their transfer to the human sphere. Most biological functionalities have their origin on the nanoscale: Periodic nanostructures such as appear on wing scales in tropical butterflies cause iridescent structural colours and thermoregulation, nanoscale nail beds on cicada wing surfaces serve as mechanical bactericide, even functional against multidrug resistant bacteria. Microscale structures cause hydrophobicity and controlled water runoff, as can be seen in Lotus leaves. Many such functionalities are structure dependent, and can be transferred to technologically relevant materials.

attachments.name: Aeroshark
attachments.description: Just by using the sharkskin technology, the global fleet of long-haul aircraft could save close to five million tons of kerosene per year. AeroSHARK is a durable bionic film that successfully mimics the skin of sharks and optimizes the airflow thus enabling significant fuel savings.   Together with the leading global chemicals and coatings manufacturer BASF, we developed a functional biomimetic technology: a film with a barely perceptible ribbed texture of small protrusions – riblets. Sized in patches for easy and targeted application, the film has millions of these prism-shaped riblets, each one 50 micrometers high.  Applied to the aircraft in a specific manner and aligned with the airflow, the riblets achieve efficiency gains, by reduced friction, similar to those of their counterparts in nature, and can also improve lift if attached on wings.  The riblet film is easy to apply, even on large commercial aircraft - approximately 800 square meters of AeroSHARK riblet film are for example applied to the Boeing 777F cargo aircraft on fuselage and nacelles by hand. Once applied, there are no special requirements for cleaning. The riblet film is extremely resilient, withstands large temperature shifts, pressure differentials and the ultra violet radiation on high flight levels.

attachments.name: Bionic Learning Network
attachments.description: In everyday factory life, automation technology performs typical tasks such as gripping, moving, and positioning goods, as well as controlling and regulating processes. Nature solves all of these tasks naturally, simply, and energy-efficiently. What could be more natural than observing its phenomena and learning from them? That's why, in 2006, we established an international research network with renowned universities and institutes, development companies, and private inventors: the Bionic Learning Network. Learn more about the network and browse our Future Concepts from recent years.

description.shortText: By using light instead of electricity to transmit data, all-photonic city networks enable ultra-fast, energy-efficient communication systems that support the high-speed demands of smart urban environments.
description.longTextHtml:
An all-photonic city network is a next-generation communication infrastructure based on photonic chips that manipulate and transmit data through light signals rather than electrical currents. These systems operate using photons, the fundamental particles of light, to perform data transmission tasks that traditionally rely on electrons in copper wires or even some fiber optic systems with electronic bottlenecks.

Unlike conventional networks, which involve conversions between optical and electrical signals (introducing latency and power consumption), all-photonic networks are designed to keep the entire transmission and switching process within the optical domain. This makes them far more efficient, with significantly lower energy losses and latency, while dramatically increasing bandwidth capacity.

These networks are particularly suited to smart city environments where massive data flows — from autonomous vehicles, IoT sensors, AI-powered infrastructure, and digital services — must be handled in real time with minimal delay. Their applications range from faster public internet and real-time traffic coordination to disaster response systems and city-wide environmental monitoring.

Future Perspectives

In the long term, all-photonic networks could serve as the invisible nervous system of hyper-connected cities. As photonic chips become more compact and scalable, cities might evolve into vast photonic organisms—processing data from billions of sensors, cameras, and devices at the speed of light.

These networks could make lag a thing of the past, enabling real-time simulation of urban environments for predictive planning, ultra-responsive AI-driven governance systems, or even immersive public holographic interfaces for citizen engagement. Intercity connections might also evolve into fully photonic national backbones, drastically reducing the energy footprint of global communication systems.

Moreover, in scenarios involving quantum communication, all-photonic infrastructures could support quantum encryption natively, providing an ultra-secure urban communication layer as threats in cyber warfare evolve.

attachments.name: Leading the World in Optical Devices and Photonics-electronics Convergence Devices While Promoting Our Technology and Increasing the Number of Like-minded Researchers
attachments.description: All-Photonics Network (APN) IOWN1.0 was launched in March 2023, marking the first commercial service of the Innovative Optical and Wireless Network (IOWN). In accordance with the IOWN roadmap, optical interconnections between racks, between boards, inside a board, inside a package, and inside a chip will be sequentially achieved, and optical devices and photonics-electronics convergence devices play key roles in these interconnections. To implement these devices in commercial networks, it is necessary to achieve Moore’s law—an empirical rule that the number of devices (such as transistors) in an integrated circuit doubles about every 18 months—in optical devices. We asked Shinji Matsuo, an NTT Fellow at NTT Device Technology Laboratories and NTT Basic Research Laboratories, about the development of membrane optical devices, which integrate compound semiconductors on a silicon-photonics circuit through heterogeneous integration, and his thoughts on fostering young and mid-career researchers.

attachments.name: Establishment and validation of optical wavelength path provisioning technology based on IOWN APN architecture for data center exchange services
attachments.description: Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corporation (headquartered in Chiyoda-ku, Tokyo; Akira Shimada, President & CEO; hereinafter "NTT") and NEC Corporation (headquartered in Minato-ku, Tokyo; Takayuki Morita, President & CEO; hereinafter "NEC") conducted a field demonstration of optical wavelength path (*1) provisioning technology based on IOWN (*2) APN (*3) architecture defined at the IOWN Global Forum (*4) for on-demand high-capacity/low-latency connections among data centers through the National Science Foundation’s (NSF) COSMOS testbed (*5) in the U.S. with Politecnico di Torino, Columbia University, Duke University, and Trinity College Dublin.

attachments.name: White Paper on Integrated Photonics
attachments.description: Electronics and photonics are important topics for the European R&D&I landscape. Growing and emerging applications in markets like Connectivity, High Performance Computing, Agrifood and Natural Resources, Safety and Security, Industrial Sensing and Automation, Health and Wellbeing, Mobility and Space as well as Consumer Electronics profit from integrated photonic solutions that combine electronics, core photonics, passive optics and other technologies into miniaturized systems using different integration technologies.

attachments.name: Optical Interposers Could Start Speeding Up AI in 2025
attachments.description: iber-optic cables are creeping closer to processors in high-performance computers, replacing copper connections with glass. Technology companies hope to speed up AI and lower its energy cost by moving optical connections from outside the server onto the motherboard and then having them sidle up alongside the processor. Now tech firms are poised to go even further in the quest to multiply the processor’s potential—by slipping the connections underneath it.

attachments.name: Chinese researchers invent silicon photonic multiplexer chip that uses light instead of electricity for communication — CCP says China's early steps into light-based chips precede 'major breakthroughs' in three years
attachments.description: The race to silicon photonics has begun to heat up, with Chinese researchers developing early light-based chips. Chinese state-run tabloid Global Times reports that researchers at Fudan University have developed a "silicon photonic integrated high-order mode multiplexer chip", or more simply put, a multiplexer that sends instructions via light rather than via electricity.

attachments.name: Photonic Integrated Circuits for Communication Systems
attachments.description: Photonic Integrated Circuits allow to meet the increasing demand of communication systems for internet which is growing at about 40% per year. This growth is driven mainly by increasing video traffic in the internet network. This growth is now further accelerated by mobile access, with video clients shipping on all smart phones and tablets, enabling video to be consumed more conveniently via network connections anywhere and anytime. This paper reviews several material platform of photonic integrated circuits and compares their performance. This paper also describes the new approaches in the design and fabrication of optical transceivers based on photonic integrated circuits for next terabit era.

attachments.name: Silicon Austria Labs Joins €400M PIXEurope Initiative To Boost Integrated Photonics With Thin-Film Lithium Niobate
attachments.description: Silicon Austria Labs (SAL) is significantly contributing to PIXEurope, the European pilot line for Photonic Integrated Circuits (PICs), through their strong expertise in thin films & integrated photonics. The ambitious initiative, backed by the European Chips Act, will invest € 400M to accelerate the development and production of photonic chips in Europe, which are critical for next-generation applications in telecommunications, AI, mobility, imaging and sensing.

attachments.name: A1 and Nokia deliver 800Gbps service transmission over 1276km across Europe on a single wavelength
attachments.description: Trial is A1's first demonstration of an 800Gbps service on single wavelength operating over a long-haul network. Achievement will help the operator meet increasing demand of its wholesale customers. A1 can reach higher bandwidth and energy efficiency and lower costs based on Nokia IP and optical chipset performance.

attachments.name: Q.ANT Gives Cloud Access to its First Photonic Chip for AI Inference
The Role of Integrated Photonics for Future 5G Networks
attachments.description: Data usage and, thus, data traffic over the mobile and fibre networks is growing exponentially every year. While the currently used optical transmission solutions are reaching their limits, a new technology is ready to be implemented. Traditional photonics (phos = light) use manipulation of light to generate, detect, or process information. More recently, integrated photonics has shown the advantage of squeezing complex functions into a single chip.  This yields a more energy-efficient and low-cost solution. Here, Giuseppe Coppola and Jorn Smeets from PhotonDelta, and Ruben Fokkema from Brainport Development, discuss integrated photonics, the landscape and the challenges that the world faces in the upcoming years. They also explain the potential of integrated photonics and what their organisations are doing speed up the development of this technology. Boudewijn Doctor, Joost Verberk and Michiel Boermans from EFFECT Photonics discuss the advantages of using their SFP module platform with tuneable transceivers in the 5G network. Field trials are being executed in the VodafoneZiggo network and in the 5G Hub to show the performance of their transceivers. But it is not only about the results now, it is about what their technology is able to do in the future.

description.shortText: A mode of transporting passengers at hypersonic speeds — speeds greater than Mach 5 — to cover vast distances in a fraction of the time of traditional airplanes.
description.longTextHtml:
Hypersonic passenger travel is a mode of air transportation at speeds greater than Mach 5 (five times the speed of sound). In comparison with traditional airplanes, hypersonic passenger vehicles could cover greater distances in a fraction of the time, significantly reducing journey times.

A hypersonic passenger aircraft works on the basis of supersonic combustion. While there are different systems, most modern hypersonic jet designs rely on a ramjet, which uses the high-speed airflow entering the engine to compress air, propelling the vehicle forward. This is coupled with a cooling system to chill the high-speed airflow once it reaches the engine. The vehicle would also need to fly at about 95,000 feet to take advantage of the thinner air pressure to balance out the dynamic pressure on the aircraft and to avoid disintegrating during flight. It incorporates an aerodynamic design to minimize air resistance and aerodynamic drag, and the tail, used to stabilize and steer the aircraft, needs to be placed in areas that can capture higher air pressure. At the same time, the materials used in the construction of the aircraft need to be advanced in their abilities to withstand extremely high temperatures. Additionally, specialized launch and landing systems are required to reach the initial speeds necessary for take-off and to slow the aircraft sufficiently for landing.

Since flying is a major contributor to climate change, for hypersonic passenger travel to be feasible, the aircraft needs to be powered by a clean fuel source; current research focuses on the use of hydrogen fuel. This could provide a solution to the clean energy issue but only if green hydrogen is used.

Future Perspectives

Hypersonic passenger travel poses several engineering and technical challenges, but if these can be overcome, it could offer extremely high-speed travel, allowing people to fly from one continent to another in a couple of hours. There is a need for renewable energy to power the aircraft; other considerations are high operational costs and the need for sufficient demand to make it commercially viable. While supersonic passenger aircrafts got off the ground and carried passengers in record times, they ultimately failed, partly because the high running costs made them economically unfeasible to the vast majority of people.

description.shortText: Interactive three-dimensional virtual objects that users can see and feel, bridging the gap between digital and physical experiences. By leveraging ultrasonic radiation pressure, these holograms create the illusion of touch, enabling users to interact with virtual objects in real time.
description.longTextHtml:
Tactile response holograms, also known as haptic holograms, are advanced interactive systems that integrate visual and tactile feedback to create three-dimensional objects that can be seen and felt. These systems employ ultrasonic radiation pressure to generate touch sensations in mid-air, allowing users to experience the illusion of interacting with holographic projections without physical contact. The technology is based on an array of ultrasonic transducers that focus sound waves at precise locations in space, producing small but perceivable vibrations that stimulate the nerves in human skin.

The visual aspect of these holograms is achieved through volumetric display techniques, where a tiny particle—often a plastic bead—levitates in mid-air using ultrasound waves and moves rapidly to create a visible three-dimensional shape. When combined with the tactile feedback, users perceive a complete interaction, as if they were physically touching the projected object. The haptic response is controlled through specialized software that adjusts the frequency and intensity of ultrasonic waves based on user interactions. By dynamically modulating these waves, different textures and pressure sensations can be simulated, enhancing the realism of the virtual experience.

Future Perspectives

Tactile response holograms have the potential to redefine how we interact with digital content, enabling more intuitive and immersive experiences across multiple industries. In design and manufacturing, engineers, architects, and product developers could manipulate and refine virtual prototypes through direct interaction, reducing the need for costly physical models and accelerating iterative processes. Remote collaboration could be enhanced by allowing teams to co-design and edit holographic objects in real-time, regardless of location.

In retail and e-commerce, customers could experience tactile previews of fabrics, accessories, and household items before purchasing them, enhancing online shopping and reducing return rates. This application could also extend to automotive and real estate sectors, where consumers could explore holographic models of vehicles or homes with tactile feedback, improving decision-making.

Education and training could be significantly enhanced with interactive holographic content. Students studying anatomy, engineering, or history could explore detailed, touchable 3D models of biological structures, mechanical systems, or ancient artifacts, making learning more engaging and accessible. In medical training, future surgeons might practice procedures on haptic holograms, refining their skills in a risk-free environment.

Entertainment and media industries could also see a revolution in how content is experienced. Video games, virtual reality, and interactive storytelling could integrate tactile holograms to create a new level of immersion, where players physically interact with game elements. Museums and cultural institutions could host dynamic exhibitions, allowing visitors to touch and explore historical artifacts that are otherwise too fragile to handle.

Ultimately, as this technology evolves, it could pave the way for fully immersive virtual environments where people interact with realistic holographic worlds. From digital workspaces to virtual tourism and social experiences, tactile response holograms may eventually replace traditional interfaces, creating new ways to engage with digital information, entertainment, and remote collaboration.

attachments.name: The Dawning of Holographic Reality
attachments.description: Holographic Reality is a necessity born from the information age. It is a new medium through which the digital world materializes into our own, allowing us to better grasp and interact with digital information.

attachments.name: Scientists Create Holograms You Can See, Hear, and Feel
attachments.description: Researchers from the University of Sussex have found a way to create cutting-edge holograms that you can not only see but also hear and even feel.

attachments.name: Scientists Create Holograms that you can Touch
attachments.description: A scientist flicks on a switch. Like magic, a small, delicate image of a fairy appears, suspended in the air.

attachments.name: Digital Holography Steps into Industrial Applications
attachments.description: Digital holography uses charge-coupled devices or complementary metal oxide semiconductor devices to replace traditional films for hologram recording. This allows numerical three-dimensional (3D) image reconstruction of an object by image processing techniques.

attachments.name: Haptics and Ultrahaptics
attachments.description: From Disney to Microsoft, NASA to MIT, corporations and institutions large and small are increasingly reviving their interest in haptic technologies, whether pursuing the edge on the next generation of smartphones, adding a piece into the puzzle of augmented reality, or engineering a robot hand that can both collect soil samples on Mars and play the violin (albeit not at the same time). Yes, haptics are making a distinct comeback. And given the vast and increasing range of applications for such kinesthetic technologies we give it a big thumbs up. Why? Read on to find out!

attachments.name: First 'touchable' hologram created in Japan
attachments.description: Advancements in haptic technology could revolutionise online communication

attachments.name: Blade Runner 2049
attachments.description: Directed by Denis Villeneuve.  With Harrison Ford, Ryan Gosling, Ana de Armas, Dave Bautista. A young blade runner's discovery of a long-buried secret leads him to track down former blade runner Rick Deckard, who's been missing for thirty years.

attachments.name: UI Urbana-champaign Tactile
attachments.description: Hoping to create circuits with the flexibility of skin, materials scientist John Rogers of the University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign, and colleagues cut up nanometer-sized strips of silicon; implanted thin, wavy strips of gold to conduct electricity; and mounted the entire circuit in a stretchable, spider web-type mesh of polymer as a support. They then embedded the circuit-polyimide structure onto a hollow tube of silicone that had been fashioned in the shape of a finger. Just like turning a sock inside out, the researchers flipped the structure so that the circuit, which was once on the outside of the tube, was on the inside where it could touch a finger placed against it.

attachments.name: Fairy Lights in Femtoseconds: Aerial and Volumetric Graphics Rendered by Focused Femtosecond Laser Combined with Computational Holographic Fields
attachments.description:
We present a method of rendering aerial and volumetric
graphics using femtosecond lasers. A high-intensity laser
excites a physical matter to emit light at an arbitrary 3D
position. Popular applications can then be explored especially
since plasma induced by a femtosecond laser is safer than that
generated by a nanosecond laser. There are two methods of
rendering graphics with a femtosecond laser in air: Producing
holograms using spatial light modulation technology, and
scanning of a laser beam by a galvano mirror. The holograms
and workspace of the system proposed here occupy a volume of
up to 1 cm3; however, this size is scalable depending on the
optical devices and their setup. This paper provides details of
the principles, system setup, and experimental evaluation, and
discussions on scalability, design space, and applications of this
system. We tested two laser sources: an adjustable (30-100 fs)
laser which projects up to 1,000 pulses per second at energy up
to 7 mJ per pulse, and a 269-fs laser which projects up to
200,000 pulses per second at an energy up to 50 μJ per pulse.
We confirmed that the spatiotemporal resolution of volumetric
displays, implemented with these laser sources, is 4,000 and
200,000 dots per second. Although we focus on laser-induced
plasma in air, the discussion presented here is also applicable to
other rendering principles such as fluorescence and
microbubble in solid/liquid materials

attachments.name: A Flexible Internet Architecture for the Next-Generation Tactile Internet
attachments.description: This paper has two main parts. The first questions two of the underlying principles of conventional transport planning on travel as aderived demand and on travel cost minimisation. It suggests that the existing paradigm ought to be more flexible, particularly if thesustainable mobility agenda is to become a reality. The second part argues that policy measures are available to improve urbansustainability in transport terms but that the main challenges relate to the necessary conditions for change. These conditions aredependent upon high-quality implementation of innovative schemes, and the need to gain public confidence and acceptability to supportthese measures through active involvement and action. Seven key elements of sustainable mobility are outlined, so that publicacceptability can be more effectively promoted.

attachments.name: Bristol University creates 3-D touchable hologram technology
attachments.description: Scientists at Bristol University have created 3-D holograms that people can touch. They are made of air using focused ultrasound.

attachments.name: Invisible 3D objects can be felt thanks to haptic holograms
attachments.description: Haptic technologies are big business these days, and joining the burgeoning scene is a team of researchers from Bristol University, who’ve found a way to create invisible “three-dimensional haptic shapes in mid-air using focused ultrasound”.

attachments.name: Contactless haptic feedback: state of the art
attachments.description: This paper discusses some of the recent advances in contactless haptic feedback. We mainly discuss two research methods to produce haptic feedback in 3D space: Air-jet and ultrasound.

attachments.name: Humans integrate visual and haptic information in a statistically optimal fashion
attachments.description: When a person looks at an object while exploring it with their hand, vision and touch both provide information for estimating the properties of the object. Vision frequently dominates the integrated visual-haptic percept, for example when judging size, shape or position, but in some circumstances the percept is clearly affected by haptics. Here we propose that a general principle, which minimizes variance in the final estimate, determines the degree to which vision or haptics dominates. This principle is realized by using maximum-likelihood estimation to combine the inputs. To investigate cue combination quantitatively, we first measured the variances associated with visual and haptic estimation of height. We then used these measurements to construct a maximum-likelihood integrator. This model behaved very similarly to humans in a visual-haptic task. Thus, the nervous system seems to combine visual and haptic information in a fashion that is similar to a maximum-likelihood integrator. Visual dominance occurs when the variance associated with visual estimation is lower than that associated with haptic estimation.

attachments.name: A tactile 3D display, created with sound
attachments.description: A new display produces stunning three-dimensional images, by illuminating a small plastic bead which is levitated a using ultrasound. This allows the display...

attachments.name: A volumetric display for visual, tactile and audio presentation using acoustic trapping
attachments.description: Science-fiction movies portray volumetric systems that provide not only visual but also tactile and audible three-dimensional (3D) content. Displays based on swept-volume surfaces1,2, holography3, optophoretics4, plasmonics5 or lenticular lenslets6 can create 3D visual content without the need for glasses or additional instrumentation. However, they are slow, have limited persistence-of-vision capabilities and, most importantly, rely on operating principles that cannot produce tactile and auditive content as well. Here we present the multimodal acoustic trap display (MATD): a levitating volumetric display that can simultaneously deliver visual, auditory and tactile content, using acoustophoresis as the single operating principle. Our system traps a particle acoustically and illuminates it with red, green and blue light to control its colour as it quickly scans the display volume. Using time multiplexing with a secondary trap, amplitude modulation and phase minimization, the MATD delivers simultaneous auditive and tactile content. The system demonstrates particle speeds of up to 8.75 metres per second and 3.75 metres per second in the vertical and horizontal directions, respectively, offering particle manipulation capabilities superior to those of other optical or acoustic approaches demonstrated until now. In addition, our technique offers opportunities for non-contact, high-speed manipulation of matter, with applications in computational fabrication7 and biomedicine8. A volumetric display that can simultaneously deliver visual, tactile and auditory content is demonstrated.

attachments.name: Holographic object feedback
attachments.description: Methods for providing real-time feedback to an end user of a mobile device as they are interacting with or manipulating one or more virtual objects within an augmented reality environment are described. The real-time feedback may comprise visual feedback, audio feedback, and/or haptic feedback. In some embodiments, a mobile device, such as a head-mounted display device (HMD), may determine an object classification associated with a virtual object within an augmented reality environment, detect an object manipulation gesture performed by an end user of the mobile device, detect an interaction with the virtual object based on the object manipulation gesture, determine a magnitude of a virtual force associated with the interaction, and provide real-time feedback to the end user of the mobile device based on the interaction, the magnitude of the virtual force applied to the virtual object, and the object classification associated with the virtual object.

attachments.name: Holographic human-machine interfaces
attachments.description: A holographic HMI allows data and commands to be entered into electronic equipment. The HMI involves no tangible physical contact between the human operator and the control elements because the input devices are holographic images of keys or other customarily touch-activated tangible input elements. Operator interaction is detected through electromagnetic means, obviating the need for direct physical contact with any solid input object or surface. Such HMIs generate a holographic image of a tangible input object of the tangible control mechanism. An illumination device illuminates the hologram to produce the holographic image. An actuation detection device detects the selection by the operator of a holographic image, and a signal generator receives the detection of the actuation detection device and provides an input signal to the electronic or electro-mechanical device thereby to produce the response. The hologram is affixed to a transparent or translucent material.

attachments.name: Holograms You Can Touch and Feel
attachments.description: Holograms that seem to have mass and can be touched have long been the stuff of science fiction. Now, they are science fact.

attachments.name: Tactile holograms are a touch of future tech
attachments.description: A piece of science fiction technology could be one step closer to reality with a new development in haptic holograms.

attachments.name: We created holograms you can touch – you could soon shake a virtual colleague’s hand
attachments.description: The TV show Star Trek: The Next Generation introduced millions of people to the idea of a holodeck: an immersive, realistic 3D holographic projection of a complete environment that you could interact with and even touch.

attachments.name: Researchers uncover physical limitation in haptic holography
attachments.description: Haptic holography promises to bring virtual reality to life, but a new study reveals a surprising physical obstacle that will need to be overcome.

attachments.name: HaptiRead: Reading Braille as Mid-Air Haptic Information
attachments.description: Mid-air haptic interfaces have several advantages - the haptic information is delivered directly to the user, in a manner that is unobtrusive to the immediate environment. They operate at a distance, thus easier to discover; they are more hygienic and allow interaction in 3D. We validate, for the first time, in a preliminary study with sighted and a user study with blind participants, the use of mid-air haptics for conveying Braille. We tested three haptic stimulation methods, where the haptic feedback was either: a) aligned temporally, with haptic stimulation points presented simultaneously (Constant); b) not aligned temporally, presenting each point independently (Point-By-Point); or c) a combination of the previous methodologies, where feedback was presented Row-by-Row. The results show that mid-air haptics is a viable technology for presenting Braille characters, and the highest average accuracy (94% in the preliminary and 88% in the user study) was achieved with the Point-by-Point method.

attachments.name: DISPLAY COMPATIBLE PMUT ARRAY FOR MID-AIR HAPTIC FEEDBACK
attachments.description: This paper presents a Piezoelectric Micromachined Ultrasonic Transducer (PMUT) array targeting mid-air haptic feedback applications. Compared to existing bulk ultrasound transducer technologies, this array implements polymer-based micromachined ultrasound transducers fabricated in a displaycompatible, large area technology. It is, thus, a good candidate for direct integration on top of large displays and allows to fabricate dense PMUT arrays for a fine non-contact haptic experience at interesting price point.

description.shortText: This solution uses responsive materials and embedded electronics to adapt to environmental and urban needs, helping cities better manage flooding, traffic, and infrastructure resilience.
description.longTextHtml:
Programmable smart pavement refers to advanced road or walkway surfaces that incorporate adaptive materials and embedded systems — such as sensors, actuators, and microprocessors — to respond in real time to changing environmental or operational conditions. These pavements are capable of dynamically modifying their structural or surface properties, such as becoming more porous during rainfall to absorb and redirect water, helping reduce urban flooding. Other functionalities include real-time traffic monitoring, automated lighting adjustments, self-healing capabilities, and communication with autonomous vehicles.

Typically, this technology combines innovations in materials science — like shape-memory alloys, programmable hydrogels, or conductive concrete — with IoT-based sensing and actuation. The modular nature of smart pavement allows for distributed intelligence, where individual units can gather data, process it locally, and coordinate responses across the infrastructure network. These adaptive roadways contribute to more efficient city operations, extending the lifespan of roads, reducing maintenance costs, and enhancing safety through real-time updates.

Future Perspectives

Looking further ahead, programmable smart pavements could evolve into fully autonomous infrastructure layers, coordinating with city-wide systems to dynamically shape traffic flow, reduce congestion, or even adapt to emergency events like earthquakes or heatwaves. Streets could morph texture or color to visually communicate with pedestrians and vehicles, optimizing mobility based on real-time needs or environmental alerts.

In more advanced futures, such pavements might become integrated into energy systems — harvesting kinetic or solar energy from traffic to power nearby infrastructure. Combined with AI-driven analytics, they could also enable predictive maintenance of cities, identify patterns in human behavior for urban planning, or even interact with wearables and implants for personalized mobility experiences.

attachments.name: Analysis of Preparation and Properties on Shape Memory Hydrogenated Epoxy Resin Used for Asphalt Mixtures
attachments.description: The objective of this investigation is to prepare the shape memory hydrogenated epoxy resin used for asphalt mixtures (SM-HEP-AM) and study its properties. The shape memory hydrogenated epoxy resin (SM-HEP) is prepared using hydrogenated bisphenol A epoxy resin (AL-3040), polypropylene glycol diglycidylether diacrylate (JH-230), and isophorone diamine (IPDA). The formulations of the SM-HEP-AM are obtained by the linearly fitted method. The thermo-mechanical property, molecular structure, and shape-memory performance of the SM-HEP-AM are studied. The glass-transition temperature (Tg) is determined using the differential scanning calorimeter (DSC). The results proved that the Tg level increased when the JH-230 content decreased. The thermo-mechanical property of the SM-HEP-AM is measured by dynamical mechanical analysis (DMA). The storage modulus of the SM-HEP-AM decreased with the increase in the JH-230 content. The above phenomena are attributed to the change in the JH-230 content. The shape memory performance results of the SM-HEP-AM indicate that specimen deformation can completely recover after only several minutes at Tg + 10 °C and Tg + 20 °C. The shape recovery time of the SM-HEP-AM increases with increased JH-230 content, and the change between the shape recovery time and JH-230 content gradually decreased as the temperature increased. The deformation recovery performance of asphalt mixture with and without the SM-HEP-AM (Tg = 40 °C) was tested by the deformation recovery test. This was used to prove that the SM-HEP-AM helps to improve the deformation recovery performance of the asphalt mixture.

attachments.name: Smart Pavement: SWCPA
attachments.description: The City of Lenexa, Kansas, population 57,000, has approved a 10-year pilot program to deploy Smart Pavement technology at five intersections in a public-private partnership with Integrated Roadways. The project involves deploying smart pavement technology through precast concrete road sections embedded with digital technology and fiber optic connectivity.

attachments.name: Measuring Infiltration Rates in Permeable Asphalt Pavement in Urban Landscapes
attachments.description: Efficient water management of roads has become increasingly important due to the escalating challenges posed by climate change. The existing body of research focusing on permeable pavements with surface layers of asphalts, concrete, and interlocking pavers, is limited, especially with respect to the use of porous asphalt as a surface layer is. Addressing the challenges and opportunities associated with permeable asphalt pavements, such as cleaning practices and maintaining infiltration efficiency is, nonetheless, essential to improve and advance urban engineering practices. This research, therefore, explores the intricate relationship between porous asphalt pavements and the dynamic behavior of infiltration rates over time. Utilizing both quantitative and qualitative data, the study revealed a variability in infiltration rates along the tested roads, affected by variables such as, pavement porosity and surface condition resulting from variation in the pavement construction process and practice.. The study, additionally, show that continuous cleaning and maintenance have a positive effect on the infiltration capability of permeable asphalt pavements, rendering surface cleaning essential, to maintain a high infiltration performance of permeable asphalt pavements.

attachments.name: Investigation of Dynamic Viscoelastic Characteristics of Permeable Asphalt
attachments.description: In order to provide a basis for the structural analysis, design and maintenance of permeable asphalt pavements, and to promote their engineering promotion and application, this study investigated the dynamic viscoelastic properties of permeable asphalt mixtures (PAC-13) under complex stress states. A Simple Performance Tester (SPT) system was used to measure the dynamic modulus of the mix under complex stress states. The displacement factor and principal dynamic modulus curves were formed by fitting Sigmoidal functions and using 1stOpt (first optimization) software, the phase angle principal curves were further determined, and the dynamic modulus was predicted for the ambient phase (15–25 °C) using the Hirsch model. The results showed that the dynamic modulus of the mixtures decreases with an increasing temperature, and the maximum decrease in the dynamic modulus is 93% when the confining pressure is 100 kPa and the loading frequency is 10 Hz. The dynamic modulus increases with an increasing confining pressure and loading frequency, the maximum increase with an increasing confining pressure is 26.1% when the temperature is 25 °C and the loading frequency is 10 Hz, and the maximum increase with an increasing loading frequency is 411% when the temperature is 25 °C and the confining pressure is 100 Hz. The dynamic modulus has a strong frequency dependence at low temperatures, while it is stress-dependent at high temperatures. Meanwhile, based on the Hirsch model, a new modified prediction model was developed, which can well predict the dynamic modulus of permeable asphalt mixtures at room temperature.

attachments.name: PAVEMENT SENSING SYSTEMS : LITERATURE REVIEW
attachments.description: In situ monitoring of pavement health has been getting much attention due to the efficiency, reliability and accuracy of data. This review consists of various embedded as well as nondestructive sensing options that have been used to perform analysis on pavement health either by simply calculating horizontal and vertical strains under pavement layers or by crack detection models inside pavement structures by supplementing information from moisture, temperature and traffic related sensors. With optimum integration of such combination sensors, engineers can predict the optimum rehabilitation time of the pavements and reduce a huge amount of budget spent on infrastructure reconstruction.

description.shortText: Biohybrid sensors using fungal mycelium offer low-energy, eco-friendly solutions for real-time environmental monitoring.
description.longTextHtml:
Living fungal sensors are a form of biohybrid technology that integrate naturally occurring fungal mycelium with electronic sensing components. Mycelium, the root-like structure of fungi, possesses innate sensitivity to environmental variables like temperature, humidity, and pollutants. This biological material is capable of forming vast, interconnected networks that not only transport nutrients but also respond to changes in their surroundings with biochemical and electrical signals.

When coupled with electronic transducers, mycelium can serve as a living substrate that reacts to external stimuli, which is then converted into readable data by integrated sensors. These sensors can detect a range of factors including volatile organic compounds (VOCs), heavy metals, and particulate matter, making them highly suitable for applications in environmental conservation, smart agriculture, air quality monitoring, and urban infrastructure. Because fungal networks are self-regenerating and biodegradable, they provide a sustainable alternative to conventional silicon-based sensing devices.

Future Perspectives

Looking toward the future, living fungal sensors may form the basis of self-sustaining environmental intelligence networks. Urban landscapes could integrate fungal sensor patches into walls, roofs, and green spaces to passively monitor pollution levels and provide feedback to adaptive infrastructure systems. In agriculture, entire farms might be lined with fungal biosensors that dynamically adjust irrigation and fertilization patterns based on real-time environmental feedback.

Speculatively, mycelial networks might evolve into organic computation systems — capable not only of sensing but also of localized decision-making. When paired with decentralized AI, such living infrastructures could become part of a broader shift toward regenerative technologies, where cities and farms behave like organisms — self-aware, responsive, and healing. This biomimetic model could pave the way for climate-adaptive habitats and long-duration space habitats, where living fungal systems monitor and regulate closed ecosystems.

attachments.name: Biohybrid robots controlled by electrical impulses — in mushrooms
attachments.description: Building a robot takes time, technical skill, the right materials – and sometimes, a little fungus.  In creating a pair of new robots, Cornell researchers cultivated an unlikely component, one found not in the lab but on the forest floor: fungal mycelia. By harnessing mycelia’s innate electrical signals, the researchers discovered a new way of controlling “biohybrid” robots that can potentially react to their environment better than their purely synthetic counterparts.

attachments.name: Electrical signal transfer characteristics of mycelium-bound composites and fungal fruiting bodies
attachments.description: Mycelium-bound composites are normally made of discrete lignocellulosic substrate elements bound together by filamentous fungal hyphae. They can be formed into bespoke components of desired geometries by moulding or extrusion. Mycelium-bound composites with live fungi have been shown to be electrically conductive with memfractive and capacitive attributes. They can be integrated into electrical circuits with nonlinear electrical properties. Advancing fungal electronics, we studied the AC conductive properties of mycelium-bound composites and fungal fruit bodies at higher frequencies across three overlapping bands; 20 Hz to 300 kHz, 10 Hz to 4 MHz and 50 kHz to 3 GHz. Measurements indicate that mycelium-bound composites typically act as low-pass filters with a mean cut-off frequency of ∼500 kHz; with ∼−14 dB/decade roll-off, and mean attenuation across the pass band of <1 dB. Fruiting bodies have between one or two orders of magnitude lower mean cut-off frequency (5 kHz–50 kHz depending on species); with −20 dB/decade to −30 dB/decade roll-off, and mean attenuation across the pass band of <3 dB. The mechanism for the frequency-dependent attenuation is uncertain; however, the high water content, which is electrically conductive due to dissolved ionisable solids is probably a key factor. The potential for mycelium-bound composites and fruiting bodies in analog computing is explored.

attachments.name: Spatial and Temporal Characterization of Living Mycelium through Dispersion Analysis
attachments.description: Mycelium, a natural and sustainable material, possesses unique electrical, mechanical, and biological properties that make it a promising candidate for biosensor applications. These properties include its ability to conduct electrical signals, respond to external stimuli such as humidity and mechanical stress, and grow integrally within structures to form a natural network. Such characteristics suggest its potential for integration into self-sensing systems to monitor vibrations, deformations, and environmental conditions in buildings and infrastructure. To understand the output voltage generated by these biomaterials in response to an applied electrical input, it is essential to characterize their spatial and temporal properties. This study introduces an electrical impedance network model to describe signal transmission through mycelium. In combination with the inhomogeneous wave correlation (IWC) method—commonly used in elastic wave propagation—we demonstrate, for the first time, the dispersion behavior of living mycelium both theoretically and experimentally. We reveal the frequency-dependent and spatial attenuation of electrical signals in living, dehydrated, and rehydrated mycelium, emphasizing the critical role of humidity in enabling effective signal sensing. Furthermore, dispersion analysis is used to assess the homogeneity of mycelium, underscoring its feasibility as a living, green sensing material. This research lays the groundwork for innovative applications of mycelium in sustainable structural health monitoring.

attachments.name: Propagation of electrical signals by fungi
attachments.description: Living fungal mycelium networks are proven to have properties of memristors, capacitors and various sensors. To further progress our designs in fungal electronics we need to evaluate how electrical signals can be propagated through mycelium networks. We investigate the ability of mycelium-bound composites to convey electrical signals, thereby enabling the transmission of frequency-modulated information through mycelium networks. Mycelia were found to reliably transfer signals with a recoverable frequency comparable to the input, in the \SIrange{100}{10000} {\hertz} frequency range. Mycelial adaptive responses, such as tissue repair, may result in fragile connections, however. While the mean amplitude of output signals was not reproducible among replicate experiments exposed to the same input frequency, the variance across groups was highly consistent. Our work is supported by NARX modelling through which an approximate transfer function was derived. These findings advance the state of the art of using mycelium-bound composites in analogue electronics and unconventional computing.

attachments.name: Reactive fungal insoles
attachments.description: Mycelium bound composites are promising materials for a diverse range of applications including wearables and building elements. Their functionality surpasses some of the capabilities of traditionally passive materials, such as synthetic fibres, reconstituted cellulose fibres and natural fibres. Thereby, creating novel propositions including augmented functionality (sensory) and aesthetic (personal fashion). Biomaterials can offer multiple modal sensing capability such as mechanical loading (compressive and tensile) and moisture content. To assess the sensing potential of fungal insoles we undertook laboratory experiments on electrical response of bespoke insoles made from capillary matting colonised with oyster fungi Pleurotus ostreatus to compressive stress which mimics human loading when standing and walking. We have shown changes in electrical activity with compressive loading. The results advance the development of intelligent sensing insoles which are a building block towards more generic reactive fungal wearables. Using FitzhHughNagumo model we numerically illustrated how excitation wave-fronts behave in a mycelium network colonising an insole and shown that it may be possible to discern pressure points from the mycelium electrical activity.

description.shortText: The next-generation wireless communication standard, designed to surpass 5G by delivering ultra-fast data speeds, significantly lower latency, and higher energy efficiency. 6G aims to support emerging technologies such as immersive augmented reality, real-time holographic communication, and AI-powered automation.
description.longTextHtml:
The sixth-generation (6G) wireless communication standard is under development to enhance data transmission speeds and minimize latency beyond the capabilities of 5G networks. While 5G networks typically offer latencies around 10 milliseconds, 6G aspires to achieve latencies in the microsecond range, enabling near-instantaneous data exchange. Operating at frequencies between 100 GHz and 3 THz, 6G aims to provide higher bandwidths and support advanced applications such as real-time holographic communications and immersive augmented reality experiences.

Currently, 6G is in the research and conceptualization phase, followed by standardization efforts. The initial deployment of 6G networks is anticipated by 2030, following the global standardization process. Key challenges in 6G development include managing energy consumption, mitigating heat generation in electronic circuits, and ensuring efficient operation at higher frequency bands.

Future Perspectives

The scientific community often mentions "wireless cognition" as a key application of 6G. This means operating communications links at frequencies that allow the transmission of real-time calculations of high-performance computers with computational capabilities similar to those of the human brain.

The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into 6G networks is expected to revolutionize wireless communication by enabling intelligent, adaptive, and self-optimizing systems. This AI-native approach will facilitate seamless interactions between humans and machines, leading to advancements in autonomous vehicles, smart cities, and personalized healthcare. Additionally, 6G's enhanced sensing capabilities could enable applications such as environmental monitoring and advanced virtual reality experiences, fundamentally transforming how we interact with the digital and physical worlds.

attachments.name: What Is 6G?
attachments.description: As 5G is deployed in the next several years, engineers and policymakers must start thinking about a 6G in the decade ahead.

attachments.name: 6G (network) | Wikipedia
attachments.description: In telecommunications, 6G is the sixth generation standard currently under development for wireless communications technologies supporting cellular data networks. It is the planned successor to 5G and will likely be significantly faster.[1] Like its predecessors, 6G networks will probably be broadband cellular networks, in which the service area is divided into small geographical areas called cells, a 6G network works in combination of 4G and 5G networks. Several companies (Nokia, Ericsson, Huawei, Samsung, LG, Apple, Xiaomi), as well as several countries  (India, China, Japan and Singapore), have shown interest in 6G networks.[2][3][4][5][6]

attachments.name: Towards User Scheduling for 6G: A Fairness-Oriented Scheduler Using Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
attachments.description: User scheduling is a classical problem and key technology in wireless communication, which will still plays an important role in the prospective 6G. There are many sophisticated schedulers that are widely deployed in the base stations, such as Proportional Fairness (PF) and Round-Robin Fashion (RRF). It is known that the Opportunistic (OP) scheduling is the optimal scheduler for maximizing the average user data rate (AUDR) considering the full buffer traffic. But the optimal strategy achieving the highest fairness still remains largely unknown both in the full buffer traffic and the bursty traffic. In this work, we investigate the problem of fairness-oriented user scheduling, especially for the RBG allocation. We build a user scheduler using Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL), which conducts distributional optimization to maximize the fairness of the communication system. The agents take the cross-layer information (e.g. RSRP, Buffer size) as state and the RBG allocation result as action, then explore the optimal solution following a well-defined reward function designed for maximizing fairness. Furthermore, we take the 5%-tile user data rate (5TUDR) as the key performance indicator (KPI) of fairness, and compare the performance of MARL scheduling with PF scheduling and RRF scheduling by conducting extensive simulations. And the simulation results show that the proposed MARL scheduling outperforms the traditional schedulers.

attachments.description: The next generation of our mobile network promises another big step forward – in capacity, reliability, and data speeds. 6G will help us digitalise further and make our society more sustainable. But what new applications does 6G offer? How can Dutch companies respond to this development? And what opportunities does 6G offer for European digital autonomy?

attachments.description: 6G is the name for the sixth generation of cellular networks, expected to be ready for commercial markets by the early 2030s. Delivering extraordinary performance and a multi-purpose platform, 6G will unleash new possibilities across telecom, technology sectors, wider industry and society.

attachments.description: The European Union needs high-performing digital connectivity infrastructure to give all citizens the best access to digital services and to maintain prosperity. In the relentless pursuit of innovation and connectivity, the development of mobile communications technologies has been a defining force in shaping the way we communicate, work, and live.

attachments.name: DEDICATE 6G
attachments.description: Reliable low latency, i.e., dependable, wireless communication links are crucial for closing the control loop between mobile sensors and actuators. They will be the “central nervous system” for the digitization of transport and manufacturing processes and must be built in a way that minimizes their energy consumption. Dependable wireless communication systems will increase the reliability and reduce the operational cost of energy efficient public transport systems, e.g., by replacing cabled safety systems with wireless links. Advanced manufacturing processes will utilize dependable wireless communication systems for controlling human-robot and robot-robot interaction. These capabilities are the key to a competitive Austrian business location with improved digital autonomy for modern industrial companies.  Fifth generation (5G) systems promised a latency of 1ms for dependable communication links but failed to deliver. Sixth generation (6G) systems aim to realize this promise and even reach 100µs latency, which is necessary for time-sensitive applications in transport and industry. The scientific challenges for dependable wireless communication systems encompass all layers of a communication system. We will specifically focus on the physical layer, i.e., radio wave propagation and distributed baseband signal processing, since all higher layers will benefit.

attachments.name: mec achieves record-breaking RF GaN-on-Si transistor performance for high-efficiency 6G power amplifiers
attachments.description: Imec, a world-leading research and innovation hub in nanoelectronics and digital technologies, has set a new benchmark in RF transistor performance for mobile applications. They present a gallium nitride (GaN) MOSHEMT (metal-oxide-semiconductor high-electron-mobility transistor) on silicon (Si) that achieves both record efficiency and output power for an enhancement-mode (E-mode) device operating at low supply voltage. The results will be presented at the 2025 Symposium on VLSI Technology and Circuits in Kyoto, Japan.

description.shortText: A proposed non-rocket space launch system that uses a continuously moving cable-like structure to lift objects into orbit without the need for conventional chemical rockets, significantly reducing costs and environmental impact.
description.longTextHtml:
The launch loop, conceptualized by Keith Lofstrom, is a ground-based space launch system designed to propel objects into orbit using an actively stabilized, high-speed circulating cable enclosed in a sheath. The structure extends approximately 2,000 km in length and is held at an altitude of up to 80 km by the momentum of its circulating belt. The system is supported at each end by magnetic bearings, which absorb the forces needed to maintain stability.

The primary function of the launch loop is to electromagnetically accelerate payloads weighing up to 5 metric tons along the flat section of the loop, reaching orbital velocities before being released into space. This approach eliminates the need for conventional rocket fuel, drastically lowering launch costs. The system is envisioned to operate over open ocean regions near the equator, minimizing risks in the event of failure.

The energy demands for a launch loop are considerable, requiring an estimated 500 MW to 17 GW depending on launch frequency. While the initial construction costs are high due to land use, material requirements, and startup power, the system could become cost-effective over its operational lifespan, provided a steady demand for space launches.

Future Perspectives

Currently in the conceptual phase, the launch loop remains a theoretical yet promising alternative to rocket-based launches. Unlike space elevators, which require advanced materials with extreme tensile strength, launch loops could be built using near-future materials. With its relatively low 3g acceleration, the system could facilitate human spaceflight, making space tourism and large-scale space colonization more feasible.

A fully operational launch loop could enable the deployment of vast amounts of cargo—potentially up to 6 million tons per year—supporting ambitious projects such as lunar bases, orbital manufacturing, and asteroid mining. Additionally, it presents a safer alternative to space elevators, as it avoids prolonged exposure to the Van Allen radiation belts.

However, the system must remain in continuous motion, requiring substantial energy input. A catastrophic failure, such as a loop collapse, could release an immense amount of kinetic energy, posing risks comparable to large-scale explosions. Despite these challenges, advancements in electromagnetics, materials science, and energy storage could bring the launch loop closer to reality.

The Launch Ring – Circular EM Accelerators for Low Cost Orbital Launch
attachments.description: Despite huge potential benefits, no electromagnetic Earth-to-orbit launcher has yet been constructed, primarily due to the difficulty of providing the enormous power required. The Launch Ring adopts circular acceleration and much of the technology of modern synchrotrons to achieve orbital speeds without the need for extremely high power. Superconducting cables and coils are employed to create a passively stable high force magnetic suspension for a maglev “sled”, which is accelerated around an enclosed, evacuated circular track of large circumference until it reaches launch speed. A projectile is then released through a tangential exit tube and, potentially, into orbit. Radial accelerations exceeding 10,000 g’s and launch speeds exceeding 10 kilometers per second appear achievable with both a relatively small accelerator for launching 10 kg micro-satellites and a larger accelerator for 1000 kg projectiles. Development of Launch Rings could lead to remotely operated assembly facilities in orbit and a radically less expensive approach to space exploitation.

This paper analyses several levitational concepts for a system that employs superconductors in the stator and on the vehicle. Both an attractive and a shear-force configuration are shown to offer static stability over the velocity range from 0 to 10 km/s.

description.shortText: Underwater farms and greenhouses leverage the stable conditions of seawater, including its consistent temperature and protection from extreme land-based weather, to cultivate crops and marine species sustainably.
description.longTextHtml:
Underwater farming is an innovative approach to cultivating plants and marine species in offshore ocean environments. It includes both underwater greenhouses and open-water restorative aquaculture. Unlike conventional hydroponics, which require active temperature regulation, underwater farms take advantage of the ocean’s natural stability. These systems operate five to ten meters below the surface, where conditions shield crops from extreme weather, reduce evaporation, and maintain a controlled, nutrient-rich environment.

Underwater greenhouses function as biospheres anchored to the seabed, close enough to the surface where sunlight can reach. This creates self-sustaining environments where humidity and condensation provide freshwater for plant growth. These underwater pods have already been used to cultivate herbs, lettuce, and strawberries, demonstrating a promising alternative to traditional agriculture, especially in regions facing water scarcity.

In addition to terrestrial crops, restorative ocean farming integrates seaweed and shellfish cultivation, including scallops, clams, oysters, and mussels. These systems act as carbon sinks, removing excess nitrogen, phosphorus, and CO₂ from seawater, thereby mitigating ocean acidification and contributing to marine ecosystem health. Seaweed farms, in particular, offer biodiversity benefits by providing shelter for marine life such as crabs and shrimp.

While underwater farming holds great potential for climate resilience and food security, challenges remain. The risk of disease, nutrient depletion, and territorial disputes over ocean farming zones need to be addressed. Additionally, pesticide use in underwater agriculture remains an area of concern. While nanobiopesticides have been proposed as a solution, their real-world effectiveness and ecological impact have yet to be fully tested.

Future Perspectives

Expanding underwater farming beyond seawater environments presents both opportunities and challenges. While oceans provide stable conditions, freshwater lakes and rivers have different ecological balances, requiring structural and biological adaptations. If successful, this could reduce land use for agriculture while supporting freshwater biodiversity.

Beyond food production, large-scale seaweed farming could play a role in climate change mitigation, serving as a renewable source for biofuels, biodegradable plastics, and methane-reducing livestock feed. Some researchers even propose sinking seaweed deep into the ocean to sequester carbon on a long-term basis.

However, geopolitical tensions may arise regarding underwater farming rights in international waters. Determining ownership, governance, and environmental impact regulations will be crucial as underwater farms scale up. Automation and AI-driven monitoring could also enhance efficiency, allowing remote management of underwater greenhouses and aquaculture farms.
