attachments.name: Analyzing the Flow of Knowledge with Sociometric Badges
attachments.description: This paper presents a collection of “best practices” for the use of “Sociometric Badges” that support automatic collection of face-to-face interaction between workers within an organization. The practices presented aim to improve data quality over legacy methods allowing insights into the processes and structures of an enterprise's de-facto communication networks. Our approach uses dynamic Social Network Analysis (dSNA) to make it easier for executives to analyze and manage communications networks. The practical applicability of the approach was evaluated by case studies conducted in three different organizations: (1) the marketing department of a medium sized bank in Germany, (2) the post-anesthesia care unit at a large US hospital, (3) teams of software developers in a Nordic European country. For the analysis, we tracked, amongst others, all personal interactions between the knowledge workers in a department or team using sociometric badges worn by each employee for the duration of the case studies. We analyzed this sociometric data as well as emails and instant messages exchanged between the employees and compared it with performance data of individuals and teams. The paper highlights 16 key lessons learnt during these studies. The first nine lessons focus on overcoming the employee's privacy concerns to set up the necessary technology infrastructure, and the final seven provide general findings for efficient management of knowledge workers based upon the results of the case studies.

description.shortText: Decentralized energy distribution points located nearer to consumers that are able to supply energy to local communities independently of large-scale energy plants.
description.longTextHtml:
Different from large-scale conventional utility plants, decentralized energy grids can transfer, store, and harvest electricity or heat in smaller units located nearer to consumers. Instead of centralizing enormous facilities that typically cause considerable sustainability issues, these grids aggregate the decentralized production of energy from distributed energy resources (DERs). From wind, solar, combined heat and power (CHP), biogas, hydropower, fossil steam, power-to-heat, to diesel engines, decentralized energy grids are an optimal solution to empower communities and individuals, so they become the holders of their energy distribution and production.

Energy storage facilities, such as batteries, thermal, compressed air, and pumped storage, could also be incorporated. With the help of IoT sensors and big data, it could monitor and optimize the grids and the networks benefiting from the energy produced, from homes and small-scale producers to businesses or industrial sites. Considering that this model allows different units to supply power to localized communities and areas, the decentralization of energy could decrease greenhouse gas emissions as the production does not exceed demand. Also, as the decentralization of energy increases efficiency due to the reduction in lost energy during transfer, it could create economic value for the producer in the long-term. However, the implementation costs are still a point of resistance. For instance, as solar panels are expensive assets, the expectancy of wide-range adoption of this energy model is still in its infancy.

Future Perspectives

As these systems become more accessible and inclusive, individual households could sell extra energy to the grid, in a peer-to-peer model, becoming a distributed energy grid. Also, these systems are evolving to become autonomous, making optimal decision and energy negotiations without human input, optimizing energy efficiency and cost, taking into consideration not only the source of power but also real-time information such as the weather.

attachments.name: Rethinking the governance of energy infrastructure: Scale, decentralization and polycentrism
attachments.description: Providing societies with reliable energy services, fighting energy poverty and mitigating climate change entail a crucial infrastructure component. Both the energy access and the low carbon challenge require more decentralized energy solutions and a change in the energy infrastructure paradigm. Yet, physical energy infrastructure co-evolves with socio-economic institutions, actors and social norms. This may produce inertia against change. The energy challenge also requires solutions at multiple scales and may entail elements of common pool resource problems. Therefore, the governance of energy infrastructure needs to be polycentric. This allows for contextualization, experimentation and innovation. The article concludes by sketching routes of further research into the energy infrastructure governance nexus in social science research. © 2014 Elsevier Ltd.

attachments.name: Real-Time Feedback-Based Optimization of Distribution Grids
attachments.description: This paper develops an algorithmic framework for real-time optimization of distribution-level distributed energy resources (DERs). The proposed framework optimizes the operation of both DERs that are individually controllable and groups of DERs (i.e., aggregations) at an electrical point of connection that are jointly controlled. From an electrical standpoint, wye and delta single- and multi-phase connections are accounted for. The algorithm enables (groups of) DERs to pursue given performance objectives, while adjusting their (aggregate) powers to respond to services requested by grid operators and to maintain electrical quantities within engineering limits. The design of the algorithm leverages a time-varying bi-level problem formulation capturing various performance objectives and engineering constraints, and an online implementation of primal-dual projected-gradient methods. The gradient steps are suitably modified to accommodate appropriate measurements from the distribution network and the DERs. By virtue of this approach, the resultant algorithm can cope with inaccuracies in the distribution-system modeling, it avoids pervasive metering to gather the state of non-controllable resources, and it naturally lends itself to a distributed implementation. Analytical stability and convergence claims are established in terms of tracking of the solution of the formulated time-varying optimization problem. The proposed method is tested in a realistic distribution system with real data.

description.shortText: Software designed to record and track the brain's electrical activity in real-time. The data collected is fed into a personalized algorithm, that is, the "mood map," which estimates a person's general mood based on their brain waves.
description.longTextHtml:
This software analyses collected data fed into a personalized algorithm, that is, the "mood map," which can estimate a person's general mood based on their brain waves. Such software has to work in tandem with wearables containing a series of small electrodes designed to record and measure the brain's electrical activity in real-time, to then send the data over for further analysis. This system works as a way of gathering data about emotional states in the medium to long term, as the algorithm is connected to a software that creates visualizations of a person's mood, thus detecting and pointing out recurring emotional patterns.

When the system detects patterns that indicate the onset of a depressive episode, for instance, it can be programmed to send a text message instantly to the user or their doctor. The system takes into consideration the networking and adaptability of the brain so that real-time neural interfaces allow the medical field to shift beyond the traditional static view and into the realm of a more precise, focused therapy.

In some cases, the wearables used to enable this software could also be mounted with neuromodulation strategies, meaning that after detecting the pervasive negative mood, it could also send small electric currents aiming to alleviate that feeling. Therefore, the algorithm is in charge of identifying moods and determining solutions to every change at a neural level without the need for physician oversight. In other cases, this emotional imaging could be connected to interactive storytelling or experiences, thus triggering outcomes in movies or games according to the user's emotional state.

Future Perspectives

Emotions are the next input in the search for more immersive, targeted digital experiences. It might come to the point in which all mixed reality headsets are integrated with mood map software, and the user's emotions could be fed in real-time to targeting algorithms. This loop could then influence everything that the user experiences in mixed reality layers. The adverts that are shown to someone who is feeling hopeless might be different from the ones shown to people that are feeling joyful, and so forth.

In a more dystopic perspective, knowing and decoding moods of happiness or sadness could be used to force individuals into a specific mood or feeling by using this technology. For example, a worker could be forced into a "happy" state to keep productivity up, or a criminal forced to face "sadness" as a punishment for their transgressions.

attachments.name: Decoding Mood from Human Brain Signals.
attachments.description: By developing a novel decoding technology, a team of engineers and physicians at the University of Southern California (USC) and UC San Francisco have discovered how mood variations can be decoded from neural signals in the human brain–a process that has not been demonstrated to date.

attachments.name: Brain Data Could Read Moods, Potentially Treat Depression.

attachments.name: Real-time decoding of mood from human large-scale ECoG activity.
attachments.description: Identifying reliable neural biomarkers that are predictive of mood dynamics in an individual is important both for personalized treatment of mood disorders and for understanding the neural processes underlying mood regulation. Here, based on semi-chronic, high-resolution, multi-site ECoG recordings obtained from epilepsy patients and simultaneous self-reports of mood (Immediate Mood Scaler), we identify network-level neural biomarkers that are predictive of mood dynamics over time in individual patients. To identify the biomarker, we first use a data-driven linear state-space modelling framework to describe neural network dynamics. Fitting the state-space model using neural features extracted from ECoG recordings, we find that a low-dimensional neural state is sufficient to describe the dynamics of large-scale ECoG. We estimate this low-dimensional neural state in real time using a Kalman filter. We then build a regression model that predicts mood variations over time from the estimated low-dimensional neural state. We find that using network ECoG activity and our modelling framework, we can decode mood variations over time in individual subjects. We further use the identified dynamical models to characterize the spatial and temporal characteristics of the mood biomarkers. Our analyses reveal subnetworks in the limbic system that are highly predictive of an individual’s mood variations over time. We also identify the time-scales of these mood biomarkers. These dynamical mood biomarkers and mood decoding algorithms can provide insight into brain processes underlying mood regulation and also enable the development of personalized stimulation therapies for depression based on feedback of the estimated mood.

attachments.name: Mood variations decoded from multi-site intracranial human brain activity
attachments.description: Mood state changes are decoded using human neural activity data from electrodes implanted in seven epilepsy patients. The ability to decode mood state over time from neural activity could enable closed-loop systems to treat neuropsychiatric disorders. However, this decoding has not been demonstrated, partly owing to the difficulty of modeling distributed mood-relevant neural dynamics while dealing with the sparsity of mood state measurements. Here we develop a modeling framework to decode mood state variations from multi-site intracranial recordings in seven human subjects with epilepsy who self-reported their mood state intermittently over multiple days. We built dynamic neural encoding models of mood state and corresponding decoders for each individual and demonstrated that mood state variations over time can be decoded from neural activity. Across subjects, the decoders largely recruited neural signals from limbic regions, whose spectro-spatial features were tuned to mood variations. The dynamic models also provided an analytical tool to compute the timescales of the decoded mood state. These results provide an initial line of evidence indicating the feasibility of mood state decoding.

description.shortText: Pods that travel inside near-vacuum-sealed pipes using linear induction propulsion systems. It works as an inter-city alternative transportation system for mass transit that could reach cruising speeds of 966 km/h.
description.longTextHtml:
A reduced-pressure sealed tube system with a near-zero friction environment for magnetic-levitating pods. These small pods would cruise at 966 km/h, propelled by a linear induction propulsion system allowing passengers to travel long distances in a short amount of time. As its regenerative braking system recovers much of the energy used during deceleration, it would generate more electricity than it consumes, providing the transportation industry and the world with a fresh perspective on clean energy production.

Reduced travel times might fundamentally alter how cities and suburbs are planned and have a disruptive impact on current inter-city transportation systems. Yet, the biggest concern when developing hyperloop projects is the high costs associated with infrastructure. Urban development and human communities must evolve along with the system for the project to be financially viable. This type of transportation solution does not depend solely on the construction and maintenance costs; it must be well-integrated with local economies and broader landscape projects.

Future Perspectives

This technological solution could alter the way the industrialized world transports cargo. Road freight creates noise pollution, a matter of concern in areas of conservation as well as cities. Replacing a significant share of shipments carried by trucks would create shared value for society. Overall, it offers an attractive shared value proposition, integrating social welfare with economic value in a successful business model.

Concerns regarding safety, costs, and engineering challenges have yet to be fully hashed out, and one of the most challenging issues revolves around regulatory restrictions along with the expensive nature of digging and building underground pipe systems. This advancement for public mobility could also generate friction with companies that rely on old transportation methods; they might be unable or unwilling to adapt to change.

attachments.name: Exploring Bridge Dynamics for Ultra-high-speed, Hyperloop, Trains
attachments.description: In this paper the dynamics of a set of ultra-high-speed (UHS) moving masses/loads traversing a continuous beam are explored. The proposed model is intended to simulate the dynamic response of continues bridges under the new Hyperloop/Transpod trains, which are proposed to travel at up to 1200 km/h. This speed introduces a range of dynamic responses that have hitherto not been observed in generic high-speed trains. The analytical results show that the dynamic amplification factors, due to train passage, are significantly larger than current trains. This is due to the combination of ultra-high-speed and continuous beam construction, which is necessary to maintain a partial vacuum in the enclosed tube. Therefore, current design recommendations are not sufficient for these UHS trains.

attachments.name: Shared Value Potential of Transporting Cargo via Hyperloop
attachments.description: This research estimates the shared value created by constructing a hypothetical Hyperloop to transport cargo along 300 km in Northern Germany. Following Porter-Kramer (2011), we identified and evaluated eight factors that create shared value: travel speed, operating costs, safety, noise pollution, air pollution, climate effect/carbon footprint, separation effect/ property efficiency, and maintenance. Using official data compiled by several German institutes and organizations, we conducted comparative analysis to quantify and compare the abovementioned factors for Hyperloop and over-the-road cargo transport in Germany. Then, we monetized the individual and collective benefits of the shared value created by Hyperloop replacing a significant share of cargo transported by truck. Our findings indicate that the hypothetical Hyperloop project in Northern Germany would create €660 to €900 million of shared value annually. Our research method establishes a framework for assessing future transportation projects like Hyperloop, and our findings can be generalized to industrialized nations beyond Germany.

description.shortText: An inexpensive and easy method to trigger mutations in DNA molecules, generating a high density of novel nucleotide diversity in the genomes of plants and animals. Chemical mutagenesis is a research area that has been investigated for functional genomic studies as well as plant breeding.
description.longTextHtml:
A method to induce genetic changes in DNA structure, affecting one or more genes, as a result of the interaction of certain environmental chemical compounds. It is an inexpensive and easy way to generate a high density of novel nucleotide diversity in the genomes of plants and animals, and as such is a research area that has been investigated for functional genomic studies as well as plant breeding. One of the most common chemicals used for mutagenesis in plants is ethyl methanesulfonate (EMS), which has already shown the ability to induce primarily single base point mutations.

Still, the high accumulation of environmental compounds have been showing genotoxic properties in short-term assays, which leads to a gap in time for obtaining information to determine if these events are responsible in tests for long-term animal mutagenicity and carcinogenicity. As such, scientists are performing comparative mutagenesis experiments with E. coli cells in vitro with and without mammalian liver preparations and in animal-medicated assays, so they can gather more accurate information on the order of the mutagenetic potency and how genotoxic factors can impact bacterial or mammalian cells.

Viruses and designer zinc-finger nucleases are another approach in mutagenetic research when trying to produce genetically modified ferrets, pigs, mice and zebrafish. With these tools, it becomes possible to target genes and combine them with somatic cell nuclear transfer and germ cell transplantation in order to generate gene-targeted animal models. In spite of being an advanced technique, it does not require the generation of embryonic stem cell-derived chimeras, thus making the production of non-mouse animal models faster for biomedical researchers.

Future Perspectives

It is possible to imagine this technology as being a "helpful assistant" to new approaches to lab experimentation and biomedical research by providing ways to analyze mutagenesis without the need for the animal itself, but in-vitro simulations that could go beyond mice, while remaining applicable to plants and possibly humans as well. More and more the mutagenicity testing of cosmetics involving minimal animal usage has shows efficiency in application without compromising the regulatory process.

attachments.name: Quantitative comparative mutagenesis in bacteria, mammalian cells, and animal-mediated assays A convenient way of estimating genotoxic activity in vivo?
attachments.description: The accumulation of environmental compounds which exhibit genotoxic properties in short-term assays and the increasing lag of time for obtaining confirmation or not in long-term animal mutagenicity and carcinogenicity tests, makes it necessary to develop alternative, rapid methodologies for estimating genotoxic activity in vivo.

attachments.name: Principle and application of plant mutagenesis in crop improvement: a review
attachments.description:
The first step in plant breeding is to identify suitable genotypes containing the desired genes
among existing varieties, or to create one if it is not found in nature. In nature, variation occurs
mainly as a result of mutations and without it, plant breeding would be impossible. In this context,
the major aim in mutation-based breeding is to develop and improve well-adapted plant varieties
by modifying one or two major traits to increase their productivity or quality. Both physical and
chemical mutagenesis is used in inducing mutations in seeds and other planting materials. Then,
selection for agronomic traits is done in the first generation, whereby most mutant lines may be
discarded. The agronomic traits are confirmed in the second and third generations through evident
phenotypic stability, while other evaluations are carried out in the subsequent generations. Finally,
only the mutant lines with desirable traits are selected as a new variety or as a parent line for cross
breeding. New varieties derived by induced mutatgenesis are used worldwide: rice in Vietnam,
Thailand, China and the United States; durum wheat in Italy and Bulgaria; barley in Peru and
European nations; soybean in Vietnam and China; wheat in China; as well as leguminous food crops
in Pakistan and India. This paper integrates available data about the impact of mutation breedingderived
crop varieties around the world and highlights the potential of mutation breeding as a
flexible and practicable approach applicable to any crop provided that appropriate objectives and
selection methods are used

attachments.name: The Use of Gamma Irradiation in Plant Mutation Breeding | InTechOpen
attachments.description: In plant breeding programs, one of the oldest methods is mutation breeding. Currently, mutation breeding has became popular among the breeders and scientists again with its use in plant biotechnology and due to some restrictions on the other techniques such as hybridization, cross breeding, and transgenic plants. Physical mutagens (X-rays, UV light, neutrons-alpha-beta particles, fast and thermal neutrons, especially gamma rays) are used more widely than chemical (ethyl methanesulfonate [EMS]) ones to artificially induce mutations (mutagenesis). However, among the physical mutagens, gamma-rays are widely used. During the irradiation of the seeds with ionizing radiation to generate mutants with desirable traits, reactive oxygen species (ROS) or free radicals can generate in cells. Although, these radicals/species generally can be very dangerous for the cell compartments, they can take an important role as a signal molecule activation of genes of antioxidant enzymes and proline, which are defense systems against these radicals in plant cells. In this chapter, usability of gamma-irradiation to provide the permanent gene expression of antioxidant enzymes and proline through the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) is discussed.

attachments.name: Chemical Mutagenesis of Seed and Vegetatively Propagated Plants Using EMS
attachments.description: Chemical mutagenesis provides an inexpensive and straightforward way to generate a high density of novel nucleotide diversity in the genomes of plants and animals. Mutagenesis therefore can be used for functional genomic studies and also for plant breeding. The most commonly used chemical mutagen in plants is ethyl methanesulfonate (EMS). EMS has been shown to induce primarily single base point mutations. Hundreds to thousands of heritable mutations can be induced in a single plant line. A relatively small number of plants, therefore, are needed to produce populations harboring deleterious alleles in most genes. EMS mutagenized plant populations can be screened phenotypically (forward-genetics), or mutations in genes can be identified in advance of phenotypic characterization (reverse-genetics). Reverse-genetics using chemically induced mutations is known as Targeting Induced Local Lesions IN Genomes (TILLING). This unit gives information on EMS treatment of seed and vegetative propagules. © 2016 by John Wiley & Sons, Inc.

description.shortText: Computer-controlled environments that grow food autonomously without human assistance.
description.longTextHtml:
A computer-controlled environment able to perform a variety of farming functions, including seeding, watering, fertilizing, and removing weeds. To increase the level of accuracy, and depending on the plants cultivated, the user can download via an open-source platform the specific amount of water to irrigate the soil, the quantity of light dosed, or any other variable that addresses the needs of a particular species.

The type of cultivation enabled by this system depends on the tools embedded in the miniaturized farming controlled environment. It can range from dry agriculture to hydroponics, which is the most popular technique applied to current examples. From seeding to harvesting, the user will only be responsible for supplying the nutrients needed to grow vegetables, fruits, and herbs, such as nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium, all already generally incorporated in the soil. With the help of machine vision, it could monitor whether plants are being excessively watered or if any fungi or bacteria have contaminated the production. It would alert the user, then require specific substances, such as fertilizers, for saving the plants.

By automating and thereby simplifying the cultivation of crops on a lower scale to meet local demand, regions that lack access to fresh produce, for instance, could be empowered to achieve food sovereignty. Also, it holds the promise to improve the diet habits of the overall population by bridging the access to healthy produce, and thus better nutrition.

Future Perspectives

If this automated farming method becomes popular enough to reach houses and areas of the most need —not just individuals that can afford to pay for it— it may eventually be a great ally in fighting hunger worldwide. Also, together with big data, interconnected gardens and urban agriculture could maintain a cyclic interrelation between food production and its broader environmental, economic, and social influences.

description.shortText: A software mounted on a wearable EEG programmed to generate audiovisual lifelogging entries, commonly presented in the form of XR glasses.
description.longTextHtml:
The digitalization and archive of a person's own experience, also known as lifelogging, is becoming ever more popular. As XR glasses grow in acceptance, so are some attempts to create a constant recording device that would store every detail of a person’s life in the form of audiovisual content.

Even though it sounds exciting and appealing, this technology has some limitations. First, the creation of videos requires a considerable amount of energy, and it loses significant quality when stored in small formats. Some argue that most of our lived moments are somewhat irrelevant and not worthy of revisiting, which is one of the reasons this software is expected to fall into discredit soon enough.

Yet, to make the lifelog process more efficient and meaningful, an EEG brainwave modulator could be connected to XR glasses. In this device, the camera would be triggered according to the user's change of emotional state, thus ensuring that only significant moments are recorded; the EEG would be trained to recognize the user’s emotional patterns. After the calibration and setup, it would be possible to trigger audio or video recording every time the user feels any emotion, such as fear, frustration, satisfaction, pleasure, and happiness. After the memory is recorded, it is labeled and tagged, according to emotional states, GPS location, date and time metadata, and then stashed in cloud storage.

Future Perspectives

As XR devices are getting ever more popular, emotional measurements will likely become embedded in their architecture. Once the energy consumption and storage challenges are solved, we can imagine a world in which all and every experience lived by a person is recorded and labeled according to a multitude of sensors, including, but not restricted to, emotion measurements. In this scenario, lying and deceiving would be impossible, as once not only a person's every lived moment could be verifiable, but also their feelings.

Correlating memories with emotional states could be a useful practice to recognize positive and negative patterns in a person's life. For instance, if most of the memories containing a specific friend are tagged with an unpleasant emotion, it might be a good idea to rethink this relationship altogether.

attachments.name: A Wearable In-Ear EEG Device for Emotion Monitoring
attachments.description: For future healthcare applications, which are increasingly moving towards out-of-hospital or home-based caring models, the ability to remotely and continuously monitor patients’ conditions effectively are imperative. Among others, emotional state is one of the conditions that could be of interest to doctors or caregivers. This paper discusses a preliminary study to develop a wearable device that is a low cost, single channel, dry contact, in-ear EEG suitable for non-intrusive monitoring. All aspects of the designs, engineering, and experimenting by applying machine learning for emotion classification, are covered. Based on the valence and arousal emotion model, the device is able to classify basic emotion with 71.07% accuracy (valence), 72.89% accuracy (arousal), and 53.72% (all four emotions). The results are comparable to those measured from the more conventional EEG headsets at T7 and T8 scalp positions. These results, together with its earphone-like wearability, suggest its potential usage especially for future healthcare applications, such as home-based or tele-monitoring systems as intended.

description.shortText: A leather-like material made of controlled fungus colonies. The fungi release a polymer-like structure similar to leather, with durable and water-repellent properties.
description.longTextHtml:
Fungi-based materials are organic, self-grown, water repellent, and antibacterial. The fungi grow by feeding on decomposing plants and vegetables, meaning they could be fed by agricultural waste or urban organic composts.

The fungi growth is exponential. It can take two months for a newly started colony to reach the size of a cow-like piece of leather and some weeks to get the size of a small object. After reaching the desired size, the fungi is harvested, and the material is heated to eliminate all remaining fungal organisms and halt the growth. The result is a dry, flexible material, available to be shaped into manifold desired forms.

By manipulating room temperature, lighting, and atmospheric gases, it is possible to control the growth of the material to achieve a specific texture and density. Fungi-based material is carbon-negative, fully biodegradable, and the leftovers are beneficial to the earth, which can be used for composting, thus closing the loop.

Future Perspectives

Fungi-grown materials point to an environmentally friendly approach to producing objects in general. While there are notorious problems in developing such products on a large scale, their development into the mainstream market could point to a radical change in the supply and production chains.

It could also, because of the nature of the material, give rise to challenges for developing cleaning systems. Both the chemicals and the machines used to clean could radically change or even become obsolete since this material is still unknown on how to clean; researchers believe it would not be needed.

Another crucial point is to consider how expensive it will be. For this to impact the market equally, its price must be accessible and able to reach the overall market. Accordingly, trademarks interested in using this material must consider the value it will have to the final consumer and how the supply chain market will be affected when deployed.

description.shortText: Blockchain-based tracking mechanism to monitor the origin source of physical assets and certificate economic, business, trading, and manufacturing practices across the global supply chain.
description.longTextHtml:
A blockchain method designed to monitor, register, and guarantee the precedence of various goods throughout the supply chain, restoring economic trust cycles and promoting new sources of value for companies that seek to be recognized as sustainable and ethical brands. The direct monitoring or backward tracking of physical assets occurs at multiple points of the supply chain using sensors and IoT devices installed at every checkpoint.

The constant tracking of assets can help ensure product provenance in a wide range of commodities such as diamonds, leather, pharmaceutical, helping prevent counterfeits and environmentally damaging products. The main benefit of relying on this technology is to improve the credibility of the origin certificates. For that, each asset is inscribed with an immutable serial number, linking to tamper-proof transaction history.

Future Perspectives

With this technology, retailers may have a real option to segment the market between responsible and non-responsible suppliers and certify as many goods as possible. Yet, blockchain may raise the cost of market segmentation, and retailers may decide to modify their certification strategy to a cheaper alternative source, which has higher rates of having non-responsible and sustainable practices. In order to maintain a fine balance, more specific policies at the international level are required.

attachments.name: Digital extraction: Blockchain traceability in mineral supply chains
attachments.description: Digital data — including technologically-mediated data generated by blockchain-enabled traceability — is performing an increasingly integral role in extractive operations, but scarce attention has been paid to the structuring effect of these digital technologies or the socio-economic spatiality of data-driven mining operations. Drawing on extensive qualitative research (interviews, participant observation, and two sets of survey data among actors relevant to these mineral supply chains), this article advances the notion of “digital extraction” to describe the collection, analysis, and instrumentalization of digital data generated under the banner of blockchain-based due diligence, chain of custody certifications, and various transparency mechanisms, situated alongside and in support of mineral extraction. The article mobilizes concepts from political geography and political ecology to argue that digital technologies of traceability in extractive processes potentially create new forms of control and exclusion or exacerbate existing social, political, and territorial dispossession through asymmetric relations of power and knowledge in mineral supply chains. Despite industry efforts to make mineral supply chains more sustainable by resorting to digital certification and traceability, the strategic uses of uncertainty, ignorance, and ambiguity undergirding blockchain-enabled traceability systems fail to challenge existing inequalities in resource use and access or fulfill the promise of transparency and accountability.

attachments.name: Analysis of the international experience of implementing blockchain technology
attachments.description: Today, blockchain technology is of interest in both the technology and business sectors. The information technology industry is developing very rapidly in our time, and new technologies appear so often that specialists often do not have time to react to their appearance. One of the striking examples of modern information technology potentially capable of changing the organization of effective economic management is the technology of distributed ledgers. Blockchain technology is “cross-cutting”, that is, one that can be applied in many areas of the economy, management, including state, municipal and social spheres. This paper determines by the provisions and the need to form the basis for the prospective assessment of the consequences of the implementation of blockchain technology, both nationally and internationally, and collect information on the state of the issue, comparison of information for a transaction using blockchain technology in the supply chain of logistics, proposing the model implementation and future research and recommendations.

attachments.name: Does Blockchain Facilitate Responsible Sourcing? An Application to the Diamond Supply Chain
attachments.description: Blockchain technology has become widely accepted to demonstrate the provenance of physical goods, but there are open questions about its practical implementation and overall effect on ethical sourcing. In the diamond industry, blockchain enables credibility of the certificate of origin and therefore, allows to charge a premium for responsibly produced goods. Thus, one would expect blockchain to be the enabler of responsible sourcing. Using a stylized economic model, we demonstrate that, counter-intuitively, blockchain implementation may reduce incentives for customers to resell diamonds on the secondary markets and increase the cost of market segmentation. As a result, blockchain implementation could change a retailer's market segmentation strategy by increasing incentives to source from non-responsible suppliers. We also demonstrate that to reduce unintended consequences of blockchain implementation, the social planner should offer blockchain as an option (and not as a requirement) to a retailer. This work shows that caution is needed with wide-scale blockchain implementation. Although it is commonly recognized that blockchain's major application is in enhancing the traceability of durable goods or goods that should have a responsible supplier, we show that, in contrast, when factors of durability and responsibility come together, blockchain may negatively influence the responsibility level.

description.shortText: A method that utilizes enzymes to break down sugar molecules and use them as a means to produce hydrogen fuel for vehicles. It is virtually as energy-efficient as traditional methods of extracting fuel from organic materials, and transforms vast amounts of agricultural waste products into energy.
description.longTextHtml:
A cost-effective method of producing hydrogen from biomass to generate fuel. The process utilizes enzymes to break down complex sugar molecules, primarily glucose and xylose, and turn them into hydrogen. It is virtually as energy-efficient as the traditional methods of extracting fuel from organic materials, and could transform vast amounts of agricultural waste products into fuel.

In order to safely and adequately store hydrogen fuel, the process could be carried out through electrolysis, where particles of oxygen and hydrogen are separated, and the latter can be blended with natural gas in an existing grid or stored separately in hydrogen fuel vessels. As wastewater treatment facilities look into generating energy as a value-added co-product, particularly where Microbial Electrolysis Cell technology is utilized, on-site hydrogen storage could become an essential and relevant consideration.

The defense and industrial sectors would benefit most from this application, as quick, low-noise vehicles that do not emit exhaust fumes offer a potential substitute for current operational vehicles. Urban mobility could also benefit from this technology. By only generating small amounts of heat and water, hydrogen fuel vehicles could cut down on pollution emissions, becoming an alternative to diesel-electric systems. Economically, this could end up being a more expensive option — especially for trains, which would require significant railway track modifications. However, with the falling costs of hydrogen fuel and batteries, the prices could potentially compete with diesel-electric vehicles.

Future Perspectives

Hydrogen technologies still face significant uphill challenges in order to meet expectations regarding viability. Yet, current research suggests that these methods and techniques can provide answers to the decarbonization of global energy systems, thus incentivizing the proper deployment of this technology. Interest in this method is rising, following the conditional promise that hydrogen is well-established in particular niches, such as forklifts. This functionality provides a ray of hope that forthcoming solutions could replicate these systems, become mainstream, and also be applied to other industries.

description.shortText: A set of algorithms that analyzes data gathered from personal devices to deeply understand the behavior patterns of an individual. It examines the political standing of the individual and automatically selects the candidate who will best serve their needs.
description.longTextHtml:
Deep learning algorithms which compare an individual's behavior patterns to the available political voting choices and select the candidate who will best serve their personal needs. Complex data cross-checking algorithms gather data from personal devices to access all available information about someone, from biometric analytics to online and offline behavior, to gain insights about the desires of each individual and provide comprehensive, tailored guidance on voting.

Providing political and overall guidance based on society's routine choices raises ethical and moral questions that need to be addressed before this technology is deployed, such as either prohibiting this technological solution even to exist or merely imposing some functioning limitations. Otherwise, personal decisions are at peril, and the free will of an individual could be questioned.

Yet as science progresses, scientific theories suggest that emotions are nothing more than biochemical data-processing algorithms. It means that all human experiences are the result of electrical brain activity, and the whole concept of free will loses relevance. If such theories become the norm, it might be easier to hand authority over to data processors, as they would be able to understand what is genuinely best for each person.

Future Perspectives

Such an immense amount of sensitive data raises fundamental questions about who ultimately has access to it. As Extended Reality evolves, for instance, lives, preferences, and relationships become even more digitized, and therefore, measurable and potentially more surveilled. With wearable and mobile devices alongside the presence of AI home assistants, machines might know us better than ever before through multiple sensors. Strong regulations and privacy measures must be implemented at every developmental stage of data gathering and processing systems to avoid possible biases within the cross-checking algorithmic process of automatic voting.

In a world where fake news is omnipresent, politicians may be confronted with situations in which they will have to convince the algorithms that their campaigns are genuine. Such a degree of automation could help increase democracy levels and assist people in pressuring candidates to maintain democratic practices while handling more accurate and specific information.
